### The rules that mattered most (compact — full detail in `measurement-discipline.md`/`peer-relay-authorization.md`/§3)
1. Relayed authorization ≠ authorization; relayed technical claims get VERIFIED, never adopted-or-dismissed. 2. A claim inherits the population it was measured on — check the denominator AND what's excluded. 3. One instrument's failure is correlated across everything reading off it. 4. Verify before refuting; suspect your own reading first. 5. A file-side inference can't rule out an explanation needing info the file lacks. 6. An unguarded per-entry loop turns one bad input into silent correlated loss. 7. When only a non-authentic guess is left, document and defer (`no-invented-fixes-policy.md`) — but a rigorous population stat can override a visual impression. 8. Don't relink `build_verify/`'s pool while another agent edits a dependency; full isolated rebuild. 9. An oracle must be able to fail. 10. Re-run every delegated result yourself from a fresh build before recording it. 11. Before trusting any gate, ask "what would a wrong answer that still passes this gate look like?" 12. A negative from a hash/name-join test is only as trustworthy as its exact input STRING + hash PARAMETERIZATION, stated explicitly. 13. One field, one name — grep every OTHER name a field carries when closing it. 14. A structural SLOT occupied by a different string each time can look like a spurious extra entry to a counter not anchored on the real boundary. 15. Confirming raw bytes/offsets EXIST ≠ confirming the correct INTERPRETATION of what they mean.

**Build/re-verify basics:** `build_verify/` holds prebuilt objects/`.exe`s (do NOT delete, read-only). Full refresh = `cl /c /W4` over `src\*.cpp`; relink tests with `build_verify\<src objs> + zlib\*.obj + d3d11/dxgi/d3dcompiler/user32/gdi32`; harnesses via `tools/validation/build_one.bat <name>`. Check: every `build_verify/*_tests.exe` ends "tests passed." Main CMake build lives in `build/` — use your OWN isolated `-B build_<name>` dir when a concurrent agent may also be building, to avoid file-lock races.

## 0. What this project is

A clean-room C++ reader library for Saints Row: The Third's on-disk data
formats, built strictly from the `spec-*.md` documents in this directory —
**never** from the game's binary, disassembly, or decompiled code. Team A
does the reverse-engineering (including Ghidra/disassembly work) and writes
it up as a spec; Team B (this codebase) implements a reader from the spec
text alone and validates it against real game data files.

**The cleanroom boundary is specifically the game's executable/code** — its
own *data* files (`.vpp_pc` archives, save files, etc., under
`D:\Project Crreish\Saints Row 3 CRREISH\`) are explicitly fair game for
testing, and this project leans on them heavily. A finding that came from
Team A's disassembly work (e.g. "flags bit 0x2 is CONFIRMED via
disassembly to mean X") is safe to implement from — you're reading their
spec, not the disassembly itself.

## 1. What's built and tested

All libraries live under `include/<namespace>/` + `src/`, are static
libraries in `CMakeLists.txt`, and each has a synthetic test suite plus (for
every format except save-data) a CLI inspector tool. **Every one of these
has been validated against real game files**, not just synthetic fixtures —
see §5.

| Format | Namespace | Spec | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.vpp_pc`/`.str2_pc` container | `vpp` | `spec-vpp-container.md` | Core, stable. Header/directory/filename-hash/zlib decompress/recursive nesting all confirmed and implemented. |
| Save data (`savedir.sr3d_pc`, `sr3save_NN.sr3s_pc`) | `sr3save` | `spec-save-format.md` | Complete for the fields the spec confirms; deliberately does not touch the large unmapped gameplay-state region. |
| `.asm_pc` manifest | `sr3asm` | `spec-asm-format.md` | Complete for non-empty sub-groups (14/14 exact match on real data); correctly detects and stops on the empty-sub-group short-record shape rather than guessing it. |
| `.fxo_pc` compiled shader wrapper | `sr3fxo` | `spec-fxo-format.md` | Complete via the scan-based recipe (not the header-length-field one — see spec §4.2's caveat). Content validator included. |
| `.cpeg_pc`/`.gpeg_pc` (+ `.cvbm_pc`/`.gvbm_pc` alias) paired texture container | `sr3texture` | `spec-texture-format.md` | Complete and validated against 2 independent real samples (see §5's offset-correction finding). Content validator included and wired into `vpp_dump`/`vpp_extract`, though no real archive has been found yet where it actually fires end-to-end (`OkUnconfirmedContent`→`ContentValidated`) — the wiring itself is proven correct by synthetic tests + the identical, already-real-data-proven xtbl/fxo pattern, just not by a live real trigger. |
| `.anim_pc` animation header (root motion; **not** the keyframe payload) | `sr3anim` | `spec-anim-format.md` | Complete for the confirmed header: **4209/4209 real files**, reproducing the spec's own population statistics exactly (see §4.3). The keyframe/track payload is deliberately out of scope — spec §6 shows the obvious model is measurably wrong and it needs the runtime sampling subsystem, not more parsing. |
| `.cmorph_pc` morph targets (full container structure; quantised deltas **not** decoded) | `sr3morph` | `spec-morph-format.md` | Complete for the container structure: **1541/1541 real files**, reproducing the spec's population statistics and correcting its §5 control figure (see §4.4). Walks outer header → "Morph" block → directory → descriptors → inline bulk runs → trailing sentinel, exposing raw 12-byte elements with only the vertex index (element `+6`) decoded. Dequantisation formula is OPEN per spec §7 and deliberately not attempted. |
| `.ccmesh_pc`/`.csmesh_pc` material block + six-array geometry block (raw extraction only, no semantic decode) | `sr3geometry` | `spec-geometry-format.md` | Complete for raw array extraction: **1803/1803 real files** (549/549 in characters.vpp_pc, 1254/1254 in customize_item.vpp_pc — the latter an independent check). See §4.2 for the three non-spec rules it depends on. No content validator (not wired into `vpp_dump`/`vpp_extract` — this format isn't reached via `decompressEntry`'s `OkUnconfirmedContent` path in practice, since real `.ccmesh_pc` content sits inside mode-(b) bundles). Arrays 1/2/3/5's *meaning* remains OPEN per spec §6 item 8 — this reader extracts them as opaque bytes, it does not decode them. |
| `.cfmesh_pc` foliage mesh (full structure; Mesh sub-block internals **not** parsed) | `sr3foliage` | `spec-foliage-format.md` | Complete: **19/19 real files** — the entire shipped population — reproducing every spec statistic exactly (see §4.5). Walks the shared material block, the outer `0x0FF1C1A1` block, inline material definitions, texture-name table and LOD/fade table. Its self-check is spec §3's oracle: the material chain must end *exactly* at the outer block's `+0x28` target. Content validator included and wired into `vpp_dump`/`vpp_extract`. Reuses `sr3geometry::MaterialBlock`. The embedded Mesh sub-block is located and version-checked but its internals are deliberately not parsed — same OPEN item `sr3geometry` holds. |
| `.ctdg_pc` mission conversation | `sr3conversation` | `spec-conversation-format.md` | Complete for the whole format. The flattest structure in the project: 8-byte header, a fixed 32-byte source-name field, and a packed array of 12-byte dialogue turns, with **no offsets and no pointer fixups anywhere**. Pinned by the exact-size identity `44 + 12 x count == size` (spec §1, 4,984/4,984), enforced by `parse()`. Speaker ids are surfaced raw — they are the rotate-6/XOR hash, but the pre-image names are OPEN (spec §6.1: 0 of 57 matched any of 3,917 candidates, control also 0). The third per-turn field at record `+0x08` is exposed by offset name only; that it is a millisecond offset is HYPOTHESIS. Content validator included and wired into `vpp_dump`/`vpp_extract`. |
| `.csc_pc` cutscene camera script | `sr3cutscene` | `spec-cutscene-camera-format.md` | Complete for the whole format: 12-byte header, packed keyframe data region, and `count` x `0x68` shot records each holding eight keyframe channels. Pinned by `record_offset + count x 0x68 == size` (spec §1, 96/96), enforced by `parse()`, plus a bounds walk over every channel pointer. **Channel 1 is surfaced as raw bytes** — its 8-byte width is CONFIRMED but its encoding is OPEN, and the obvious quaternion reading was actively *refuted* (0 of 31,898 keys, against a control firing on 30.2%), so `decodeFloats()` deliberately *refuses* it. Channels 3–7 decode as floats (4-byte width CONFIRMED) but are named by index, since "depth of field" is HYPOTHESIS. Content validator included and wired in; note this format has **no magic number**, so its check rests on the size identity and pointer walk rather than a header sniff. |
| Shared "Mesh" sub-block: index buffer + per-vertex channels | `sr3mesh` | `spec-vertex-format.md` | Complete: **549/549 paired meshes** in characters.vpp_pc, full g-segment walk with both check-value bookends, stride law 549/549, indices-in-range 4,312,125/4,312,125, normals unit-length and weight/index lanes 100% (see §9.7). Decodes position, normal, tangent (+handedness sign), skinning weights/indices, and signed int16/1024 texcoords. Also decodes the **draw-range/LOD-group** partition (§9.10) — required for correct geometry, not just batching. Synthetic suite added (§9.17): 9 tests built from the spec's layout, validated by mutation testing — 6 of 6 reader mutations caught, one of which exposed a blind lane in the fixture itself. |
| `.rig_pc` skeleton | `sr3rig` | `spec-rig-format.md` (v2) | Complete: **585/585 real rigs**, reproducing every published statistic exactly — 22,274 bones, hash table matching lowercased names 585/585, 286/585 with attachments, 12,473/12,480 unit quaternions (see §9.11). Bone hierarchy, model-space rest positions, parent links, engine-hash lookup, attachment/IK targets. The spec’s "rest rotation" triple is **not a rotation** — it is the negated parent-relative offset, verified 22,274/22,274 (§9.15), so the bone record carries no orientation at all and spec §10 item 1 is dissolved rather than answered. Synthetic suite added (§9.16): 10 tests built from the spec’s layout, validated by mutation testing — 4 of 4 genuine reader mutations caught. |

**The evidence behind every population figure above lives in
`tools/validation/`** — the harnesses that ran the readers over the shipped
archives and compared the output against the specs' own statistics. They
are standalone diagnostics, deliberately *not* wired into `CMakeLists.txt`
(they need game archives, and they print numbers for a human rather than
asserting pass/fail); `tools/validation/README.md` says how to build one
and `build_one.bat` does it. They previously lived only in the session
scratchpad, which is temp and does not survive the session — so this
document was citing evidence that was about to evaporate. Anything quoting
a real-data number should live there from now on.

Plus the shared `vpp::ByteView` utility (`include/vpp/byte_view.h`) used by
every format library: a non-owning, bounds-checked byte-range view
(`at()`, `readU16LE()`, `readU32LE()`, `subview()`, `cStringLength()`), all
throwing `std::out_of_range` rather than reading past a buffer. Any new
format library should use this, not raw pointer arithmetic.

## 2. Central design pattern: `DecodeStatus` and content-validation corroboration

This is the single most important thing to understand before touching
`vpp::Container` or adding a new format's content validator.

**The problem:** Team A found that in a multi-entry, mode-(a) (independent
zlib streams) container, only entry index 0 is reliably confirmed to
decode to *correct* content. Other entries can pass every check this
library can do on its own (no zlib error, decoded length matches the
declared uncompressed size) while the actual bytes are silently
truncated/corrupted. This is a real, still-only-partially-understood
container-format issue (see `spec-vpp-container.md` §3.2/§6 item 1) — not
something this reader library can fix by itself.

**The response:** `vpp::DecodeStatus` (`include/vpp/container.h`) has two
extra states beyond the obvious `Ok`/error ones:

- `OkUnconfirmedContent` — decoded with no zlib error and the right byte
  count, but is a non-first entry in a multi-entry mode-(a) container (the
  exact at-risk shape). Data is returned, but flagged distinctly.
- `ContentValidated` / `ContentValidationFailed` — a format-specific
  structural check (see below) ran on an `OkUnconfirmedContent` result and
  either corroborated it or **confirmed** it corrupt.
  `ContentValidationFailed` clears `data` — it's known-bad, not merely
  unconfirmed, and callers (`vpp_extract`) refuse to write it to disk.

**The corroboration pattern**, used identically by three formats so far
(`vpp::refineWithXtblValidation`, `sr3fxo::refineWithFxoValidation`,
`sr3texture::refineWithCpegValidation`):

```cpp
DecompressResult r = container.decompressEntry(i);
if (looksLikeXFilename(entry.name)) {
    r = refineWithXValidation(std::move(r));
}
```

Each `refineWithXValidation` function: (1) is a no-op unless
`status == OkUnconfirmedContent`, (2) runs a format-specific structural
check (XML well-formedness for `.xtbl`, D3D9 version/end-token scan for
`.fxo_pc`, magic+size-invariant parse for `.cpeg_pc`), (3) upgrades to
`ContentValidated` or downgrades to `ContentValidationFailed` accordingly.
**Every one of these has been confirmed on real data to catch genuine
corruption**, not just theoretical — e.g. a `.fxo_pc` entry that decoded
with the right byte count but whose 6th embedded shader started with a
real token and CTAB marker and then never reached a valid end token before
running out of declared content.

**If you add a new format:** if it has any self-describing structure at
all (a magic number, an exact-size invariant, anything that would fail to
parse on truncated/corrupted-but-same-length data), add the same
`looksLikeXFilename` / `validateXContent` / `refineWithXValidation` trio,
wire it into `vpp_dump.cpp`/`vpp_extract.cpp`'s `else if` dispatch chain
(see either file — both currently chain `xtbl → fxo → cpeg`), and update
both `CMakeLists.txt` and the manual build script (§6).

## 3. Other conventions to keep consistent

- **Confidence discipline.** Every spec rates each fact CONFIRMED / HIGH
  CONFIDENCE / HYPOTHESIS / OPEN-UNKNOWN. Only CONFIRMED facts drive
  parsing/control-flow or throw `FormatError`. HYPOTHESIS/OPEN fields are
  either not read at all, or read and exposed as raw/opaque values with a
  comment citing the spec — never given an interpreted meaning the spec
  itself didn't commit to. See `sr3save::SlotRecord`'s three
  `fieldX_rawXxxHypothesis` members for the pattern.
- **Trust real bytes over spec prose — always verify before calling
  something done.** Twice this session a spec's own stated field
  offset/size turned out to be wrong when checked against real files it
  claimed to have used, and both times the fix was found by hex-dumping
  real extracted bytes, not by re-reading the spec harder:
  - `spec-asm-format.md`: an undocumented 4-byte gap between two fields,
    found by tracing real bytes by hand.
  - `spec-texture-format.md` §3: the "total compressed size" field is
    documented at `+0x22`, but is actually at `+0x24` on two independent
    real samples (confirmed via direct hex inspection, cross-checked
    against the spec's own worked-example numbers and the offset-chaining
    invariant between consecutive texture records). See
    `include/sr3texture/texture_pair.h`'s file-level comment for the full
    trace. **This correction has been relayed to Team A but the spec
    document itself may not be corrected yet — trust the code/header
    comment over the spec text on this one field until it is.**
  Always cross-check a new reader against whatever real sample(s) the spec
  itself claims to have used, not just synthetic self-consistency tests.
- **Search outward from a documented estimate, not linearly from a scan
  window's edge**, when locating an approximately-known-position field by
  plausibility (see `sr3asm`'s `deltasByDistance()` in `src/manifest.cpp`).
  Linear left-to-right scanning locked onto a coincidental false match 2
  bytes early on real data; searching outward from the spec's own
  estimated offset fixed it.
- **Never trust a "success rate" without a random-shuffle control
  baseline.** Earlier hypothesis-testing work in this project (ruling out
  hash-sort and alphabetical-sort as the mode-(a) physical packing order)
  found that a naively-impressive "6/30 matches" result was statistically
  indistinguishable from chance once compared against a random-shuffle
  control. If you're ever testing "does X property predict Y" against real
  archive data, run the same test against a randomized control group
  before believing the result.
- **Degrade gracefully, don't guess past the last confirmed byte.** When a
  format has a genuinely ambiguous or only-partially-specified region
  (e.g. `sr3asm`'s archive-record scanning, or a directory entry with an
  unexpected shape), stop and report partial success
  (`recordsFullyParsed() == false`, an empty-but-valid result, etc.)
  rather than extrapolating from one sample. `sr3asm` correctly refuses to
  guess the short-record shape used by empty sub-groups (one real sample
  isn't enough to be confident) — that was explicitly called out and
  approved rather than corrected.
- **`vpp::hashFilename()` is broadly reused, but it is NOT the engine's
  only string hash.** It lives in namespace `vpp` only because the
  container format is where this project first needed it. It is confirmed
  across unrelated formats: archive filenames, 22,274/22,274 `.rig_pc`
  bone names (`spec-rig-format.md` §5), the `.cfmesh_pc` mesh-registry key
  (`FUN_00da7890`, now CONFIRMED by disassembly rather than inferred), and
  `.ctdg_pc`'s in-file speaker ids.
  *Scope correction (2026-09-10, from Team A's `.ctdg_pc` pass):* an
  earlier version of this bullet — and of `hash.h`'s comment — said any
  name-keyed lookup "should call it rather than reimplement it," which
  overclaimed. The engine has **at least two** string hashes: this
  rotate-6/XOR one and a table-driven CRC-32 over the lowercased string
  (`FUN_00d9e8b0`) keying the mission-conversation registry. `.ctdg_pc`
  uses **both at once**. Don't assume an unidentified 32-bit name hash is
  this one; `spec-vpp-container.md` §2.2, `spec-rig-format.md` §5, and
  `spec-conversation-format.md` §6 all carry the correction.
  **Cheap identification technique, worth reusing:** this hash can be
  identified *algebraically* from very few samples — under
  `h = rotl32(h, 6) XOR c`, two strings differing only in their final
  character produce hashes differing by exactly that character's XOR
  value, a property CRC-32 provably lacks. One matching pair settles it
  with no search at all; that identity is what cracked the `.ctdg_pc`
  speaker ids after a 3,917-candidate brute force had returned nothing.
- **Validate a new reader by reproducing the spec's own population
  statistics, not by checking it doesn't crash.** When a spec states
  numbers over a whole population — "4209/4209 normalize to 1.0",
  "167/167 gated files hold a valid offset", "12 files under 0x48, 0 of
  them setting the flag" — have the validation harness recompute each one
  and print it beside the spec's figure. This catches whole classes of
  quiet wrongness that a parse-without-throwing check sails past, and it
  costs almost nothing once you're already walking every file. It also
  surfaces *reciprocal* findings: doing this for `.anim_pc` turned up a
  number of the spec's own that doesn't reconcile (§4.3's 1,953-vs-1,954),
  which is useful back to the spec team. Where a spec re-ran a control
  baseline, re-run that too — a control that still scores ~1% while the
  real field scores 100% is what makes the 100% mean something.
- **A failed test with two plausible causes is evidence about neither
  until one is eliminated.** This bit twice in the engine phase, in two
  different disguises, and both are in §9:
  - A "half-float plausible (|v|<8)" band reported 90.53% and looked like
    support for the half-float texcoord reading. It was worthless: a
    denormal decodes to ~0.0001, which sits *inside* the band, so the
    acceptance region contained the exact failure mode that refutes the
    hypothesis (§9.8).
  - A mesh↔rig cross-check failed at 0.2%, and that was reported as
    evidence of a bone-palette indirection. But a coordinate-space
    mismatch between the two formats produces an identical failure, and
    that mismatch turned out to be real — so the test could not
    discriminate, and the conclusion was not established (§9.12).
  **The check to run before trusting a result:** ask what *else* would
  produce this same number. If a second cause fits equally well, the
  measurement has not decided anything yet — design one that separates
  them, or report the ambiguity rather than picking a side. A negative
  result is only informative when the test could have come out positive
  for exactly one reason.
- **If a statistic does not move when you scramble the input it supposedly
  measures, it is measuring something else.** The cheapest way to find out
  whether a metric means anything is to run it a second time against
  deliberately corrupted data and check that the number gets *worse*. In
  §9.14 this exposed four of five metrics in one pass: two were clean under
  scrambled blend indices (so they were testing the arithmetic, not the
  data) and two returned a byte-identical maximum in both arms (so they
  were describing one degenerate edge, not the deformation). None of that
  was visible from the passing run alone — every one of those metrics
  looked like a green check. **Build the corrupted-input control before
  trusting the result, not after it surprises you.**
- **When you locate a structure by search-and-check, report how many
  candidates survived — a match rate without an ambiguity count is not a
  measurement.** "Found a run in 3,954 / 3,954 records" sounds conclusive
  and carries no information on its own, because it never asks how many
  *other* positions would have satisfied the same test. Split by run
  length, that 3,954 was two populations: 1,285 where exactly one position
  tied for best, and 300 where **six or more tied in every single case** and
  the answer was being chosen arbitrarily (§9.22.1). The hit rate was
  identical across both. Whenever a field is pinned by "search for the
  offset where the invariants hold", the number that matters is **how many
  offsets held**, and a search that cannot distinguish one survivor from
  six has found nothing. Corollary: if the ambiguous cases turn out to be a
  real subpopulation — there, placeholder meshes with no binding to find —
  the honest output is *no answer*, not the best of six.
- **An invented threshold inside your own tooling is a denominator bug that
  reports N/N.** Team A carried an arbitrary group-count cap of 64 — chosen
  for character meshes, where nothing approaches it — which silently
  rejected **286 of 372 vehicles**. Every vehicle figure they published was
  computed on a 23% subset selected by a number they had made up, and the
  harness reported a confident N/N while never naming what it dropped.
  Vehicles reach **311 groups**, so the cap was nowhere near the data.
  This is the denominator lesson with the filter moved into the *tool*,
  where it is far harder to see: a published rate at least shows its
  denominator, but a harness that `continue`s past the awkward cases shows
  nothing at all. **Count your exclusions and print them next to the
  result** — `skipped: 0` is a finding, and it is not the same statement as
  a report that never mentions skipping. Audited here after the fact
  (§9.30): `sr3mesh`'s own caps do not bind (max ranges in a group is 32
  against a limit of 4096; draw groups located 372/372), but that was
  established by measuring rather than by trusting the caps were generous.

  **The hardest variant: a denominator INHERITED from the pass you just
  invalidated.** §9.33.1 — a spec section split a population in two, fixed
  its headline rate from 90.2% to 99.89%, and then in the next paragraph
  measured the follow-up claim against `399`, the combined count from
  *before* the split, when the claim's own population was `397`. Nothing
  hinged on it (84.0% vs 84.4%) and nobody was careless: `399` was simply
  the number already in hand, and it reads like the right denominator right
  up until you notice the section had just finished proving it isn't one
  population. **When a correction re-cuts a population, every figure carried
  over from the previous pass needs re-deriving, including — especially —
  the ones inside the correction itself.** A stale number is at its most
  convincing while sitting next to the analysis that refuted it.

  **And this lesson was itself one level too shallow when first written
  here.** It originally said the *denominator* needs re-deriving. Team A
  then re-measured rather than re-dividing and found the **numerator was
  contaminated the same way** — one of the 335 recoveries was itself one of
  the two non-bit clips, so the honest figure is `334/397 = 84.1%`, not
  `335/397 = 84.4%`. Dividing by the corrected denominator would have
  produced a number that was still wrong, and wrong in a way that now
  *looked* audited. **After stratifying, re-derive every downstream figure
  from the restricted set by measuring it again — never by recomputing it
  from a total gathered before the split.** Worth noticing the shape: the
  fix for a one-level-too-shallow error was itself one level too shallow,
  which is not irony so much as the default — a correction inherits the
  frame of the thing it corrects, so the question to ask is always *what
  else came from the same pass?*, not just *is this figure's denominator
  right?*
- **A guard doing its job looks identical to a feature failing to work —
  only the reason tells them apart, so record the reason next to the
  number.** `MaterialBindings` locates bindings on 3 of 372 vehicles, which
  reads like a broken reader and is the opposite: it accepts only when the
  run count matches the declared material count, and the vehicle
  material↔run association is a documented OPEN item, so 369 files
  correctly report *no binding* rather than runs nobody can attribute
  (§9.27). Another team reported "finds runs on all 372" for the same
  bytes; both are true, and the difference is what each does with them.
  **Loosening a guard to improve a count is manufacturing a result** — and
  a low number with a stated reason is worth more than a high one without.
  Corollary for anyone reading these figures cold: a coverage number in
  this document is never evidence on its own, because the refusals are
  deliberate.
- **A property shared by every failure is not a cause until you check the
  successes lack it — and a failures-only sample structurally cannot tell
  you.** Chasing the six-array bug (§9.26), every failing vehicle printed
  geometry version 42, which looked exactly like the discriminator. Scoring
  the *passing* set too: 205 passing were v42 as well. All 372 were v42, so
  it separated nothing. The trap is built into how diagnosis usually starts
  — you print the failures, look for what they have in common, and the
  successes are never on screen. **Always measure the property on both
  sides.** Close cousin of the denominator lesson below, but distinct: there
  the population was mixed, here it was never sampled at all.
- **A model fitted to a handful of samples can score WORSE than the thing
  it replaces.** Also §9.26: ten failing meshes fitted `align8(blobEnd + 1)`
  *exactly*, which felt conclusive. On the full population it got 185/372
  against the existing rule's 205/372 — not merely unproven, **actively
  worse than doing nothing**. "It explains every example I looked at" is
  compatible with being a net regression, and the only way to find out is
  to score the candidate and the incumbent on the same full population.
  Team A hit the identical shape from the other direction: a keyframe model
  that reproduced two clips exactly, including a reversal symmetry between
  a door-open/door-close pair, and was still refuted at scale.
- **Illustrating with examples silently drops the exceptions — a distinct
  failure from a small sample, even when it looks the same on the page.**
  §9.47.1: I read a ratio pattern off six *chosen* examples out of ~20
  printed and called it "multiples of one half"; recomputing all 20 found
  one (4.733) that breaks it. Nobody picked a small sample on purpose — the
  full 20 were sitting right there — an exception just never got checked
  because prose examples stand in for a claim more easily than they support
  one. The fix is mechanical, not statistical: when a sentence is about to
  say "the pattern is X", recompute over every value already in hand before
  writing it, not a hand-picked subset of them.
- **"OPEN" and "wrong but confident" are different failures, and only one
  of them is safe.** From a distance both read as *field not fully
  understood*, so it is easy to treat a mistaken characterisation as merely
  an incomplete one. It is not. An OPEN marker tells the next reader to go
  and look; a confident wrong statement tells them not to bother — it
  actively spends the attention that would have found the truth. `sr3anim`
  carried *"+0x28 is observed zero everywhere"* while the field was non-zero
  in 394 shipped clips and pointed at a real table (§9.31), and that
  sentence is worse than having said nothing, because "observed" claims a
  measurement that was never made. **Whenever a claim is corrected, check
  whether the old wording asserted more than was measured** — and if a field
  is genuinely unexamined, say unexamined, not "observed to be X".
- **A scan that finds nothing has ruled out its WINDOW and its SHAPE,
  not the hypothesis.** §9.21 reported a relayed field as "could not reproduce"
  after scanning ±256 bytes around the structure it was described relative
  to. The field was real and sat in the *parent* structure, outside the
  window (§9.22). The precise claim — "not within the window I searched" —
  is much weaker than the one that got written down, and the difference
  matters when someone else reads it as a refutation.

  **The SHAPE half is the more insidious one** (§9.31). The original
  `.anim_pc` pass searched for an **ascending run** of indices at header
  `+0x28`, found none, and recorded "no such table exists". The real table
  is a **permutation** — `[0,1,3,4,2,6,7,5,9,10,8,14,15,17]` in one shipped
  clip — so that predicate could never have found it whether or not the
  table was there, and the field sat mischaracterised for two full passes.
  A window is visibly a parameter you chose; *"the indices ascend"* reads
  like a property of the thing rather than an assumption you smuggled in.
  **State the predicate in the negative result**: "no ascending run here",
  never "no table here".
- **Some claims you can check; some can only be checked by doing the very
  thing you are not doing. Those are a third state, not a failure to
  engage.** The standing rule is *verify a relayed claim before adopting
  it*, and twice it paid off exactly as written (§9.22, §9.31 — the second
  proving one of this project's own comments wrong). But §9.33 is the other
  shape: Team A resolved what header `+0x30` points at, and the only
  evidence that would actually bear on it is the per-track walk — which
  **is** the parked keyframe decode. There was no honest small measurement
  available; every candidate either tested something else or was the parked
  work wearing a different name.

  So the resolution is neither adopt nor dismiss but **record the claim,
  its tier, and why it was not checked here**. "Not verified in this
  codebase, because verifying it requires work that is parked" is a
  complete, publishable epistemic state — and it is *more* informative than
  a silent OPEN, because it tells the next reader the evidence exists and
  where it lives.

  The trap this avoids is subtle and worth naming, because it is pressure
  toward **doing more work, not less**: writing "I did not verify this"
  feels like an admission, and an adjacent measurement is always available
  to make the paragraph look diligent. Reaching for one would have meant
  starting parked work in order to avoid writing an honest sentence.
  **Check whether the measurement you are reaching for actually bears on
  the claim, or merely discharges the discomfort of not having one.**
- **When quoting another team's figure, restate WHAT WAS COUNTED, not just
  the count.** §9.35: `spec-vertex-format.md` §8.4.1 cited this project's
  measurement — *runs `<` count in 369/372, never `>`* — as evidence that
  `runs ≤ materialCount`. Ours was a **binding-run** figure; the claim was
  about **draw runs**. Measured directly, draw ranges *exceed*
  `materialCount` in **371/372** — the opposite one-sided relation, from the
  same four words.

  This is not a denominator problem, a control problem or a guard problem;
  it is a **shared term with two referents**, and it needs its own place in
  this list. What makes it hard to catch: **both documents were internally
  consistent.** Each side's usage of "run" was locally correct, so no single
  document contained an error — the defect lived only at the citation
  boundary, which is precisely where nobody is reading both halves at once.
  A borrowed number arrives stripped of the definition that made it true.
  The tell is never the number looking odd; it is re-deriving both
  quantities and finding they disagree.

  **Team A's tighter version, which would have caught this project's own
  instance directly: NEVER SUBTRACT ACROSS POPULATIONS YOU DID NOT BOTH
  DEFINE.** §9.38.1 — this project estimated a sub-population at "~69" by
  subtracting *their* outright-failure count from *its own* landing count.
  The real figure was 55. Neither input was wrong; the subtraction was
  meaningless because the two counts were taken over differently-defined
  sets. Restating what was counted is the general rule; not subtracting
  across a boundary is the specific habit that enforces it.

  **And the tell that catches the whole family: exact numeric identity
  between two quantities in one analysis usually means they ARE one
  quantity.** Three instances in a day, in three different positions:
  a control returning **9,878** against a real reading of 9,878 (the control
  could not fail — §9.34); Team A's `.czn_pc` bracket test where the
  "brackets the Mesh block" count and the "walk got this far" count were
  both **830**, so the test restated its own precondition; and an exact
  digit match between a predicted ceiling and a measured one that turned out
  to be coincidence (§9.37.2). **When the same number appears twice in an
  argument, check whether it is the same measurement twice before treating
  it as agreement.**

  **Companion rule, from Team A (§9.35.1): check a citation against the
  argument you wrote AROUND it, not just against its source.** §8.4.1
  contained its own refutation one sentence earlier — the prose predicted
  `runs ≥ materials` while the conclusion said `≤` — and a borrowed number
  bridged the two convincingly enough that neither half got re-read against
  the other. **Your own prose arguing against your own conclusion is a free
  proof-read, if you re-read it.**
- **An EXACT numeric coincidence is weaker evidence than a matching average,
  not stronger.** From Team A (§9.37.2): they solved a reported ceiling
  backwards to a specific field width and presented it as arithmetic rather
  than a guess, and the digit match was coincidence — the figure was just
  `8 × 64 × 4 × SCALE` for an unremarkable value on the axis they happened to
  pick. **One matching number is a sample of size one.** Exactness is
  persuasive in a way magnitude is not, while carrying no more information,
  which is exactly what makes it dangerous: the same error as the aggregate
  lesson below, with the sample size reduced to one, and it *feels* more
  convincing rather than less.
- **Two aggregates agreeing is not a relation — and an inference that
  delivers several wanted things at once deserves MORE scrutiny, not less.**
  From Team A, §9.35.3: their median runs/vehicle (~48) sat near declared
  `materialCount` (~44) while ours (~26.5) sat near referenced (~22), which
  looked like a clean explanation — our locator finds only the referenced
  half. Tested per file instead of trusting the medians: **257 `>`, 110 `<`,
  26 `==`** — no relation at all. Two medians landing close is compatible
  with many item-level structures including none, and they withdrew it before
  publishing.

  The part worth carrying is *why it was seductive*: it arrived
  pre-packaged explaining the 2× discrepancy, validating their own scan, and
  supporting the pairing hypothesis — **three wanted results from one
  number.** That conjunction is not corroboration; a number doing that much
  work at once is the one to distrust first. This project's own version was
  the ten-sample `align8(blobEnd + 1)` fit that scored *worse* than the code
  it would replace (§9.26) — both felt conclusive on arrival, and in both
  cases the disconfirming test was cheap and one level down from the
  summary.
- **Verify before REFUTING, and suspect your own reading first.** §3 has
  long said to verify a relayed claim before adopting it. The mirror was
  never written down and cost real time on 2026-09-11 (§9.37.1): this
  project published a refutation of a spec formula, and the defect was its
  own — a missing `*64` and `*4` in an expression the spec stated only as a
  range. The reasoning that led there was half right, which is what made it
  dangerous: an arithmetic ceiling of 36° really *is* impossible for
  character animation, so something was certainly wrong. **The jump was from
  "something is wrong" to "the spec is wrong", skipping the cheaper and far
  likelier candidate — my own implementation.** A refutation is a claim like
  any other and deserves the same bar as one you are adopting; publishing it
  spends someone else's time replicating a result that may not exist. Ask
  what the failing case would look like for *your own reading* before
  concluding it is the other one that fails.
- **A claim inherits the population it was measured on, and stops there —
  whether the claim is about an IMPLEMENTATION or a PROPERTY.** Three
  instances of the identical check today, unified because it is the same
  question asked of different subjects: *what population did this actually
  run over?*
  * §9.45 — two implementations disagreed on 14 clips; I preferred the
    shipping reader because it had been "validated" against 3,687 clips that
    land on the format's declared endpoint. **Not one of those 3,687
    contains the disputed construct.** A validation that never exercised the
    behaviour in dispute confers no authority over it — "this is what we
    ship" silently became "this is correct".
  * §9.42 — translation tracks looked non-rigid; in fact 90.5% of tracks
    carry **no** translation data at all, so the tracks that exist are
    exactly the ones that vary. A property confirmed on "the tracks that
    have this field" is not confirmed on "bones" in general.
  * §9.50 — tangent handedness is CONFIRMED at 100.0000% on characters/items
    and was written into the header as a carrier-independent rule. It holds
    at 17.98% on vehicles. Confirmed on one carrier, assumed on all.
  In every case a true statement about a subset silently became a statement
  about the whole, and in every case the fix was the same question, asked
  before trusting the label rather than after something broke: **which
  population does this evidence actually cover, and does the thing I am
  about to apply it to sit inside that population?**
- **A probe that carries its own copy of production logic is a SECOND
  IMPLEMENTATION, and second implementations drift.** §9.40: a probe asked
  its private `walkN()` whether a clip's walk completes, while a census
  asked the shipping `Payload::walk()`. They disagreed on **14 clips**, and
  the probe's answer had already been written up as a finding.

  **The corollary is the part that stings: "re-measure it directly" only
  beats "infer it" when the direct measurement uses the AUTHORITATIVE
  implementation.** Same section: an inference was rejected as
  methodologically unsound and replaced by a direct measurement — and the
  inference had been right, while the replacement was wrong, because the
  replacement ran on the private copy. Swapping an unvalidated inference for
  an unvalidated measurement feels like rigour and is not.

  Deliberate divergence is fine and sometimes necessary —
  `validate_vehicle_runs.cpp` keeps a pre-tightening copy of a reader on
  purpose, documented, so it can measure what the reader now filters
  (§9.34.1). The failure mode is the *undocumented* copy, assumed identical
  and never compared. **If a harness must duplicate reader logic, make it
  assert agreement with the reader and print the disagreement count.**
- **A correction must replace the LABEL, not merely add prose. Audit by
  label, not by prose.** From Team A: a geometry-spec bullet carried a
  properly written correction in its prose — old claim quoted, refutation,
  population, pointer to the superseding document — while its own trailing
  confidence label still read HIGH CONFIDENCE **for the exact reading the
  prose had just refuted**. These documents are skimmed by label, so the
  correction was invisible to the reader most likely to act on it, and the
  stale label actively pointed them at the wrong evidence.

  **Audited this file on the same rule and found one** (§9.37, fixed
  2026-09-12): the sub-heading *"Rotation — the never-run replay, and it
  FAILS"* survived for hours after §9.37.1 retracted exactly that claim. The
  top-level heading had been corrected and the retraction written; the
  sub-heading had not. The defect is a **mismatch between two parts that
  each read fine in isolation**, which is why reading the prose to check the
  prose never finds it — the audit has to enumerate labels and headings
  independently of the text they sit on.
- **A check must GATE the action, not merely accompany it.** From Team A: a
  patch script printed `patched` *and* `anchor hits: 0` on the same run. The
  write succeeded, the edit matched nothing, and they acted on the
  reassuring half of two facts that were both on screen. Printing a
  diagnostic next to a success message leaves the reader to reconcile them,
  and readers reconcile in the direction they were hoping for.

  This project hit the identical shape twice in one day and only survived it
  by luck: `build_one.bat` invoked through `cmd /c` from the Bash tool
  printed a banner, **exited 0**, and left the old binary in place — caught
  only because the rebuilt harness still printed its old string. And a
  mutation run's "6 checks failed" is indistinguishable from a compile
  failure, since both exit 1; that one was handled correctly, by asserting
  the executable existed *before* reading the failure as a catch. **Make the
  tool refuse to report success when its own precondition failed**, rather
  than reporting both and trusting whoever reads it.
- **A uniform zero is a plumbing signature, not a data signature.** Also
  from Team A: an extraction reporting "0 of 41 recovered" turned out to be
  a file-path mismatch — the parser had read the wrong file. Real format
  surprises are **partial**: a wrong field reading gives 12%, or 63%, or
  90.06%, because some cases coincidentally survive. Total silence almost
  always means the data never arrived. This project's own instance the same
  day: `validate_anim_field28.exe` run with no arguments printed
  `files examined: 0` — which was read for a moment as a result rather than
  as "you didn't pass it an archive". **Before investigating why a
  measurement found nothing, confirm it was looking at something.**
- **A refutation is scoped to the CONJUNCTION it tested. Write down which
  compound claim failed, or it drags its innocent components down with it.**
  From Team A, and §9.47 is the case: spec §6 refuted
  `payload ≈ +0x06 × tracks × bytes_per_key` and that refutation is correct.
  But it was remembered as *"the arithmetic does not support `+0x06` being a
  frame count"*, which **poisoned the field for two sessions**. `+0x06` is
  the clip's total duration; the uniform-array model was wrong for an
  unrelated reason (keys are sparse and each holds for a variable number of
  frames). **The same arithmetic that killed the compound claim is what
  predicts the component one** — a 2× over-count is exactly the mean gap
  between keys.

  A refuted `A ∧ B ∧ C` licenses nothing about `A`. The habit that prevents
  it: state the failing conjunction explicitly in the refutation, rather than
  naming the field or the idea that happened to be in it.
- **A population size cannot distinguish a real negative from a fake one —
  only an independent route can.** Also Team A: one session produced two
  genuine all-zero findings and two FAKE all-zero findings in a single
  afternoon (a wrong length-field origin; an offset assumed absolute when it
  was blob-relative). **26,601/26,601 is exactly what a wrong base address
  also produces.** The genuine ones were separated from the fakes only
  because disassembly independently showed the walker never touches those
  bytes. So a clean 100% negative earns its tier from a *second route*, never
  from its denominator — and "N is large" is not that route.
- **An AMBIGUITY COUNT is a control, and needs the same test as one: can it
  fail?** §3 has long required reporting how many candidates tie, and that
  rule caught real errors. §9.44 is where it caught this project instead: an
  ambiguity of *exactly 1.00* was reported as proof of a location, over a
  candidate space **512 wide**. Running the search from a deliberately wrong
  start achieved the same ambiguity of 1.00 in **333/518** clips against the
  real start's 328 — the wrong start did *better*. Uniqueness was a property
  of the search.

  **The uncomfortable part is that this was diligence failing, not diligence
  missing.** The ambiguity count was computed *because* §3 demands one, and
  reported as the headline finding. What was never asked is the question §3
  asks of every other instrument: **what would a failing case look like?**
  A discipline adopted as a habit stops being a check the moment it is
  performed without that question. **Every number offered as evidence needs
  its own falsifying control — including the numbers you produced to be
  rigorous.**
- **Check that your control CAN FAIL. A control agreeing suspiciously
  exactly with the real measurement is a bug report about the control.**
  §9.34 ran two controls against the vehicle run scan. The misalignment one
  collapsed to 0 runs, as a working control should. The other — shifting the
  name base by one byte — returned **9,878 runs, byte-identical to the real
  scan.** Not a near miss: the same number. The cause is that the name guard
  accepts any printable string containing a dot, so a one-byte shift merely
  produces *different truncations*, which it accepts equally; the control was
  structurally incapable of failing.

  This is nastier than an absent control, because a passing control reads as
  reassurance rather than as something to interrogate. Had the misalignment
  control not run alongside it, the honest summary — *one working control,
  one broken instrument* — would have been written up as *two controls, both
  consistent*, which is a far stronger claim. **Before believing a control,
  ask what result would have made it fail, and confirm that result was
  reachable.** Corollary, and the tell that caught this one: exact agreement
  between a control and the real measurement is not confirmation, it is
  evidence they are measuring the same thing.
- **Mutation-test the test, and distrust a mutation that reports
  "not caught".** A suite that passes against a correct reader has shown
  nothing about whether it would fail against a wrong one; the only way to
  earn a green result is to break the code on purpose and watch the suite
  notice (§9.16 — four deliberate reader bugs, four caught). But the
  *mutation run itself* has two failure modes that both masquerade as
  "the suite did not catch this":
  - **The catch arrives as a crash, not an assertion.** A reader that
    rejects a valid fixture throws, the exception escapes `main`, and the
    process fast-fails with `0xC0000409` and no message. A grep for
    `CHECK FAILED` finds nothing and the mutation is recorded as uncaught.
    Wrap the positive path so an unexpected error is *reported*, not fatal.
  - **The mutation never applied.** If the search pattern does not match
    the real source, the build runs on unmodified code and prints "all
    tests passed" — byte-identical to a mutation that ran and was
    correctly tolerated. **Assert that the text actually changed before
    trusting the outcome.**
  And when a mutation genuinely is not caught, that is a *question*, not a
  verdict: it may be semantically equivalent (§9.16's lowercase fold was —
  the hash function already folds case, so removing the fold changed
  nothing). Go and read the code before calling it a hole.
- **When two causes are in play, look for the measurement whose two
  outcomes point in opposite directions.** Having named topology and
  mesh↔rig pairing as candidate explanations for one anomaly (§9.14), the
  way out was not more of the same test but a *pose-free, rig-free* count
  of the mesh's own connected shells — a number that had to come out one
  way if topology was the cause and the other way if it was not. Naming
  two candidates is the start of the work; finding the measurement that
  splits them is the work.
- **"It ran successfully" and "it did what I asked" are different claims —
  and this project has now been bitten by the gap twice.** Both times the
  exit code was 0 and the real defect was that the code did the wrong
  thing, silently and plausibly:
  - `sourceNameTruncated()` tested a condition the engine never produces,
    so it returned false for all 4,984 files and reported a clean negative
    that was actually dead code (§5 item 8).
  - `sr3_viewer`'s positional index argument used `arg.size() > 1`, which
    silently ignored every single-digit index. It exited 0 while rendering
    texture 0 no matter which one was requested.
  The two were caught by the same thing and it was not the return value:
  **comparing the output against an independent expectation.** The first
  needed a whole-population statistic (0 truncated names vs the spec's
  1,187); the second needed one glance at the picture and the texture name
  printed beside it. Neither was catchable by checking that the call
  succeeded, because in both cases it did.
  The practical rule: when a tool reports success, verify it against
  something that did **not** come from the tool itself — a published
  statistic, a rendered image, a known-good sample. A success code only
  tells you the code finished; it tells you nothing about whether it
  finished doing the right job.
- **Real-data validation only ever exercises the success path — it is not
  a substitute for testing failure modes.** These two kinds of checking
  cover genuinely different ground, and the overlap is smaller than it
  looks. A clean sweep over a complete shipped population sounds
  exhaustive, but shipped files are (by definition) well-formed: they walk
  the happy path and prove the *model* is right. Error paths are reached
  only by malformed input, which real data does not contain, so untested
  assumptions accumulate there indefinitely. Worse, the harnesses that run
  these sweeps typically `catch (const std::exception&)` broadly — so even
  if a real file *did* fail, the harness could not tell you *which*
  exception it got. Concretely: `sr3foliage` passed 19/19 on the entire
  shipped population while throwing the wrong exception *type* out of
  every material-block failure, and only a synthetic test feeding
  deliberately malformed input and asserting on the specific type exposed
  it (§5 item 7). When a reader is "validated against all real data", that
  is a statement about its success path only. Ask separately what happens
  when it is handed something broken.
- **The per-entry raw sentinel (+0x10) outranks the container's
  shared-stream flag (0x2), always.** The flag describes stream *layout*
  for entries that are compressed; it does not declare that any entry is
  compressed. The two signals are independent, and real archives combine
  "flag set" with "every entry raw" — `preload_anim.vpp_pc` is 4,209 raw
  entries in a flags-0x2 container (spec §5.9). Any code deciding
  raw-vs-compressed must read the sentinel and must not consult the flag;
  `PayloadLocator::locate()` is the single place that decision is made.
- **A caught infinite loop, not a caught crash, is the dangerous class of
  bug.** See §5's `Z_NEED_DICT` writeup — a hang doesn't announce itself
  the way an exception does. If you add a new decode/scan loop with a
  library call that has more than 2-3 possible outcomes (zlib's `inflate()`
  has ~7 return codes), explicitly enumerate what happens for every one of
  them, don't just handle the ones you expect and assume "else keep
  looping" is safe.

## 4. Current status

Everything in §1's table is built and compiles clean, all **twelve**
synthetic suites pass, and the tree is free of build artifacts. Rebuilding
from a clean checkout (via `CMakeLists.txt`+`cmake`, or the manual script —
see §6) should reproduce all of it as-is.

**`sr3foliage` (`.cfmesh_pc`) is fully integrated — see §4.5.** It was
previously the one exception: real-data validated but outside the build
and untested. It is now wired into `CMakeLists.txt` and the manual build
script, has its own synthetic suite (`tests/synthetic_foliage_test.cpp`),
and has a content-validation corroborator wired into `vpp_dump`/
`vpp_extract` like the xtbl/fxo/cpeg ones. Writing those tests immediately
found a real exception-type bug that real-data validation had been masking
— see §5.

**`sr3conversation` (`.ctdg_pc`) and `sr3cutscene` (`.csc_pc`) are the
last readers built — see §4.6.** Both were built, wired and unit-tested
from the start (no repeat of foliage's mixed status), and both are
validated against their **complete** shipped populations: 4,984/4,984 and
192/192 respectively, zero failures, reproducing every published statistic
exactly. Each format is pinned by its own exact-size identity, which
`parse()` enforces per file. That full sweep also caught a real bug in the
conversation reader that synthetic tests structurally could not — §5
item 8, worth reading for the reason why.

**Every reader in §1's table is now validated against real game data as
well as synthetic tests**, each against the largest population available
to it. The per-format numbers are in §4.1–§4.6.

Three honest caveats carried forward on otherwise-finished work:
- `.cmorph_pc`'s dequantisation formula is OPEN (spec §7) — the reader
  extracts the quantised elements but does not decode them. Same for the
  `.anim_pc` keyframe payload and `.ccmesh_pc` arrays 1/2/3/5. These are
  scope boundaries, not gaps in what's built.
- No real archive has been found where the `.cpeg_pc` content validator
  actually fires end-to-end (`OkUnconfirmedContent` → `ContentValidated`).
  The wiring is proven by synthetic tests and by the identical,
  real-data-proven xtbl/fxo pattern — but not by a live trigger. §1 table.
- `.anim_pc`'s "1,954 files with exactly zero translation" (spec §2)
  doesn't reconcile with what this reader measures (1,953 exact, plus 7
  within 1e-4). Relayed to Team A; no bearing on parsing. §4.3.

### 4.1 Whole-game extraction sweep — COMPLETE, full results

A `vpp_extract` pass across all 38 `.vpp_pc` archives in
`D:\Project Crreish\Saints Row 3 CRREISH\packfiles\pc\cache\` (~8.5GB
compressed total) finished cleanly. Each archive was extracted to a scratch
directory on `D:\`, its final `Done. containers=... decodeFailures=...`
stats line recorded, then the extracted output deleted immediately
(several archives decompress to many GB — the aggregate stats were the
goal, not a permanent extraction; nothing from this sweep is kept on disk).
Processed smallest-archive-first so partial progress stayed useful
throughout.

**This sweep is also what surfaced the `Z_NEED_DICT` infinite-loop bug
(§5, item 2)** — the first run hung silently on `dlc3.vpp_pc` for over 8 hours
before being noticed and killed; the numbers below are from the *second*,
post-fix run, which completed all 38 archives without a single hang.

**Aggregate totals, all 38 archives combined** (recursive — counts every
container/entry at every nesting depth, not just top-level):

| Metric | Total |
|---|---|
| Containers opened (root + every nested `.str2_pc`) | 6,431 |
| Nested containers opened | 6,393 |
| Raw leaf entries written | 9,740 |
| Entries decompressed successfully (`Ok`) | 6,248 |
| `OkUnconfirmedContent` (non-first entry, multi-entry mode-(a), no validator available) | 23 |
| `ContentValidated` (structural check corroborated) | 1 |
| `ContentValidationFailed` (CONFIRMED corrupt, not written) | 116 |
| Recovered via mode-(b) shared-stream heuristic | 378,929 |
| Hard decode failures (`NoValidZlibHeaderAtOffset`/`ZlibStreamError`) | 4,244 |

**Top-level container mode breakdown** (38 archives): 28 are fully raw/
uncompressed at the top level (no corruption exposure at all — includes
both city-streaming archives, all DLCs, `characters`, `customize_item`,
`customize_player`, `items`, `skybox`, `vehicles`, all the `sounds*`/
`voices`/`cutscene*` archives, etc.), 9 are mode-(a) independent-stream
(`startup`, `da_tables`, `cutscene_tables`, `sound_turbo`,
`vehicles_preload`, `patch_compressed`, `misc_tables`, `shaders`, `misc` —
these are where essentially all of the 4,244 hard failures and 116
confirmed-corrupt entries concentrate), and 1 is mode-(b) shared-stream
(`soundboot`, which fully recovered — 929/930 entries via the recovery
heuristic).

**What this confirms about the scope of the mode-(a) corruption issue**:
it is real but narrow in which archives it touches — almost entirely
gameplay/config *tables* (`misc_tables.vpp_pc` alone accounts for 1,338 of
the 4,244 hard failures — that's the archive holding `vehicles.xtbl`,
`customization_items.xtbl`, etc., per `spec-vehicle-data.md`/
`spec-customization-data.md`) and shader wrappers (`shaders.vpp_pc`: 1,585
hard failures + 106 confirmed-corrupt, out of 1,693 entries — only 2
entries in that whole archive came back trustworthy). The bulk-content
archives that make up the vast majority of the game's actual bytes —
textures, meshes, audio, the entire open-world city streaming system — are
either fully raw or mode-(b), and none of them showed a single hard
failure or confirmed-corrupt entry in this sweep. The 378,929
mode-(b)-recovered count (dominated by `sr3_city_1`: 184,366,
`sr3_city_0`: 129,835, `cutscenes`: 32,168, `dlc2`: 10,578) is the real
scale of "content that would be unreadable without the recovery heuristic
this project built" — a substantial fraction of the game's total content,
now fully readable.

### 4.2 `sr3geometry` (`.ccmesh_pc`/`.csmesh_pc` raw-array extractor) — complete, 1803/1803 real files

Built per the redirect below (originally scoped at `.gcmesh_pc`, moved to
`.ccmesh_pc` after real-data tracing showed that's where the actual
structure lives). `MaterialBlock` (`include/sr3geometry/material_block.h`)
parses the shared material-reference block; `GeometryBlock`
(`include/sr3geometry/geometry_block.h`) parses the `0x424BD00D` block and
extracts all six arrays (spec §4.1) as opaque byte blobs — no semantic
interpretation of any array's content, per the task's own scope.

**Real-world validation:** every `.ccmesh_pc` found recursively in
`characters.vpp_pc` (**549/549**) and in `customize_item.vpp_pc`
(**1254/1254**) parses correctly — **1803 real files, zero failures**. The
second archive is an independent check: none of it was used in deriving
any of the rules below.

**Three things in this reader are NOT from the spec text — found
empirically, and exactly the kind of gap a fresh session needs to know
about before touching this code:**

1. **The 16-byte pad between the material block and the geometry block is
   a mandatory minimum gap, not a no-op when already aligned.** When the
   material block's end already lands on a 16-boundary, a *full extra* 16
   bytes of pad follow, so the magic sits 16 further out than a plain
   `roundUp16` predicts. `GeometryBlock::parse()` therefore **searches**
   nearby 16-byte-aligned candidates for the real `0x424BD00D` magic
   rather than computing its position — a 4-byte exact match is an
   extremely strong anchor on its own. Measured: 21 of 549 files in
   `characters.vpp_pc` and 84 of 1254 in `customize_item.vpp_pc` need this,
   and in every single one the magic is at exactly naive+16.
2. **"BlobA" must be skipped via its own length field** (spec §4.1.2
   finding 2, Team A/disassembly). Between the gating fields and array 1
   sits a length-prefixed blob holding the embedded second (mixed-case)
   copy of the material names: a 4-byte length at geometry-block `+0x88`,
   then 5 pad bytes, then that many content bytes. Read the length; do not
   try to re-derive it. See §5 item 6 for the bug that came from trying.
3. **Array alignment has two different rules, and both matter.** Between
   arrays: 16-byte aligned, and an **empty array occupies nothing and
   triggers no padding at all** (it is skipped, not "placed with zero
   bytes then padded"). The final step, from the last populated array to
   the Mesh sub-block, is **8-byte** aligned, not 16 — spec §4.1 says
   exactly this ("an 8-byte alignment for the final trailer step"); it is
   simply invisible on simple meshes, where the last array happens to end
   on a 16-boundary anyway. Both rules are exercised by dedicated
   regression tests in `tests/synthetic_ccmesh_test.cpp` so a revert to
   uniform-16 fails loudly.

A note if you compare findings with Team A: they independently reported
21/549 files as "tiny degenerate/censor meshes with an all-zero geometry
block." Those are the *same* 21 files as rule 1 above, and they are not
degenerate — they are ordinary meshes (3–5KB, 6–9 textures; only 3 of the
21 even have zero textures) that parse completely once the extra pad is
accounted for. A direct `roundUp16` just lands on the pad's zero bytes and
looks like an empty block. Verified by parsing all 21 in full. **No
genuinely geometry-less `.ccmesh_pc` exists in either archive** — an
earlier `looksLikeNoGeometryPlaceholder()` helper written for that
supposed case was removed once it matched 0 of 1803 real files.

No content-validation corroborator was built for this format (unlike
xtbl/fxo/cpeg) — real `.ccmesh_pc` content sits inside mode-(b)
`custmesh_*.str2_pc` bundles, which are never subject to the
`OkUnconfirmedContent` risk in the first place (same situation already
noted for `.cpeg_pc`/`.cvbm_pc` in §4.1), so there's no real scenario this
project has found yet where that pattern would have something to do.

**Original redirect, for context:** this task was originally scoped at
`.gcmesh_pc`/`.gsmesh_pc` (per Team A's disassembly findings,
`spec-geometry-format.md` §4.1/§4.1.1). Byte-tracing the spec's own real
worked example (`cm_hand_f_leather.ccmesh_pc`/`.gcmesh_pc`, extracted from
`customize_item.vpp_pc`) found that the `0x424BD00D` magic, its six-array
system, AND the nested "Mesh" sub-block all live inside the small
`.ccmesh_pc` file, not `.gcmesh_pc` — the redirect to `.ccmesh_pc` (this
section) is a direct result of that finding, already relayed to and
approved by the peer session before implementation started.

### 4.3 `sr3anim` (`.anim_pc` header) — complete for the confirmed header, payload deliberately out of scope

`Animation::parse()` (`include/sr3anim/animation.h`) covers exactly what
`spec-anim-format.md` confirms: the `ANIM` magic, the version-must-be-14
rule (both enforced, since the real loader enforces both), the flags byte,
the root-motion quaternion at `+0x0C` and translation at `+0x1C`, the
`+0x30` in-file offset, and the optional section at `+0x40` that flags bit
`0x10` gates.

**It deliberately does not touch the keyframe/track payload**, and that is
a scope decision, not an omission. Spec §6 tested the obvious
`frames × tracks × bytes-per-key` model against the whole population and
found it *measurably wrong* (median 0.55 bytes per frame-track, sd 0.34 —
no consistent value, and a nominal half-byte per key that cannot be a
literal uncompressed key). Decoding it needs the runtime animation
*sampling* subsystem, not more parsing. Same posture as `sr3save` with the
save-snapshot's unmapped gameplay region: take the confirmed fields, leave
the rest alone.

Fields whose meaning is OPEN or merely hypothesised (`+0x06`, `+0x08`,
`+0x09`, `+0x0A`, `+0x0B`) are exposed as `field_0xNN_rawCount()` — named
by offset on purpose. Spec §6 actively undermines the "frame count"
reading of `+0x06`, and the per-bone-track-count reading of `+0x0A`/`+0x0B`
is explicitly HIGH CONFIDENCE but unconfirmed; giving them interpreted
names would assert something the spec declines to.

**Validation against all 4,209 real files** in
`test-fixtures/preload_anim.vpp_pc` reproduces the spec's own population
statistics, which is a much stronger check than "it parsed":

| Spec claim | Spec | This reader |
|---|---|---|
| Files parsed | 4,209 | **4209 / 4209** |
| Version is exactly 14 | all | **all 4209** |
| Root quaternion normalizes to 1.0 (±1e-4) | 4209/4209 | **4209 / 4209** |
| Files with flags bit `0x10` set holding a valid `+0x40` offset | 167/167 | **167 / 167** |
| Ungated files with offset-shaped bytes at `+0x40` (by chance) | 3.4% | **137 → 3.4%** |
| Sub-`0x48`-byte files | 12 | **12** |
| …of which set the flag | 0 | **0** |
| `+0x30` holds an in-file offset | 4209/4209 | **4209 / 4209** |
| Rare flag values beyond the main eight | "four rarer values" | **exactly 4** (`0x0c`, `0x1c`, `0x5d`, `0x9d`) |

The flags histogram differs from spec §2's by exactly the 12 short files
(spec's counts are over the 4,197 *full-header* files; mine are over all
4,209, and §8 item 6 notes all 12 short files are flags `0x09` — 2167 + 12
= 2179, which is what this reader reports). Not a discrepancy, just a
different denominator.

**One genuine loose end, reported rather than smoothed over:** spec §2 puts
"exactly zero translation" at 1,954 files; this reader finds **1,953**
exactly zero, plus 7 more within 1e-4 of zero (magnitudes 3e-06 … 9e-05).
So the spec's 1,954 matches neither an exact-zero nor a 1e-4 threshold
cleanly. It is a one-file difference in a descriptive statistic about a
field whose *interpretation* the spec itself rates HIGH CONFIDENCE rather
than confirmed, and it has no bearing on parsing correctness — flagged for
Team A, not chased further from this side.

### 4.4 `sr3morph` (`.cmorph_pc`) — complete, 1541/1541 real files

Validated against the full shipped population across all seven archives
spec §2 surveyed. Every structural claim reproduces exactly, and the run
also turned up a real correction to the spec's own control statistic
(below).

`MorphFile::parse()` (`include/sr3morph/morph_file.h`) walks the whole
container per spec §3: outer header (`0x1337BEEF`, version 5) → "Morph"
block header (`0x0BADBEEF`, version 3, mode, target count) → directory
(`count × 0x10`) → descriptors (`n × 0x28` per target) → inline bulk runs
(align 16, `N × 12`, align 16) → trailer (align 4, `0x0BADBEEF` sentinel).

Only one field *inside* an element is decoded: the vertex index at `+6`,
which spec §5 confirms at 25,789/25,789 records against a control that
scored 1.3%. The three quantised components are exposed as raw `u16`s and
deliberately **not** decoded — spec §7 leaves the dequantisation formula
open (whether the descriptor's float triples are `(min,extent)`,
`(offset,scale)` or `(scale,center)`, and whether the 16-bit values are
biased or two's-complement, are all undetermined), and closing it needs the
runtime code that *applies* a morph. Same posture as `sr3geometry`'s six
arrays and `sr3anim`'s keyframe payload.

**Two implementation points that are easy to get wrong:**

1. **Alignment here is the CONDITIONAL form** — pad 0 when already
   aligned. This is explicitly *not* the mandatory-minimum pad that
   `.ccmesh_pc` uses at its material/geometry boundary (§4.2 finding 1).
   Spec §3 calls the difference out directly because the loader's own
   arithmetic shows it. Using the wrong one breaks the exact-size replay.
2. **`parse()` is itself the structural proof.** Spec §4's headline result
   is that this walk predicts the exact byte size of 1,541/1,541 real files
   with zero residual, with the sentinel at the predicted end. `parse()`
   re-checks *both* on every file and throws (reporting the residual)
   rather than trusting the walk. So a successful parse *is* that
   verification — which is why the validation run below was worth doing:
   it either confirmed the model on 1,541 files or produced a residual
   localising exactly what was wrong (spec §10 item 3: "a residual is a
   measurement"). It confirmed — see the table below.

**Modes 0 and 2 are deliberately not implemented.** They are real loader
capability but place the bulk in a secondary `.gmorph_pc`, of which the
game ships **zero** (spec §6: 2,946 `.cmorph_pc`, 0 `.gmorph_pc`). Every
shipped file is mode 1. `parse()` rejects 0/2 with an explicit message
rather than writing an unverifiable path blind.

**Measured results**, all seven archives, deduped by `(name, size)`:

| Spec claim | Spec | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| Entries / unique by (name, size) | 2,946 / 1,541 | **2946 / 1541** |
| Parsed | — | **1541 / 1541**, 0 failures |
| Exact-size replay lands on EOF + sentinel | 1541/1541 | **1541 / 1541** |
| `.gmorph_pc` files anywhere | 0 | **0** |
| Size range | 324 … 805,236 | **324 … 805,236** |
| Most common size | 17,220 × 218 | **17,220 × 218** |
| Every file mode 1 | yes | **1541 mode 1** |
| Index at `+6` ascending / unique / max matches `+0x06` | 100% | **45243 / 45243** on all three |
| Total elements, all with `+10` < 4096 | 10,415,507 | **10,415,507 / 10,415,507** |

**A real correction to spec §5's control statistic.** The spec reports the
`+0` control — the "what would an arbitrary `u16` field score?" baseline
that makes the `+6` result meaningful — as **324 / 25,789 = 1.3%**. Both
numbers reproduce exactly, but they are measured over records with `N ≥ 1`,
and **322 of those 324 hits are single-element records**, which pass
"strictly ascending" *vacuously*. Measured only where the test can actually
fail (`N ≥ 2`), the genuine by-chance rate is **2 / 25,467 = 0.008%** —
roughly 165× lower than stated.

This *strengthens* §5's conclusion rather than weakening it: the real
contrast isn't 1.3% vs 100%, it's 0.008% vs 100%. Directly measured
breakdown, which reconciles every figure on both sides:

| N | records | of which `+0`-ascending |
|---|---|---|
| 0 (empty, no bulk) | 19,454 | — (excluded from spec's denominator) |
| 1 (single element) | 322 | **322** — all vacuous |
| ≥ 2 (test is meaningful) | 25,467 | **2** |
| **≥ 1 (spec's denominator)** | **25,789** ✓ | **324** ✓ |

**A second finding the spec doesn't cover: 19,454 of 45,243 records (43%)
have `N == 0`** — descriptors declaring a target that affects no vertices
at all. That these readings are correct is not an assumption: a wrong `N`
anywhere would break the exact-size arithmetic, and the replay lands on EOF
for all 1,541 files. Plausibly a full slider set declared per file with
only some sliders actually deforming a given garment, but that reading is
inference, not confirmed.

The validation harness is `tools/validation/validate_morph.cpp` (+
`build_validate_morph.bat`) — ephemeral, but the shape is worth reusing;
see §6.

**Answering the paired-file question raised with this target:** spec §6
notes the secondary `.gmorph_pc` is legitimately absent for *every* morph
in the game, and asks whether this project's dispatch tolerates a missing
secondary. **It does, by construction — there is no paired-file dispatch
to break.** Every reader here takes the primary file alone:
`TexturePair::parse()` takes only the `.cpeg_pc` and makes the `.gpeg_pc`
an opt-in second argument (`validateAgainstGpeg()`, and `texture_dump`'s
optional `argv[2]`); `sr3geometry` reads `.ccmesh_pc` only and never needs
the `.gcmesh_pc`; `vpp_dump`/`vpp_extract` walk entries independently with
no pairing logic at all. A missing secondary is simply a call not made, not
an error path. Worth keeping that way.

### 4.5 `sr3foliage` (`.cfmesh_pc`) — complete: real-data validated 19/19, build-integrated, unit-tested

Now fully integrated. It was for a while the tree's one mixed-status
component — real-data validated but outside the build and untested — and
that split is closed:

- **The parser is validated against the complete shipped population**,
  reproducing every statistic in `spec-foliage-format.md` exactly (table
  below). Nothing in it is failing.
- **It is now part of the tested build surface**: in `CMakeLists.txt` and
  the manual build script, with its own synthetic suite
  (`tests/synthetic_foliage_test.cpp`) and a content-validation
  corroborator wired into `vpp_dump`/`vpp_extract`.
- **Writing those tests immediately earned their keep**, which is the
  argument for not treating real-data validation as a substitute: the
  first run of the new suite crashed, and the cause was a real bug that the
  19/19 real-data run had been structurally incapable of noticing. See §5.

**Measured, all 19 files (the entire population, in
`sr3_city_0.vpp_pc`'s `awld_compact.str2_pc` bundle):**

| Spec claim | Spec | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| Files (complete population) | 19 | **19 found, 19 parsed, 0 failures** |
| `.gfmesh_pc` files | 0 | **0** |
| Size range | 1,564 … 24,564 | **1,564 … 24,564** |
| Embedded Mesh sub-block reads version 9 | 19/19 | **19 / 19** |
| Material records | 33 | **33** |
| Distinct shader hashes / variant hashes | 2 / 13 | **2 / 13** |
| Material shapes (A,B,C) | (3,9,11)×23, (1,1,3)×10 | **exactly that** |
| Material flags | 0xC2 plants, 0x40 litter | **0xc2 ×10, 0x40 ×23** |
| Texture bindings | 79 | **79** |
| Distinct `slot_hash` / distinct `.tga` names | 3 / 16 | **3 / 16** (names match §6.3's list exactly) |
| Materials per file / LOD records per file | 1–4 / 1–3 | **1–4 / 1–3** |

Because `parse()` enforces spec §3's oracle — the material sub-record chain
must end *exactly* at the outer block's `+0x28` target — 19/19 parsing
means that chain check also held 19/19, including the 16-byte alignment
after the runtime slot array that spec §9 records as the step the spec
team's own first replay got wrong.

**Re-validated after the §5 item 7 exception fix**, rather than assuming a
change to an error path couldn't reach the success path: the full run was
repeated against `sr3_city_0.vpp_pc` and returned 19 found / 19 parsed /
0 failures (exit 0), with every statistic identical to the table above.

The flags/shape pairing also cross-checks §6.3's semantic claim: the 10
`(1,1,3)` records carrying flags `0xC2` bind a single texture (plants,
diffuse only), and the 23 `(3,9,11)` records carrying `0x40` bind three
(litter: diffuse, specular, normal).

**What exists:**
- `include/sr3foliage/errors.h`, `include/sr3foliage/foliage_mesh.h`,
  `include/sr3foliage/content_validation.h`
- `src/foliage_mesh.cpp`, `src/foliage_content_validation.cpp`
- `tools/foliage_dump.cpp`
- `tests/synthetic_foliage_test.cpp`
- All of it wired into `CMakeLists.txt` (library `sr3foliage`, tool
  `foliage_dump`, test target `sr3foliage_tests`) and the manual build
  script. `sr3foliage` depends on `sr3geometry` for `MaterialBlock`.

**The synthetic suite** locks in the shapes real data alone can't reach:
the mandatory ≥1-byte pad to the outer block, the 16-byte alignment after
the runtime slot array, length-prefixed material sub-records at their three
internal alignments (bindings 4, constant hashes 4, vec4s 16), and the
exact `+0x28` chain check. Its builder deliberately mirrors
`src/foliage_mesh.cpp`'s own layout logic step for step — the same way
`synthetic_ccmesh_test.cpp` mirrors `geometry_block.cpp` — so a change to
one that isn't matched in the other fails loudly. Coverage includes a
well-formed file, a multi-material file using both of spec §6's observed
shapes, a zero-material/no-Mesh-block/no-LOD-table file, and seven
negative cases: bad outer magic, bad outer version, Mesh sub-block not
reading version 9, a null required offset, a material declaring size 0, a
chain that misses the `+0x28` target, and truncated content.

**The corroborator** (`looksLikeCfmeshFilename` / `validateCfmeshContent` /
`refineWithCfmeshValidation`) follows §2's pattern exactly. Its structural
check is simply "did `parse()` succeed", which is stronger here than that
phrasing suggests: `parse()` enforces the `+0x28` chain oracle, so a pass
is real corroborating evidence rather than a loose shape match. Matches
`.cfmesh_pc` only — spec §2 confirms no g-side extension exists (0/19), so
unlike `sr3texture` there is no paired-file case to consider.

- The real-data validation harness is `tools/validation/validate_foliage.cpp` —
  ephemeral, rebuild as needed (§6). Note it takes **~50 minutes** to walk
  `sr3_city_0.vpp_pc` (1.5 GB); it prints nothing until it finishes, so an
  apparently-silent run is normal, not a hang.

**Design intent, for whoever picks it up.** It reuses
`sr3geometry::MaterialBlock` for the block at `+0x00` rather than
duplicating it, locates and version-checks the embedded "Mesh" sub-block
without parsing its internals (same boundary `sr3geometry` holds, same open
item), and walks the inline material definitions, texture-name table and
LOD/fade table. Its central self-check is spec §3's oracle: the material
sub-record chain must end **exactly** at the outer block's own `+0x28`
target, which held 19/19 for the spec team once the alignment after the
runtime slot array was 16 rather than 8 (spec §9). `parse()` enforces that
and reports the residual on mismatch.

**On the risk that was flagged and did not materialise.** Before the result
came back this section warned that the reader had been written from a spec
without ever meeting real bytes, and that this project has repeatedly found
specs and real files disagreeing in load-bearing ways — the texture
format's `+0x22`/`+0x24` offset, the geometry format's BlobA, the morph
spec's control statistic. That caution was right to state; it simply
didn't pay out here. `spec-foliage-format.md` proved accurate in every
respect this reader touches. Worth recording precisely because the
opposite outcome is what the earlier sections document — a spec being
right first time is the less common case in this project, not the default.

**One further thing it confirms**, independent of its own correctness:
spec §3 states the mandatory-pad rule outright — pad to the next 16-byte
boundary, *always at least one byte* — which is exactly the behaviour
