`sr3geometry` had to derive empirically from 21 of 549 files sitting at
naive+16. That cross-confirmation is noted in
`include/sr3geometry/geometry_block.h` and stands on its own.

### 4.6 `sr3conversation` (`.ctdg_pc`) and `sr3cutscene` (`.csc_pc`) — complete: both validated on their full populations (4,984/4,984 and 192/192)

Two formats built in one pass, both structurally complete. Unlike §4.5's
foliage, these were integrated into `CMakeLists.txt`, the manual build
script, the `vpp_dump`/`vpp_extract` corroborator chain and their own
synthetic suites **from the start** — there was no window where either sat
on disk outside the tested surface.

**Both are pinned by an exact-size identity, which is what makes them
cheap to trust.** Neither reader has to infer a layout: the file's own
count field determines the total size exactly, so a successful parse *is*
the spec's replay re-run per file.

| | `.ctdg_pc` | `.csc_pc` |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | `44 + 12 × count == size` | `record_offset + count × 0x68 == size` |
| Spec's replay | 4,984/4,984 | 96/96 |
| Magic | `0x56414344` (`DCAV`) | **none** — only a `u16` version |
| Offsets/fixups | **none anywhere** | record array + 2 pointers per channel |

**`.ctdg_pc` is the strongest corroborator target in the project.** Magic,
version, a bounded count, *and* a size identity accounting for every byte
with no offsets anywhere to leave slack — a corrupted decode has nowhere
to hide. `.csc_pc` is the weakest header-wise (no magic at all), so its
check leans on the size identity plus a bounds walk over every channel
pointer instead. Both are noted honestly in their
`content_validation.h` files rather than presented as equivalent.

**What is deliberately left raw**, per the usual convention:
- `.ctdg_pc` speaker ids — they *are* the rotate-6/XOR hash (spec §6
  proves it algebraically), but the pre-image names are OPEN: 0 of 57
  matched any of 3,917 curated candidates, with the control also at 0, so
  the search was unsuccessful rather than mis-calibrated. Recovering them
  needs the validator's string table.
- `.ctdg_pc` record `+0x08` — CONFIRMED stored per turn, HYPOTHESIS that
  it means milliseconds. Exposed as `field_0x08_raw` with an
  `field_0x08_asInt32()` helper that performs a bit-level reinterpretation
  and makes no semantic claim.
- `.csc_pc` channel 1 — 8-byte width CONFIRMED, encoding OPEN. Note this
  is a *refuted* reading, not merely an unidentified one: the obvious
  compressed-quaternion interpretation matched 0 of 31,898 keys against a
  control that fires on 30.2% of known-non-quaternion bytes. So
  `decodeFloats()` **throws** if handed channel 1 rather than silently
  halving it — a guess dressed as a decode is worse than no decode.
- `.csc_pc` channels 3–7 — 4-byte width CONFIRMED so they decode as
  floats, but they are named by index. "Depth of field" is HYPOTHESIS.

**One property deliberately *not* enforced:** `.csc_pc` shots tile the
timeline exactly (1,309/1,309 consecutive pairs, first shot at 0.0 in
96/96). That is a CONFIRMED property of *shipped data*, not a rule the
engine's parser checks — so `parse()` accepts a non-contiguous file and
exposes `Shot::isContiguousWith()` for callers who want to test it.
Rejecting it would invent a constraint the format does not have.

**Real-data validation — read the two formats separately, they are not at
the same level of coverage.** Their populations live in different archives
(`.csc_pc`: `cutscenes.vpp_pc` plus 6 in DLC; `.ctdg_pc`:
`sr3_city_0.vpp_pc` 4,096, `dlc2` 604, `dlc3` 253, `dlc1` 31), so a sweep
of a subset reproduces only that subset's share of the spec's published
totals — compare like with like before calling a number a mismatch.

**`.csc_pc` — COMPLETE population, 192/192 parsed, 0 failures.** Note the
harness counts all 192 *entries* where the spec counts 96 *distinct* files,
so every figure below is exactly double the spec's — and the doubling being
exact is itself independent corroboration of spec §2's "every duplicate
byte-identical" claim.

| Spec claim (96 distinct) | Spec | Measured (192 entries) |
|---|---|---|
| Files parsed | 96 | **192 / 192, 0 failures** |
| `.gsc_pc` files | 0 | **0** |
| Size range | 148 … 45,240 | **148 … 45,240** (exact) |
| Total shots | 1,405 | **2,810** = 2×1,405 |
| Shots per file | 1 … 82 | **1 … 82** (exact) |
| First shot starts at 0.0 | 96/96 | **192 / 192** |
| Null channel pointers | 0 of 22,480 | **0 of 44,960** = 2×22,480 |
| Multi-key tracks strictly ascending | 1,999/1,999 | **3,998 / 3,998** |
| Channel 0 keys | 14,703 | **29,406** = 2×14,703 |
| FOV keys in (0, π) | all 2,345 | **4,690 / 4,690** = 2×2,345 |
| Optional group absent/single/multi | 396 / 914 / 95 | **792 / 1,828 / 190** = 2× each |

**`.ctdg_pc` — COMPLETE population, 4,984/4,984 parsed, 0 failures.** Run
as two sweeps (`sr3_city_0.vpp_pc` 4,096, then DLC 888) and summed. Every
published total reproduces exactly:

| Spec claim | Spec | Measured (4,096 city + 888 DLC) |
|---|---|---|
| Files | 4,984 | **4,984, all parsed, 0 failures** |
| Total records | 19,440 | **16,234 + 3,206 = 19,440** (exact) |
| Size range | 56 … 248 | **56 … 248** (exact) |
| Records per file | 1 … 17 | **1 … 17** (exact) |
| Distinct speakers per file | 2 in 4,149; 3 in 673; 1 in 114; 4 in 48 | **4,149 / 673 / 114 / 48** — exact on all four |
| Line ids distinct within file | 4,983 of 4,984 | **4,096/4,096 + 887/888 = 4,983 / 4,984** (exact) |
| `field_0x08` zero | 19,109 of 19,440 | **15,911 + 3,198 = 19,109** (exact) |
| Distinct speaker ids | 57 | **34 + 23 = 57** |
| Distinct line ids | 4,153 | **3,531 + 622 = 4,153** |

The last two rows are worth a note: the two sweeps measured their sets
separately, so those are sums, not directly-observed unions. That they sum
to *exactly* the spec's totals means the city and DLC sets are disjoint —
DLC conversations use their own speakers and their own line ids, sharing
none with the base game. Consistent, but recorded as an inference rather
than a direct measurement.

**The full sweep earned its keep: it found a real bug in this reader.**
See §5 item 8 — `sourceNameTruncated()` was testing the wrong condition
and could never fire. The tell was the one row that did *not* reproduce:
0 truncated names against spec §1's 1,187.

**Two reciprocal findings for Team A on `field_0x08`** (neither affects
parsing — the field is surfaced raw regardless):
1. **Its range is wider than stated.** Spec §4 says "roughly −500 … +600";
   measured across all 331 non-zero values it is **−1,300 … +800**.
2. **Not all non-zero values are multiples of 100.** Spec §4 characterises
   them as "signed multiples of 100"; measured, **304 of 331 are, and 27
   are not**. The shape claim is a strong tendency, not a rule — which
   matters if anyone tries to use it as a validation constraint.

**Both apparent discrepancies from this pass resolved in the spec's
favour** — worth recording because the checking, not the result, is the
transferable part:

1. **Shot contiguity, 2,612 of 2,618 — NOT a spec error.** Against spec
   §4's 1,309/1,309 (2,618 doubled) this looked like six real violations.
   Measuring the residuals settled it: all six are near-misses, largest
   0.000107 s (~7 float32 ULP at t≈206 s), **zero** gaps above 1 ms, in
   just 3 distinct files (`01_in`, `02_in`, each counted twice). The spec
   is right; `Shot::isContiguousWith()` uses exact float equality and is
   simply stricter than the tolerance the spec used.
   **API sharp edge, know about it:** that method therefore returns
   `false` for 6 of 2,618 genuinely-contiguous real pairs. It is left as
   exact equality deliberately — picking a tolerance would be inventing a
   rule the spec does not state — so **any caller doing timeline logic
   should compare with its own epsilon**, not with this method.
2. **`field_0x08` reaching 800** (in
   `dlc2_m02_2nd_action_1_convo_bm.ctdg_pc`), outside spec §4's "roughly
   −500 … +600". All 8 non-zero values seen are multiples of 100, which
   matches the spec's shape claim; only the stated *range* understates the
   maximum. Since this is 8 of the population's ~331 non-zero values, the
   true range is likely wider still. Reciprocal finding for Team A; no
   bearing on parsing, since the field is surfaced raw either way.

## 5. Real bugs found and fixed this session (read before repeating them)

1. **zlib trailer requirement.** Real archives' compressed streams don't
   reliably include a trailing Adler-32 checksum within their declared
   compressed length. Fixed by targeting the exact declared uncompressed
   byte count as the stop condition (`Container::inflateToSize`) instead
   of requiring `Z_STREAM_END`.
2. **`Z_NEED_DICT` infinite loop — the most serious bug found this
   session.** `Container::inflateToSize`'s decode loop only explicitly
   handled 3 of zlib's ~7 possible `inflate()` return codes
   (`Z_STREAM_ERROR`/`Z_DATA_ERROR`/`Z_MEM_ERROR` as fatal,
   `Z_STREAM_END` as done); everything else fell through to "keep
   looping." The mode-(b) shared-stream recovery heuristic
   (`tryRecoverSharedStreamTail`) tries candidate "owner" byte offsets that
   are only ever heuristically plausible, not certain — `looksLikeZlibHeader`
   is a deliberately loose CMF/FLG sniff, and coincidental false-positive
   matches on ordinary compressed bytes are expected/already handled
   elsewhere. But when such a coincidental match's FLG byte also happened
   to have the FDICT bit set, `inflate()` returned `Z_NEED_DICT` — not
   handled — and since this format never uses a preset dictionary, calling
   `inflate()` again on unchanged state returned `Z_NEED_DICT` again,
   forever. Hit for real on `dlc3.vpp_pc` during the whole-game sweep: the
   process sat at ~100% CPU with a flat, small (~114MB) working set for
   **over 8 hours** before being noticed and killed — no crash, no error,
   just silent CPU burn. Confirmed the exact mechanism (not guessed) by
   building an instrumented copy of the decode loop that printed the raw
   zlib return code each iteration: `ret=2` (`Z_NEED_DICT`) repeating with
   `avail_in`/`avail_out`/`total_out` all frozen. **Fix:** treat any
   `inflate()` return other than `Z_OK`/`Z_STREAM_END` as an immediate
   decode failure, closing the loophole categorically rather than
   special-casing `Z_NEED_DICT` alone (see `Container::inflateToSize` in
   `src/container.cpp` for the full comment). Verified: the same file that
   hung for 8 hours now completes in 47 seconds.
3. **`.fxo_pc` filename-matching gap.** Real `shaders.vpp_pc` has ~50% of
   its entries as `.fxo_pc_dx11` (a DX11 variant) plus a couple of bare
   `.fxo` files — an exact `.fxo_pc` suffix match silently skipped all of
   them. Fixed to "extension starts with fxo" (same class of gap as
   `.xtbl` vs `.cte_xtbl`, which the xtbl matcher already handled
   correctly).
4. **`.fxo_pc` false-positive shader detection.** The D3D9 version-token
   scanner had no lower bound on the major-version byte, and found a
   spurious "shader model 0.0" (not a real D3D9 version) on real data.
   Fixed with a `kMinPlausibleMajorVersion = 1` constraint (D3D9 versions
   only ever ran 1.0–3.0, public/documented fact).
5. **Texture format's `+0x22`/`+0x24` offset error** — see §3 above.
6. **Re-deriving a length that the format already declares.** The
   `sr3geometry` reader originally located array 1 by *walking* the
   embedded name copy as N null-terminated strings (mirroring the material
   block's own genuinely-simple format) plus an ad-hoc padding search,
   because the spec section being worked from didn't mention that this
   region — "BlobA" — carries its own explicit 4-byte length field at
   `+0x88`. That guess worked by coincidence on simple meshes and failed
   outright on richer ones: 82% pass rate, and for the failures a
   full-file brute-force scan found *no* valid position anywhere, because
   the model of the region's internal layout was simply wrong rather than
   slightly off. Two lessons worth carrying: (a) a clean brute-force
   "nothing matches anywhere" result is strong evidence the *model* is
   wrong, not that the search needs widening — that reading was correct
   here and is what got it escalated instead of tuned; (b) when a
   structure resists a formula, check whether the format already declares
   the answer before inferring it. Fixing this exposed the two alignment
   rules in §4.2 item 3 as well, taking the reader from 82% to 1803/1803.
   Credit where due: Team A's disassembly pass identified BlobA; this side
   independently verified its offset, length field and pad byte-for-byte
   on real files before trusting it.
7. **`sr3foliage` threw the wrong exception type across a namespace
   boundary — and real-data validation structurally could not see it.**
   `FoliageMesh::parse()` calls `sr3geometry::MaterialBlock::parse()` to
   read the shared block at `+0x00`. `sr3geometry::FormatError` and
   `sr3foliage::FormatError` are *unrelated sibling classes* — both derive
   from `std::runtime_error`, neither from the other — so every
   material-block failure escaped `FoliageMesh::parse()` as a
   `sr3geometry::FormatError`, sailing straight past any
   `catch (const sr3foliage::FormatError&)`. That silently defeated
   `foliage_mesh.h`'s own documented contract ("Throws FormatError if the
   material block fails to validate"), and defeated the new corroborator's
   catch clause too — `validateCfmeshContent` would have let the exception
   escape instead of reporting `NotWellFormed`. **Fix:** catch and rewrap
   at the call site in `src/foliage_mesh.cpp`.
   The instructive part is *why it survived a 19/19 real-data validation*:
   that harness catches `const std::exception&` broadly, so it never cared
   which of the two types it got, and none of the 19 real files fail
   anyway. Only a test that deliberately feeds malformed input **and**
   asserts on the specific exception type could expose it — which is
   exactly what the first run of `synthetic_foliage_test.cpp` did, by
   crashing (`0xC0000409`, the same uncaught-exception fast-fail signature
   as §4.2's). Treat this as the concrete case against "it validated
   against real data, so it doesn't need unit tests": real data exercises
   the success path, and error paths are where unexercised assumptions
   accumulate.

8. **A detector that tested a condition the engine never produces —
   caught only by a whole-population sweep.**
   `sr3conversation`'s `sourceNameTruncated()` flagged a source-name field
   that filled all 32 bytes with *no terminator*. But the engine clips an
   over-long authoring name to 31 characters **and still writes the NUL**,
   so a truncated name has length 31; the length-32 case never occurs in
   shipped data. The flag was dead code: it returned false for all 4,984
   files, against spec §1's count of 1,187 truncated names.
   **What actually caught it** is the point. Every other statistic in the
   `.ctdg_pc` sweep reproduced its published figure exactly — records,
   size range, speakers-per-file, line-id distinctness, `field_0x08`
   zeros — and this one row read 0 against 1,187. Nothing else would have
   surfaced it: the format parsed fine, the size identity held 4,984/4,984,
   and the synthetic tests passed because the test fixture exercised the
   same wrong assumption the reader held (it built a 40-character name and
   asserted the length-32 behaviour). A validation harness that only
   checked "did it parse" would have reported total success.
   Two lessons worth carrying: (a) **§3's "reproduce the spec's own
   statistics" rule is what has repeatedly caught quiet wrongness** —
   here, an 18% sample had shown 0 against 1,187 too, but that was
   ambiguous (the truncated files could all have been elsewhere); only the
   complete population made it unarguable. (b) **A test fixture written
   from the same misreading as the code under test cannot catch that
   misreading** — the synthetic suite was green throughout. Real-population
   statistics are the independent check that synthetic tests structurally
   cannot be.
   **Fix:** detect length ≥ 31, with the accessor documenting that a name
   genuinely 31 characters long is indistinguishable from a clipped one —
   the clip discards the evidence — so it reports "at the clip limit",
   the strongest claim the bytes support. Regression tests added for the
   31-character case, the 32-character case, and two negatives.

## 6. Build system

`CMakeLists.txt` at the project root is the **authoritative** build
definition — use it in any environment that has `cmake` available
(`cmake -B build && cmake --build build`, then `ctest` from `build/` for
the test suite). It declares: `vpp_container` (core), `sr3save`, `sr3asm`,
`sr3fxo`, `sr3texture`, `sr3geometry`, `sr3anim`, `sr3morph`, `sr3foliage`,
`sr3conversation`, `sr3cutscene` static libraries, one CLI tool per format,
and one test executable per format registered with `ctest`. `sr3foliage` is
the only library that depends on another format library (`sr3geometry`, for
the shared `MaterialBlock`); everything else depends only on
`vpp_container`.

**This particular dev sandbox has no `cmake`/`g++`/other compiler besides
MSVC** (`cl.exe` via `C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\
BuildTools\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvarsall.bat x64`), so this session used a
hand-written batch script mirroring `CMakeLists.txt`'s target graph,
compiling each `.cpp` and linking manually. That script is **not part of
the deliverable** — it lives in the session's own scratchpad directory
(ephemeral, tied to this conversation), not in the project tree. If you're
in a similarly cmake-less environment, you'll need to either install
`cmake`+a compatible generator, or reconstruct an equivalent manual script
from `CMakeLists.txt`'s target list (source files, include dirs, and link
order are all given there). One real gotcha if you do: every combined
compile+link `cl.exe` invocation (i.e. anything with `/Fe` but no `/c`)
needs its own explicit `/Fo"<builddir>\\"` too, or MSVC silently drops the
intermediate `.obj` in the current working directory instead — this
littered the actual project root with stray `.obj` files for most of this
session before being caught and fixed (every step in this session's own
script now passes both flags).

Vendored `third_party/zlib` (1.3.1) is used as an unmodified, off-the-shelf
RFC 1950 zlib codec — never reimplemented, per task scope.

**Real-data validation harnesses (ephemeral — rebuild as needed).** The
per-format real-file checks referenced throughout §4 were run from one-off
harnesses in the session scratchpad, not the project tree, since they're
throwaway analysis rather than deliverables. They all follow one shape:
walk a `.vpp_pc` recursively with `vpp::Container`, pick out entries by
extension, run the *real* library parser over each, and tally results
against the spec's own published figures. If you need them again they're
quick to reconstruct from that description; the pattern is worth reusing
for any new format, and §3's "reproduce the spec's own statistics" bullet
explains why. All of them have now been run to completion: `validate_anim`
(4209/4209, §4.3), `validate_morph` (1541/1541, §4.4),
`validate_ccmesh_broad` (1803/1803, §4.2) and `validate_foliage` (19/19,
§4.5). Budget real time for the foliage one in particular — walking
`sr3_city_0.vpp_pc` (1.5 GB) takes **~50 minutes** and prints nothing at
all until it finishes, so silence is not a hang.

## 8. Where the corruption investigation stands (context, not this session's active work)

The mode-(a) non-first-entry silent-corruption issue (`OkUnconfirmedContent`,
§2) is Team A's ongoing investigation, not something this reader library
attempts to fix. This session's own black-box hypothesis tests (continuous-
stream decoding, hash-sort and alphabetical-sort physical packing order)
were all ruled out with rigorous random-control-baseline comparisons — see
§3's note on the hash-sort false lead. The mode-(b) shared-stream recovery
heuristic (`tryRecoverSharedStreamTail`) is a real, working mitigation for
a *related* but distinct shape (2 confirmed real instances, always a direct
owner→entry pair) — it is not a fix for the general mode-(a) problem.

The whole-game sweep (§4.1) is the best current evidence of the issue's
real-world *scope*, not its cause: it's concentrated almost entirely in a
handful of gameplay-table and shader-wrapper archives
(`misc_tables.vpp_pc`, `shaders.vpp_pc`, and a few smaller ones), while the
large majority of the game's actual content (every raw and mode-(b)
archive — textures, meshes, audio, the whole open-world city) is fully
readable today with zero corruption exposure. If Team A's investigation
resumes, `misc_tables.vpp_pc` (1,338 hard failures out of 1,342 entries —
the single worst archive in the sweep) is the highest-value real sample to
work from.

## 9. Engine/renderer phase (started 2026-09-11)

**Phase change.** The reverse-engineering/implementation phase closed with
§1–§8. This section covers the follow-on work: turning the readers into an
actual engine/renderer. Same clean-room boundary as before — specs and
game *data* files only, never the executable or disassembly.

**New confidence tier: CONFIRMED ON-SCREEN.** Forward-engineering needs a
stronger top tier than the RE phase had, and rendering supplies one. A
format hypothesis that produces a coherent, recognisable image is
confirmed in a way no amount of byte arithmetic can match — and, crucially,
this tier can close spec items that arithmetic provably *cannot* (see
§9.3). It is also a discipline: "it renders" means an image was produced
and looked at, never that an API call returned `S_OK`.

`spec-texture-format.md` §4 (§9.4), plus the texcoord encoding, the

### 9.1 Architecture decisions (settled, don't re-litigate)

**Graphics API: D3D11.** Not a preference — a constraint. This sandbox's
Windows SDKs (10.0.22621 / 10.0.26100) ship `d3d11.h`, `dxgi.h` and
`d3dcompiler.h` but **not `d3d9.h`**; D3D9 would need the deprecated
standalone DirectX SDK, which isn't installed. (`d3d9.lib` is present
without its header, which is a trap worth knowing about.) Two reasons it is
the right call anyway: D3D11's **WARP** software rasterizer guarantees a
device with no GPU and no interactive session, and BC1/BC3 are core
formats — exactly what SR3's texture codes turn out to be.

*Consequence, accepted:* the game's own `.fxo_pc` shaders are D3D9 SM1-3
bytecode and **cannot** be fed to D3D11. This engine writes its own HLSL.
Reusing the shipped shaders would need either a D3D9 path (no header) or an
SM1-3 bytecode translator; neither is required for current milestones.

**Headless-first, with render → readback → PNG as the verification
backbone.** The primary path renders to an offscreen target, reads the
pixels back and writes a PNG. This is deliberate: it makes every milestone
produce an artefact a human or agent can *look at*, and it runs with no
window and no display. `png_writer.cpp` reuses the already-vendored zlib
for DEFLATE and CRC-32, so no new dependency was introduced.

*Observed:* the device comes up as **HARDWARE (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090)**
here, but nothing depends on that — `RenderDevice::kind()` reports which
rasterizer was obtained rather than assuming.

**Files.** Renderer: `include/sr3render/` + `src/` — `png_writer`, `device`,
`texture_upload`, `quad_renderer`, `window`, `swap_chain`, `mesh_renderer`.
Format readers added this phase: `sr3mesh` (`src/mesh_block.cpp`) and
`sr3rig` (`src/rig.cpp`). Driver tool `tools/sr3_viewer.cpp`, with
subcommands `clear`, `list-textures`, `texture`, `view` (windowed),
`mesh` (`--mode uv|checker|normal|textured`, `--rig`, `--yaw/--pitch`).

### 9.2 Milestone 1 — rendering scaffold: DONE, confirmed on-screen

Device creation, offscreen render target, clear, CPU readback, PNG out.
Verified two ways rather than one: every pixel of the readback was checked
against the requested clear colour in code, *and* the PNG was viewed. The
clear colour (40,90,160) is deliberately asymmetric so a channel-order bug
would show as the wrong hue instead of a plausible image — it came out
blue, not orange, so RGBA ordering is correct.

### 9.3 Milestone 2 — real texture on screen: DONE, and it closed an open spec item

`sr3_viewer texture <archive> <name.cpeg_pc> <out.png> [index]` runs the
whole path in memory — open archive, find the `.cpeg_pc`/`.gpeg_pc` pair
(descending into nested containers), decode with the validated
`sr3texture` reader, upload to the GPU, draw a fullscreen quad, read back,
write PNG. Nothing is extracted to disk.

**Rendered and visually confirmed:** `decal_cracks.tga` (code 402) renders
as coherent radiating impact cracks; `vfx_blast_decal_01_n.tga` (code 400)
as a sharp radial blast pattern; `ds_skidmark01.tga` as tyre tread.

**This closes `spec-texture-format.md` §6 item 1 for codes 400 and 402.**
That item was open because, in the spec's own words, "the raw pixel bytes
were not decoded/rendered to visually confirm which specific compressed
encoding is in use" — and it *could not* be closed by arithmetic, since
byte ratios cannot distinguish BC1 from any other 4-bit-per-pixel scheme.
Rendering settles it: block-compressed data read with the wrong block
layout does not degrade gracefully, it produces structured noise and 4×4
block artefacts. Sharp, coherent, recognisable images at 256×256 are strong
evidence the mapping is right.

| Code | Mapping | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | `DXGI_FORMAT_BC1_UNORM` (DXT1) | **CONFIRMED ON-SCREEN** |
| 402 | `DXGI_FORMAT_BC3_UNORM` (DXT5) | **CONFIRMED ON-SCREEN** |
| 403 | — | still OPEN; deliberately **not** guessed at |

Code 403 (seen once: 800×324, 518,400 bytes = exactly 2.0 bytes/pixel, no
mip chain) is refused by `uploadTexture()` rather than mapped to a
plausible 16-bit layout. Several fit that ratio; rendering one and getting
something that "looks fine" would manufacture false confidence.

### 9.4 Three corrections to `spec-texture-format.md` §4, found by building it

All three come from the same measurement: computing each texture's mip
chain size and comparing it against the record's declared size.

1. **Mip chains terminate at 4×4, not 1×1.** §4 describes a "complete mip
   chain … down to 1×1". The 2×2 and 1×1 levels are never stored.
2. **The spec's "rounding" was not rounding.** §4 hedges that its
   arithmetic matches "closely enough … within the small rounding expected
   from block-compression's fixed minimum block size". That hedge was
   covering for finding 1: assuming 1×1 overshoots by *exactly* the two
   missing levels — 16 bytes for BC1, 32 for BC3, every time.
3. **Some textures carry no mip chain at all.** `ds_skidmark01.tga` (64×64,
   code 402) declares 4,096 bytes = precisely its base level, nothing more.

So there is no single chain-length rule to apply. **The record's declared
size is authoritative for how many levels are present**, and reading the
count out of it covers all cases without guessing — the same lesson as the
geometry format's "BlobA" (§5 item 6): when a structure resists a formula,
check whether the format already declares the answer.

**Result: computed mip-chain totals now match declared sizes EXACTLY on 13
of 13 real textures** (the 12-texture `decals.vpp_pc` sample plus the 8×8
`startup.vpp_pc` sample), zero residual — strictly stronger than the spec's
"closely enough", and the exactness is itself corroboration that the
BC1/BC3 block sizes are right.

### 9.5 A further observation: code-400 normal maps store two channels

`vfx_blast_decal_01_n.tga` decodes with **blue exactly 0 across every
pixel** (R mean 126, G mean 126, B min 0 max 0, A 255) — the signature of a
two-channel tangent-space normal map storing X and Y with Z reconstructed
at runtime. It renders olive/green rather than the familiar lavender for
exactly that reason; this is correct data, not a decode error.

This does **not** mean code 400 implies "normal map" — the spec already
rejected that (`misc-static.tga` is code 400 and is not one), and this
engine confirms it: that texture decodes as flat grey (R 107, G 103, B 107)
with a normal blue channel. Code 400 is simply BC1; whether a given BC1
texture holds colour or packed normals is a property of the asset.

*Practical consequence for the renderer:* a shader sampling a `_n` texture
must reconstruct Z rather than reading B. Noted here so it is not
rediscovered later as a lighting bug.


### 9.6 Interactive window + swap chain: DONE

Win32 window (`window.h/.cpp`) plus a DXGI swap chain (`swap_chain.h/.cpp`),
driven by `sr3_viewer view <archive> <name.cpeg_pc> [index]`. Real window,
real present loop, Escape or the close button to quit, resize handled.

**Added alongside the headless path, not replacing it.** The offscreen →
readback → PNG route remains the verification backbone, for a reason worth
being explicit about: *a window proves something to a person watching, but
nothing to an automated check.* Rendering to a file is the stronger
evidence and the only kind that survives being reported second-hand.

**So the windowed path was made verifiable too.** `SwapChain::capture()`
reads the back buffer into the same layout `writePng()` expects, and
`view` takes `--frames N` and `--capture <png>`, so a windowed session can
run bounded and write out exactly what it presented. Verified that way:
512×512 window, 60 frames presented, captured image shows
`decal_cracks.tga` correctly (point-sampled up from 128×128, so the 4×
magnification is visibly blocky — that is the sampler doing what §9.1 asks
of it, not an artefact).

Two implementation details that are easy to get wrong and are worth not
rediscovering:

* **Capture before `Present()`.** With `DXGI_SWAP_EFFECT_DISCARD` the back
  buffer's contents are undefined afterwards, so capturing after presenting
  reads garbage on some drivers.
* **Release every back-buffer view before `ResizeBuffers()`.** It fails
  outright while any view still references the buffers. `resize()` also
  treats a 0×0 size (a minimised window) as "no change" rather than passing
  it to DXGI, which would be an error.

Window creation is allowed to fail with a clear message rather than
producing an invisible window: a non-interactive or session-0 context is a
normal thing to run in here, and the headless path covers it.

*Build note:* the Win32 window needs `user32.lib` and `gdi32.lib` on the
link line, which the D3D11-only milestones did not.

### 9.7 Milestone 3 — a real game asset on screen: DONE, confirmed on-screen

`brad.ccmesh_pc` renders as a recognisable Saints Row: The Third
character: black suit, white shirt and tie, lapels, a chest badge, brown
hands, black shoes, each landing on the right part of the body. Geometry
decode, texcoord decode, strip topology and the BC1 texture pipeline all
working together on shipped assets, end to end from the archive.

**New library, `sr3mesh`** (`include/sr3mesh/`, `src/mesh_block.cpp`) —
reads the shared Mesh sub-block's index buffer and per-vertex channels.
This is the structure `sr3geometry` and `sr3foliage` deliberately located
but did not parse.

**The pre-header offsets were measured, not assumed.** `spec-vertex-
format.md` §2 says a check value, a c-length and a g-length sit
"immediately before the header" without fixing their offsets relative to
the version field. Rather than guess, they were pinned against an external
oracle — the g-file's first `u32` *is* the check value and its size *is*
the g-length — giving check at `+0x04` and g-length at `+0x0C` in
**400/400** real paired meshes. Two independent 32-bit values landing at
fixed offsets across 400 files is not something a wrong reading produces.

**Real-data validation, `characters.vpp_pc` (549 paired meshes):**

| Check | Measured | Spec |
|---|---|---|
| Full segment walk + both check-value bookends | **549 / 549** | 1937/1937 |
| Declared g-length == actual g-file size | **549 / 549** | 1937/1937 |
| Indices < vertex count | **4,312,125 / 4,312,125** | 1.000000 |
| Stride law `base + 4×texcoords` | **549 / 549** | 26601/26601 |
| Positions finite | **1,773,744 / 1,773,744** | all |
| Normals unit length (6% tol) | **1,773,744 / 1,773,744** | 1.000 |
| Blend-weight sums in [250,260] | **1,773,744 / 1,773,744** | all |
| weight-zero ⟺ index-255, per lane | **7,094,976 / 7,094,976** | 1.000000 |

The semantic check is as convincing as the statistics: `brad` decodes to a
**1.385 × 1.735 × 0.404** bounding box with minimum Y ≈ −0.013 — a
correctly-proportioned human standing on the origin plane — and head LODs
sit at minimum Y 1.523 and 2.120, i.e. at head height on differently-sized
characters.

**Stride comes from the record, not the layout table.** The spec's stride
law is checked and disagreement is reported, but the channel record's own
size bytes (`+0x04` + `+0x07`) win. Same lesson as BlobA (§5 item 6) and
the mip chains (§9.4): when a structure declares its own size, read it.
It also means the unprobed layout codes (11, 13, 24) still get a correct
stride even though their field layout is unknown — `decodeChannel()`
refuses those rather than reading fields at guessed offsets.

### 9.8 Two spec corrections arrived mid-build — and one of them exposed a flaw in my own test

`spec-vertex-format.md` was corrected twice on the day it was issued.
Both corrections landed after the corresponding code was already written.

**Texcoords are signed 16-bit fixed point at scale 1024, not half-float.**
Independently re-measured here before adopting: **92.64%** of coordinate
values have a half-float exponent field of zero (spec: 94.6%), so under
the half-float reading essentially the whole population would decode as
denormals at ~0.0001 and collapse every mesh to a point. **4.74%** of raw
values exceed 32767 (spec: 2.79%), which is why the reading must be
signed. Both numbers differ slightly from the spec's because this was a
different archive subset — the conclusion is identical.

**The flaw worth recording is in the test I wrote, not in the spec.** My
first harness reported "half-float plausible (|v|<8): 90.53%" and I nearly
took that as support. It is worthless: a denormal decodes to ~0.0001,
which sits *inside* the |v|<8 band, so the acceptance region contained the
very failure mode that refutes the hypothesis. **A plausibility band that
contains the null hypothesis is not a test.** The discriminating
measurement — the exponent field — is the one that had to be looked at
directly. This is the same family as §3's control-rate lesson and as
Team A's own note about a ratio whose denominator is affected by the
hypothesis under test.

**+12 is the NORMAL, +16 is the TANGENT**, settled from the fourth bytes:
the one at +16 takes exactly two values (0/255) and is a handedness sign;
the one at +12 carries 113 distinct values of real content. `Vertex`
exposes `tangentHandedness` and a `bitangent()` helper so the sign is not
dropped — dropping it makes mirrored UV islands light inside-out. The
normal's own fourth byte stays OPEN, now known *not* to be handedness.

### 9.9 The index buffer is a triangle strip — and one consequence for Team A

Topology was resolved to a **triangle strip** with separate strips joined
by degenerate (repeated-index) triangles. `MeshBlock::triangleListIndices()`
expands the strip, drops the degenerates and alternates winding.
Measured non-degenerate triangles per vertex: **1.492** (`brad`), **1.762**
(`brad_head_lod`), **1.440** (`brute_flamethrower`) — in the band the strip
reading predicts, and nowhere near the ~0.53 a list reading gives, which
is topologically impossible for a surface.

This also retroactively explains the 38% of index counts not divisible by
three: strips have no divisibility requirement. That statistic was the
format telling us it was not a list, and it was being read as an anomaly.

**A finding to pass back: the open "per-material draw ranges" item is not
purely cosmetic — it affects geometric correctness.** Drawing the whole
index buffer as one continuous strip produces spurious triangles bridging
unrelated parts of the model (visible as thin spikes from hands to feet).
Measured, as triangles with an edge exceeding 20% of the bounding-box
diagonal:

| Mesh | Bridges | Triangles | Material textures |
|---|---|---|---|
| `brad` | 55 | 7,527 | 8 |
| `brute_flamethrower` | 32 | 8,318 | 8 |
| `brad_head_lod` | 3 | 548 | 3 |

Bridge count scales with material complexity, and a low-material mesh
renders essentially clean — `brad_head_lod` produces a flawless head with
eyes, nose, brow and jaw.

**This was reported to Team A as a correctness issue rather than a cosmetic
one, and that call was right — it sent them looking, and they found the
cause. §9.10 has the resolution. RESOLVED: bridges are now 0.**

*(Superseded guess, kept because the reasoning is instructive: this section
originally concluded the ranges lived in arrays 1–3 of the outer six-array
structure. Wrong — array 1 is absent on the very meshes showing the
artifact. The correlation with material count was real and the inference
from it was reasonable, and still landed in the wrong place. Correlating an
artifact with a plausible cause is not the same as locating it.)*

### 9.10 Draw ranges / LOD groups — the fix, and two traps in reading the spec

The index buffer is **partitioned into draw ranges**, and the partition
lives inside the **Mesh sub-block itself**, not in the outer six-array
structure. Drawing the buffer as one continuous strip reads across range
boundaries and fabricates the bridging triangles.

**Structure** (spec-vertex-format.md §8.2): Mesh header `+0x04` is a group
count; groups are `0x30`-byte records after the channel array (and after
the flag-bit-1 arrays), 16-byte aligned; each group's first `u32` is how
many ranges it owns; all group records come first, then all ranges, 20
bytes each — `{material id, start index, index count, min vertex, max
vertex}`.

**Result: `brad`'s bridge triangles went 55 → 0.** Group 0 yields 5,278
triangles with zero long-edge outliers. Structure found exactly as
documented: `brad` has 4 groups of 5/5/5/4 ranges, `brad_head_lod` has 1
group of 1 range.

**The group offset is SEARCHED, not computed.** The spec places the groups
"after the channel array (and after the flag-bit-1 arrays when present)"
without stating those arrays' size, so there is no offset to compute.
`MeshBlock::parse()` scans 16-byte-aligned candidates and accepts only one
satisfying every invariant at once: ranges contiguous from 0, covering the
index buffer exactly, and `minVertex ≤ maxVertex < vertex count`. Four
simultaneous constraints are not passed by accident. Same technique as the
pre-header pinning in §9.7 and the geometry-magic search in §4.2.

**Two traps, both of which cost a failed attempt here:**

1. **Contiguity runs across ALL ranges in group order — it does not restart
   per group.** Reading "ranges contiguous from 0" as per-group and
   requiring each group to begin at 0 rejects every multi-group mesh.
   `brad`'s 19 ranges form one continuous partition 0…12,373 spanning all
   four groups.
2. **A group is therefore a contiguous SLICE of the buffer, not an
   independent full copy of the model.** Requiring every group to cover the
   whole buffer also rejects everything.

Both failures presented identically — "groups not located" — which is worth
knowing: a validator strict enough to be trustworthy is also strict enough
to reject the truth if one of its premises is wrong.

**Third trap, flagged by Team A and taken on trust rather than rediscovered:**
on multi-channel meshes the range vertex bounds are relative to the
**largest** channel, not channel 0. This reader bounds against the largest.

### 9.11 `sr3rig` (`.rig_pc` skeletons) — reader complete and fully validated

New library `include/sr3rig/`, `src/rig.cpp`. Header, per-bone hash table,
bone array (name, model-space rest position, rotation triple, parent), and
the attachment/IK-target array. Every published statistic reproduces
exactly:

| Check | Measured | Spec |
|---|---|---|
| Rigs parsed | **585 / 585**, 0 failures | 585 |
| Bones total | **22,274** | 22,274 |
| Hash == engine hash of lowercased name | **585 / 585** rigs | 22,274/22,274 |
| Bone count range | **1 … 109** | 1 … 109 |
| Rigs with attachments | **286 / 585** | 286/585 |
| Attachment quaternions unit ±10% | **12,473 / 12,480** | 12,473/12,480 |
| Rotation components within ±π | **66,685 / 66,822** | 117 bones excepted |

`parse()` enforces the tree invariants (parent < child, parents in range)
because the spec confirms them across all 585 rigs. The **rotation triple
is surfaced raw and never converted to a matrix** — its convention (Euler
order vs axis-angle) is OPEN, spec §10 item 1.

### 9.12 Bind-pose skinning: what it is worth, and a claim I overstated (resolved in §9.13)

**First, why "bind-pose skinning" is not a milestone by itself.** Skinning
evaluates `v' = Σ wᵢ · (Poseᵢ · InverseBindᵢ) · v`. In bind pose
`Poseᵢ == Bindᵢ`, so every product is the identity and `v' == v` exactly.
A mesh "skinned in bind pose" is pixel-identical to the same mesh drawn
with no skinning. Wiring a skinning shader to produce the same image would
have been a fake milestone; the real test is whether the two formats agree.

**They did not agree at first, and the cause was a coordinate mismatch —
resolved in §9.13.** Measured on `brad`:

```
rig  bbox: 1.340 × 1.706 × 1.126   X[-0.67 0.67] Y[-1.71 0.00] Z[-0.13 1.00]
mesh bbox: 1.385 × 1.735 × 0.404   X[-0.69 0.69] Y[-0.01 1.72] Z[-0.22 0.19]
```

X matches closely and **Y matches under negation** (rig Y spans [-1.71, 0]
where mesh Y spans [0, 1.72]), but Z does not — 1.126 against 0.404. The
skeleton drawn over the mesh confirms it visually: it does not line up.

**A CORRECTION TO AN EARLIER CLAIM OF MINE, recorded because the error is
the instructive part.** A mesh↔rig cross-check (do vertices weighted to
bone B sit near bone B's rest position?) returned 1.12× against control and
a nearest-bone rank test of 1/422 (0.2%), below chance. I reported that as
evidence that blend indices do not index directly into the rig bone array —
i.e. that a bone palette indirection exists.

**That conclusion was not established.** Two independent causes could
produce that failure — wrong indices, or a coordinate-space mismatch — and
I attributed it to one without ruling out the other. Any nearest-bone test
across a mismatched space fails regardless of whether the indices are
direct, so the test could not discriminate. The palette hypothesis may
still be correct (max blend index 61 against 94-bone rigs is suggestive),
but it is unproven and was reported with more confidence than the evidence
carried.

*The general form, worth keeping alongside §3's other measurement lessons:*
**a failed test with two plausible causes is evidence about neither until
one is eliminated.** Same family as the half-float plausibility band in
§9.8 — both are cases of a measurement that cannot distinguish the
hypotheses it is being asked to decide between.

### 9.13 RESOLVED: the transform, and why the bounding-box approach misled me

Team A resolved both blockers; both were re-verified here before adoption.

**The transform is `mesh = (rig.x, −rig.y, −rig.z)`** — a plain 180° rotation
about X. No scale, no translation.

**The Z "mismatch" I measured was one bone.** `brad`'s rig contains a bone
named `camera` at (0, 0, 1) — a camera helper a metre in front of the
character, parented to nothing. That single bone accounted for the entire
rig Z extent of 1.126. Excluding it, rig Z is [−0.126, 0.100] against mesh
Z [−0.219, 0.185]: a clean match needing nothing beyond the sign flips.

**Verified independently here** rather than taken on trust, and both
measures moved sharply in the right direction:

| Measure | Before transform | After |
|---|---|---|
| Mean distance, vertex → its own bone | 1.9607 | **0.6831** (2.9× better) |
| Rank test (nearest bone to a weight cluster's centroid is that bone) | 1/422 (0.2%) | **63/422 (14.9%)** |

14.9% against a chance rate of ~1.06% for 94-bone rigs is ~14× above
chance. It is not 100% and should not be: a joint sits at the *end* of a
limb while the skin weighted to it spans the whole segment, so the nearest
bone to a cluster centroid is frequently a neighbour. Team A gives ~0.10–
0.14 m as the expected median residual for a correct skin, with helper
bones (twist, spinebend, handprop) scoring worse by design.

**BLEND INDICES ARE DIRECT — there is no palette indirection.** Team A
tested constant offsets −6…+6 with independently refit transforms across
six characters; shift 0 wins cleanly. My §9.12 retraction was the right
call, and the answer it was hedging toward is simply "no indirection, the
original mapping was fine."

**The methodology lesson, which is the part worth carrying.** I tried to
identify the transform by comparing **bounding boxes**, and that is what
produced the phantom Z discrepancy: helper and attachment bones sit
*deliberately* outside the mesh volume, so a bbox comparison will always
show a mysterious scale error that is really one outlier. **Fit by
correspondence, not by extent.** The blend indices already say which bone
owns which vertices — take the weighted centroid of a bone's own vertices
and match it against that bone's rest position. That turns a vague
shape-matching problem into a per-bone score that can actually be
validated, and it is robust to outliers because each bone is scored
separately.

This is the same failure family as §3's newest bullet: my bbox measurement
had two candidate explanations (wrong axis convention vs one outlier bone)
and could not distinguish them, so it was never going to decide the
question.

**Also now CONFIRMED (was HIGH CONFIDENCE):** rig rest positions are
model-space, not parent-relative accumulation — median residual 3.04
accumulating down the parent chain versus 0.126 using the stored vector
as-is. `sr3rig` already reads them as model-space, so no change was needed.

**Still open / parked:** the rotation-triple convention (needed for real
posing, not for bind pose), and keyframe animation — which needs the
`.anim_pc` payload, one of the items the user explicitly parked. **Do not
start animation without new authorisation.**

### 9.14 Making skinning falsifiable WITHOUT `.anim_pc`: the synthetic-pose test

Bind pose is the identity (§9.12), so it cannot fail. `purrsian-44`
proposed the way around that: author a pose **by hand** — rotate one bone
and its descendants by a fixed angle about that bone's own rest position —
and check the deformation structurally. No keyframe data, so the parked
`.anim_pc` item stays parked. Built as
`tools/validation/validate_pose.cpp`.

**Why it is possible at all, and what it therefore cannot decide.** The
rotation convention is OPEN, so there are no bind *rotations* available.
The test does not need them. With bind transforms taken as pure
translations `T(p_i)`, every bone in the rotated subtree shares one
skinning matrix:

```
Pose_i * InverseBind_i = T(p)*R*T(-p)*T(p_i) * T(-p_i) = T(p)*R*T(-p)
```

— "rotate about the joint", containing no bind rotation. So the test
**sidesteps the open convention and cannot decide it either.** It tests
blend indices, blend weights, the parent hierarchy, and the §9.13
coordinate transform. Nothing more.

**Every metric is run twice: real indices, then deliberately scrambled
ones** (`b -> (7b+13) mod boneCount`). Without that control the test is
just a picture that looks plausible.

**The first run was a failure, and the control is what proved it.** Real
and scrambled scored alike, which by §3's rule makes the result evidence
about neither. Four separate bugs, all mine:

| Bug | Symptom | Why it fooled the eye |
|---|---|---|
| No renormalisation after a lane is dropped | 332 zero-weight vertices "moved" | The vertex collapses toward the origin by exactly the missing weight — looks like deformation |
| Stretch measured as a **ratio** on near-degenerate edges | Max stretch **328.28x, identical in both runs** | A 0.001-long edge whose ends separate by 0.33 reports 328x; the number described the edge, not the pose |
| Coherence measured over "moved at all" (`d > 1e-5`) | 753 components | A vertex with 0.01 weight twitches; those stragglers shatter the count in *both* runs |
| Adjacency built only from draw group 0 | Coherence understated | A limb vertex no group-0 triangle references has no edges, so it counts as its own component |

An identical max in both arms is the tell worth remembering: **if a
statistic does not move when you scramble the input it supposedly
measures, it is measuring something else.**

**Result after the fixes** (45° about Z at `l-upperarmtwist1`, an 18-bone
subtree):

| Mesh | Coherence, real | Coherence, scrambled | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `brad` | **67.3%** | 19.1% | 3.5x |
| `brute_flamethrower` | **74.9%** | 17.3% | 4.3x |
| `nightblade` | 7.0% | 3.5% | 2.0x |

**Which metrics actually earn their place — only one of five.**

* **M1** (zero-weight vertices must not move) and **M2** (vertices fully
  inside the subtree preserve their radius to the pivot) both come out
  **clean — 0, and ~2e-5% — but they come out clean under SCRAMBLED
  indices too.** They validate the arithmetic, not the data. Reporting
  them as skinning evidence would be the §9.12 mistake again.
* **M4** (max edge stretch) and **M5** (max absolute tear) are dominated by
  a single outlier edge and barely separate the two arms. Void as stated.
* **M3b** (largest connected component / limb vertices) is the only one
  that discriminates, and it does so 3.5–4.3x.

**The honest reading:** on two of three characters the one sound metric
separates real from scrambled sharply and in the right direction, which is
real evidence that blend indices, weights, hierarchy and the §9.13
transform compose correctly. `nightblade` separates only 2x with both arms
low. That is **unexplained**. Plausible causes are many disconnected
material shells in its LOD0, or a mesh↔rig pairing this harness matched
only by name stem — and *I have eliminated neither, so no claim is made
about it.* Two of three is the finding; three of three is not.

Also incidentally confirmed: **no blend index exceeds the paired rig's bone
count** in any of the three (`OOR idx: -1`), and weights sum to 1 within 1%
for 5,044/5,044, 5,777/5,777 and 6,768/6,768 vertices.

**Still parked:** this does not open `.anim_pc`. A real pose needs the
rotation convention, which this test explicitly cannot supply.

#### 9.14.1 RESOLVED: `nightblade` was mesh topology, not skinning

§9.14 left `nightblade`'s 7.0% coherence with two candidate causes and
eliminated neither — the exact failure §3 warns about, so it was not
allowed to stand. The way out was a measurement taken with **no pose, no
skinning and no rig at all**: count the connected shells of the LOD0
surface itself. The two hypotheses predict opposite results, which is what
makes it a real test rather than another plausible story.

| Mesh | Shells in LOD0 | Referenced verts | Largest shell | Limb coherence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `brad` | 27 | 3,302 | 599 (18.1%) | 67.3% |
| `brute_flamethrower` | 53 | 3,796 | 607 (16.0%) | 74.9% |
| `nightblade` | **268** | 6,768 | 510 (**7.5%**) | **7.0%** |

**`nightblade`'s LOD0 is shattered into 268 disjoint shells averaging 25
vertices each** — against `brad`'s 27 shells averaging 122, roughly a
tenfold difference in fragmentation. Its limb coherence of 7.0% sits
essentially *at* the whole mesh's own largest-shell fraction of 7.5%: the
arm is about as connected as that surface allows anything to be. **The
coherence metric was measuring mesh topology, and the skinning pipeline is
exonerated.**

Note what makes this an elimination rather than another guess: the shell
count is computed without touching the rig, so it cannot be contaminated
by a bad mesh↔rig pairing. Had the pairing been the problem, `nightblade`
would have shown `brad`-like fragmentation with only its limb score
depressed. It shows the opposite.

**What is still NOT claimed.** Topology is *sufficient* to explain the
number, which is not the same as proving the name-stem pairing is correct
— both could be true at once, and the pairing remains unverified. It is
simply no longer needed to explain anything. Supporting this reading: the
real-vs-scrambled ratio stays at 2.0x in the correct direction (7.0% vs
3.5%), where a genuinely mismatched rig would be expected near 1.0x.

**So the §9.14 headline is now 3 of 3, not 2 of 3** — with the third
carrying a ceiling its own geometry imposes. The correction runs in the
favourable direction, which is exactly why it was worth pinning down
rather than leaving as a caveat.

### 9.15 The rotation convention did not get answered — the field is not a rotation

Team A relayed (via `purrsian-44`) that the bone record's `+0x14` triple,
which `spec-rig-format.md` §4 calls a **"rest rotation"** with its
convention marked OPEN in §10 item 1, is not a rotation at all: it is the
**negated parent-relative offset**, fully derivable from data already in
the record.

**Their updated spec never landed.** Both copies on disk —
`TEAM A/spec-rig-format.md` and `TEAM B/spec-rig-format.md`, same
timestamp — still read *"HIGH CONFIDENCE — a rotation in radians (Euler or
axis-angle); OPEN — which convention"* at line 64, and §10 item 1 still
lists the convention as open. So this was verified from scratch rather
than adopted, as every relayed correction has been.

Harness: `tools/validation/validate_rotfield.cpp`. Identity under test:

```
child : triple == -(restPosition - parent.restPosition)
root  : triple == -restPosition
```

| Set | Match at 1e-5 | Max error | Wrong-parent control |
|---|---|---|---|
| Child bones | **20,564 / 20,564 (100%)** | 3.8e-06 | 2.61% |
| Root bones | **1,710 / 1,710 (100%)** | 0.0 | 0.41% |
| **Components beyond ±π** | **117 / 117 (100%)** | 3.8e-06 | 3.42% |

**CONFIRMED, and Team A's figures reproduce exactly.**

**The third row is the one that settles it, and it was sitting in the spec
the whole time.** §4 recorded 117 of 22,274 components exceeding ±π, all
in vehicle rigs, and §7 offered *"plausibly rotor/spin bones stored beyond
one turn"* — a story that only makes sense if the field is an angle. The
two hypotheses split cleanly there: under the rotation reading those 117
are anomalies needing a special explanation; under the offset reading they
are simply long bones, and must obey the identity like everything else.
They obey it 117/117. The examples are unambiguous once seen —
`avatar_wings/l-wingc` at (−3.3933, 3.9743, −2.4434) and
`sp_vtol01_cs/engine_coverLB` at (−1.5775, 0.5348, −4.1548) are a wing and
an aircraft panel, metres from their parents. **A wing is not spinning; it
is just far away.**

Non-triviality was checked before trusting the match: median |triple| is
0.1105 and only 2,574 / 22,274 are ~zero, so ~88% of the population
carries a value large enough to have been wrong.

**Consequences for this codebase** (all applied):

* `Bone::restRotationRaw` → **`Bone::negatedParentOffset`**, with
  `parentRelativeOffset()` for the useful sign. A field name that asserts
  something false is worse than a vague one.
* `rig.h`'s header comment said orientation work "needs that convention
  resolved first". Replaced: **the 40-byte record contains no orientation
  at all.**
* **Bind pose as pure-translation composition is not a simplification
  awaiting a better answer — it is exact.** §9.14's model was right, and
  the 3/3 result rests on firmer ground than when it was reported. Nothing
  to redo.
* §9.14's caveat that the synthetic-pose test "is structurally blind to the
  rotation convention" still stands but no longer matters: there is no
  convention for it to be blind to.
* Real orientation data does exist in this format — in the **attachment
  array**, whose records carry genuine unit quaternions (12,473/12,480
  unit within 10%). Useful for mounting a prop to a bone. It is not in the
  bone array.

**What this does NOT unlock.** Per-frame skeletal animation still needs
per-bone rotation over time, which exists only in the `.anim_pc` keyframe
payload — **still parked, still needs the user directly.**

**The methodology lesson, which is Team A's to claim:** their original
"rest rotation" reading rested on *every component within ±π*. That is
true of rotations in radians **and** of bone offsets in metres, because
human limbs are short — a range check that cannot distinguish two
hypotheses is evidence for neither. This is §3's standing lesson again,
and note where the disconfirming case was: **the vehicle-rig exceptions
were recorded in their own spec at the time and not followed up.** The
refutation was already written down. Worth asking, of any long-standing
OPEN item, whether its own documentation already contains the anomaly that
breaks it.

### 9.16 A synthetic suite for `sr3rig` — and mutation-testing the suite itself

`sr3mesh` and `sr3rig` were the two readers with no self-contained tests,
which made them the largest untested surface in the project — and `sr3rig`
had just had a public field renamed (§9.15) with nothing but a real-data
sweep behind it. `tests/synthetic_rig_test.cpp`, wired into
`CMakeLists.txt` as `synthetic_rig_test`.

**Fixtures are built from the spec's stated layout, never from
`src/rig.cpp`.** This is not pedantry; the project has paid for ignoring it
once. The `.ctdg_pc` `sourceNameTruncated` bug survived a green suite
because the synthetic fixture had inherited the reader's own misreading —
a fixture derived from the parser only ever proves the parser agrees with
itself. Two checks here are anchored to values computed independently *in
the test file*:

* the name hash is recomputed from the algorithm as written in
  `spec-vpp-container.md` §2.2, so a drift in `vpp::hash` fails the test
  rather than being mirrored by it;
* the `+0x14` field is written as `pos(parent) − pos(bone)` per spec §4
  from positions chosen arbitrarily in the fixture, so the reader must
  invert it correctly — the guard the §9.15 rename was missing.

**Ten tests:** round-trip, the parent-offset identity, hash table (with a
deliberately mixed-case bone name, so a reader that skips the lowercase
fold fails), `findBone` case-insensitivity, padding, the `+0x2C` detail
index, six rejection cases, no-attachment rigs (260/585 shipped), multi-root
rigs (275/585), and a bone whose offset exceeds π — the vehicle case from
§9.15, now a regression guard so nobody re-reads that field as an angle.

**The fixture uses THREE bones on purpose.** `0x50 + 3×4 = 0x5C` is not
8-aligned, so it exercises spec §3's pad-to-8 rule. An even bone count
would let a reader that forgot the padding pass anyway — the test would
have been decorative.

#### The suite passed on the first run, which is exactly when to distrust it

A test that has never failed has not been shown to be capable of failing.
So the reader was deliberately broken, one mutation at a time:

| Mutation | Caught? |
|---|---|
| Read `+0x14` from `+0x18` | **Yes** |
| Drop the pad-to-8 before the bone array | **Yes** — 8 failures |
| Read the parent index from `+0x1C` | **Yes** — 9 failures |
| Read the attachment quaternion from `+0x24` | **Yes** |
| Hash the stored spelling instead of the lowercased name | **No — and correctly so** |

**The last row is the interesting one.** It looks like a hole and is not:
`vpp::hashFilename` folds case internally, so the `lowercased()` call in
`rig.cpp` is redundant and removing it changes no behaviour. **An uncaught
mutation that is semantically equivalent is not a test gap** — but the only
way to know which kind it was was to go and read the hash function. An
uncaught mutation is a question, not a verdict.

**Two defects in my own work, found only because the mutation run happened:**

1. *The suite detected a broken reader by crashing.* Dropping the pad made
   `parse()` reject a valid fixture; the exception escaped `main` and the
   process fast-failed with `0xC0000409` and no message. A detection, but
   an illegible one — and a grep for `CHECK FAILED` found nothing, so the
   mutation initially looked **uncaught**. Fixed with a `run()` wrapper
   that reports an unexpected `FormatError` on a valid fixture as a normal
   failure.
2. *Two mutations never applied at all.* The `-replace` patterns did not
   match the real source (I guessed `hashFilename(lowered)`; it is
   `hashFilename(lowercased(bone.name))`), so a run on **unmutated** code
   printed "all tests passed" and would have been recorded as "mutation
   not caught". Every mutation now asserts that the text actually changed
   before its result is trusted.

Both are the same failure in different clothes: **a negative result from a
test that never ran is indistinguishable from a negative result from a test
that ran and passed, unless you check.** Same family as §3's other
measurement lessons.

**One self-inflicted scare worth recording:** reverting the mutations via
PowerShell `Get-Content -Raw` + `WriteAllText` corrupted `src/rig.cpp`'s
encoding — Windows PowerShell 5.1 read the UTF-8 file as ANSI, so every
`§` came back as `Â§` and the file grew 6,827 → 6,876 bytes. Comments and
error strings only, but it is corruption. Restored byte-exact from a backup
and verified byte-identical. **Round-trip text through PowerShell only with
an explicit encoding on both ends**, or use `Copy-Item` — the same class of
tooling trap as the `sed`/`perl` newline mangling in §3.

### 9.17 A synthetic suite for `sr3mesh` — and the mutation that exposed the fixture

`tests/synthetic_ccmesh_vertex_test.cpp`, wired in as
`synthetic_mesh_vertex_test`. With §9.16 this closes the last of the
project's untested readers: **every format library now has a self-contained
suite that runs without game data.**

Nine tests, fixtures built from `spec-vertex-format.md` rather than from
`src/mesh_block.cpp`: the §2 pre-header and `0x70` header, the §3 channel
record, the §4 g-segment walk (check value → align 16 → index buffer → each
channel aligned to 16 → align 4 → check value, totalling the declared
g-length), the §5 stride law, the §6 element encodings, and §8's strips and
draw ranges.

Two are there because the spec establishes them *with a control* and a
reader could plausibly invert them:

* **A weight lane is zero exactly when its index lane is 255**
  (70,054/70,054 in the population; control 0.1498). The fixture satisfies
  it by construction, so reading the two fields from swapped offsets breaks
  the agreement.
* **Texture coordinates are signed** — the unsigned reading differs by a
  *wrap*, not a rescale, so a negative coordinate is the whole test.

**The slope, not the bases.** Spec §5 is explicit that the per-code bases
are *measured* and only the 4-bytes-per-texcoord-set slope is predictive,
so `testStrideLawSlope` walks codes 0, 2 and 3 across texcoord counts 0–3
and asserts each increment costs exactly 4. Asserting the bases would have
been circular.

**Alignment is exercised, not assumed.** `testAlignmentActuallyExercised`
uses three indices — 6 bytes, not a multiple of 16 — so the pad before the
channel data is load-bearing. A fixture whose sizes happened to be
16-aligned would pass with the alignment removed.

#### The mutation run found a hole in the fixture, not the reader

Six deliberate reader bugs, all caught **after one fix**:

| Mutation | Caught? |
|---|---|
| Read texture coordinates unsigned, **u lane** | **No → then yes** |
| Read texture coordinates unsigned, **v lane** | Yes |
| Skip the trailing check-value bookend | Yes |
| Drop the align-to-16 before channel data | Yes — 7 failures |
| Wrong UBYTE4N divisor (128 instead of 255) | Yes — 2 failures |
| Read blend weights from the index offset | Yes — 3 failures |

The first row is the lesson. The fixture had a negative coordinate in the
**v** lane only, so a mutation dropping the sign on **u** passed unnoticed.
The reader was correct throughout; the *test* was blind on one axis.
Generalised:

> **A property must be exercised in every lane that carries it.** One
> negative number proves the sign is handled *somewhere*, not everywhere.
> The same applies to any per-component decode — x/y/z, u/v, the four
> blend lanes: a fixture that varies only one component tests only one
> component, however many assertions are written about it.

That hole was invisible from the passing run. It took deliberately breaking
a single lane to find it, which is the whole argument for mutation-testing
a suite rather than trusting a green result — and note it argues for
mutating at a *finer grain* than feels necessary. A coarse "break the
texcoord decode" mutation would have been caught and would have certified a
fixture that was half-blind.

**One mutation was skipped, not passed:** `kTexcoordScale = 1024.0f` lives
in `mesh_block.h`, not the `.cpp` being patched, so the pattern never
matched and the run reported it as such rather than as a silent pass —
the guard added in §9.16 doing its job.

### 9.18 Per-material draw calls: a correction to my own framing, and a blocked mapping

I described this task to both the user and `purrsian-44` as *"a real
correctness gap, not a feature — group-0-only is a subset of the mesh."*
**That was wrong, and it was wrong from the spec, not from ambiguity.**

`spec-vertex-format.md` §8.2: *"The groups are level-of-detail steps... pick
one group, then issue one indexed draw per range in it."* Groups are LOD
levels. **Drawing group 0 alone is the correct behaviour** — it is the
highest-detail representation of the whole mesh, not a fragment of it. The
renderer was never dropping geometry. I read "group 0 only" as "part of the
model" when §8.2 says plainly that a group *is* the model at one detail
level, and the spec even warns about that exact misreading two paragraphs
later ("a group is a contiguous *slice*... not an independent full copy").

I had already recorded that trap in §9.10 after hitting it once. Reading my
own warning did not stop me restating it as a defect. **A lesson written
down is not the same as a lesson applied**, and the gap between them is
worth more attention than the original mistake.

#### What per-material drawing actually needs, and why it is blocked

Issuing one draw per range instead of one per group changes nothing
geometrically — `triangleListForGroup` already restarts the strip at every
range boundary, which is why bridge triangles are 0 (§9.10). The *only*
thing separate draws buy is **binding different state per range**, i.e. a
texture per material. That needs `materialId → texture`, and that mapping
is **not established**.

Spec §8.2 says the range's `+0x00` "indexes the material set". The material
block (`spec-geometry-format.md`) offers a flat list of **texture names** —
a different kind of thing, since one material normally owns several
textures. `textureNames[materialId]` is a guess, so it was measured first
(`tools/validation/validate_material_map.cpp`, 549 meshes):

| Measurement | Result |
|---|---|
| Material ids dense from 0 | **549 / 549** |
| `max(materialId) < textureSlotCount` | 546 / 549 — **3 counterexamples** |
| `textureSlotCount % materialCount == 0` | 291 / 549 |
| …of those, meshes with only ONE material (trivially divisible) | **272** |
| **Multi-material meshes with an integer ratio** | **19 / 277 = 6.9%** |

**6.9% is chance.** A fixed number of texture slots per material is
refuted. `brad` is the clean illustration: **5 materials, 8 texture names**,
and the names say why —

```
[0] brad_sm_upper_d   [1] brad_sm_upper_n   [2] cloth_matte_02_sb
[3] skin_ca_02_sb     [4] reflection_01_sb  [5] brad_sm_lower_d
[6] brad_sm_lower_n   [7] leather_02_sb
```

— two `_d`/`_n` body pairs plus shared `_sb` surface maps. Materials
clearly *share* entries and take differing numbers of them. And the 3
meshes where `max(materialId) ≥ textureSlotCount` kill direct indexing
outright: there is no slot to point at.

The geometry block's array 2 (spec §8.2 calls arrays 2–3 "per-material
float data") does not supply the count either — `brad` has 5 materials
against array 2's 11 entries, `brute_flamethrower` 7 against 12,
`nightblade` 7 against 11. *(Array 3 is more interesting: its count is 68
for `brad` and 94 for `nightblade` — exactly those characters' bone counts.
Noted, not claimed.)*

**Status: `materialId → texture` is OPEN.** Binding
`textureNames[materialId]` would render something plausible-looking and
wrong, which is worse than rendering untextured — the failure would be
invisible in a screenshot. Not implemented, and this is the honest reason
rather than a scoping decision.

**What was done instead** is in §9.19: per-range draw calls with each
material id given a distinct flat colour, which verifies the *partition*
on screen without asserting anything about textures.

### 9.19 Per-range draw calls, and the material partition CONFIRMED ON-SCREEN

Since `materialId → texture` is OPEN (§9.18), the renderer does the part
that is actually supported: **one indexed draw per draw range** (spec
§8.2's "issue one indexed draw per range in it"), with each material id
given a distinct flat colour. `MeshDrawMode::MaterialIdAsColour`,
`sr3_viewer mesh ... --mode material`.

A colour rather than a texture is the whole point. Binding
`textureNames[materialId]` would produce a plausible-looking character and
a wrong one, and **that failure would be invisible in a screenshot** —
the worst kind, because the verification method cannot see it. A flat
colour asserts only what is CONFIRMED: the buffer is partitioned into
ranges, each carrying a material id.

**Honest note on what the separate draws buy.** Geometrically, nothing:
`triangleListForRange` already restarts the strip at every boundary, so
the pixels are identical to the single-call path (§9.10). Separate draws
matter only because per-range state can now be bound. Every other draw
mode still issues one call, deliberately — splitting them would look like
progress and be none.

#### The result, which is corroboration rather than decoration

| Mesh | Materials | What the colours land on |
|---|---|---|
| `brad` | 5 | jacket+arms, trousers, gloves, shoes, hair |
| `nightblade` | 7 | hair, torso+arms, long coat, bracers+scabbard, trousers+boots, gloves, neck detail |

**Every boundary follows a garment or accessory edge.** Nothing in the
decode forces that. The material ids come out of a 20-byte record at an
offset this reader *searched* for rather than computed, and the ranges are
spans of an index buffer. That those spans coincide with where a clothing
seam falls is independent evidence the field is being read correctly — the
same shape of argument as the mesh↔rig cross-check in §9.11: two things
derived without reference to each other agreeing.

This also quietly corroborates **§9.14.1**. `nightblade`'s LOD0 was 268
disjoint shells against `brad`'s 27, which was the evidence that its 7.0%
limb coherence was topology rather than skinning. The material render
shows why: a separate coat, scabbard, bracers, gloves and boots are
*exactly* what a heavily fragmented surface looks like. A prediction made
for one reason, confirmed by a picture rendered for another.

#### A bug caught by looking at the output, not the exit code

The first render reported success and wrote a file called `--mode`. The
`mesh` sub-command takes its output path **positionally** at `argv[4]`, so
`--mode material --out file.png` made `"--mode"` the filename, left
`"material"` as a stray token, and the flag loop **silently ignored it** —
producing a *checker* image while being asked for material colours. Exit
code 0, wrong picture: precisely the failure §3 already records from the
texture-index bug, and it went the same way — the return code was clean
and only opening the image revealed it.

Two guards added, because the tool should not have permitted this:

* the argument loop now **refuses** an unrecognised token instead of
  dropping it;
* an output path beginning with `--` is rejected with a message saying the
  path is positional.

Both verified: the exact bad invocation now exits 2. **A tool that silently
ignores what it does not understand will eventually produce a confident
wrong answer**, and the cost of a catch-all `else` is one branch.

### 9.20 LOD selection — and "the groups are LOD levels" upgraded to CONFIRMED ON-SCREEN

`spec-vertex-format.md` §8.2 marks the *structure* of draw groups CONFIRMED
but flags the interpretation as **"HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred that the
groups are LOD levels specifically, from the shrinking index counts and the
single-group LOD meshes."** Shrinking index counts are consistent with LOD
levels — and also with a mesh split into progressively smaller *parts*, or
with groups holding some other partition. The inference was never tested;
it was reasonable, which is a different thing.

`--group N` on `sr3_viewer mesh` selects the group (`MeshRenderer::upload`
takes `drawGroup`, default 0), which makes the question answerable by
looking.

**`brad`, four groups:**

| Group | Indices | Triangles | Materials | What it renders as |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 8,424 | 5,278 | 5 | the character |
| 1 | 2,625 | 1,517 | 5 | the character, simplified |
| 2 | 884 | 478 | 5 | the character, clearly faceted |
| 3 | 440 | 218 | **4** | the character, coarse — hair dropped |

**Each group is a complete, self-contained character.** Same pose, same
proportions, same silhouette, same five materials in the same places, with
detail falling away — at group 2 the hair is a single strip and the hands
are blocky; at group 3 the hair material is gone entirely, which is exactly
why the range counts read `5 5 5 4`.

That is what settles it. **A part-wise split would have rendered a
fragment** — a torso, or a limb, or the character with pieces missing. Every
group renders the whole figure. Combined with the monotone 8,424 → 2,625 →
884 → 440 cascade (roughly 3× per step, the standard LOD ratio), the LOD
reading is now **CONFIRMED ON-SCREEN** rather than inferred, and the
competing "these are parts" reading is refuted by the pictures.

Worth noting what made this cheap: the material colouring from §9.19 was
built for a different purpose, and it is what makes the comparison legible
— the five materials staying in their places across four levels of detail
is far more convincing than four grey silhouettes would have been. The
per-group index counts are printed next to the render (`lod : g0=… g1=…`)
so the numbers sit beside the picture instead of relying on the eye.

**What is deliberately NOT implemented:** choosing a group automatically
from camera distance. That needs the distance thresholds, which are not in
this file and are not in any spec this project holds. Selecting a group is
supported; deciding *which* one the engine would pick is not, and guessing
a threshold would be inventing data. `--group` exposes the choice and
leaves it to the caller.

### 9.21 Breadth sweep: a proxy corrected, a hard boundary, and a claim I could not reproduce

`tools/validation/validate_pipeline.cpp` runs the whole chain — container →
material block → geometry block → Mesh sub-block → channel decode → draw
groups → triangle expansion — and reports failures rather than successes,
broken down **by layout code**, because "561 meshes passed" hides that 546
of them are the same code path.

#### 1. The bridge metric was a proxy, and it needed its own control

The first run reported **197 of 546 code-3 meshes with "bridge" triangles**
and I nearly wrote that up as a partition defect. It is not one.

Almost every flagged mesh was a `*_head_lod`, and spec §8.2 records that
those have **exactly one group holding exactly one range**. *A single-range
mesh has no boundary to bridge across* — so whatever the metric was
counting, it could not be a partition error. The long-edge test is a
**proxy** for "two unrelated pieces got joined", and a proxy has to be
checked against the thing it proxies for.

The measurement that means something is the **difference** between
expanding the buffer the wrong way and the right way:

| Code | Meshes | 1-range | whole-buffer → per-range | Removed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 3 | 0 | 170 → 50 | 70.6% |
| 1 | 3 | **3** | 8 → 8 | **0.0%** |
| 3 | 546 | 261 | 12,566 → **1,634** | **87.0%** |

**Code 1 is the control and it lands exactly where it must.** All three of
its meshes are single-range, so the partition has no boundary to act at and
removes precisely nothing — 0.0%, not "nearly nothing". Meanwhile respecting
the partition removes **87%** of long-edge triangles on code 3. The 1,634
that survive are 0.09% of 1.8M triangles and are concentrated in the 261
single-range meshes, where a partition error is impossible by construction.

**No partition failures found across 561 meshes.** The residual is geometry.
*Had I reported the first number, it would have been a false alarm on 197
meshes — generated entirely by a threshold tuned on body meshes being
applied to compact head meshes.*

#### 2. Vehicles are not reachable, and this is a format boundary

The point of sweeping vehicles was layout codes **100/101** — a rigid part
index where characters carry blend weights — which no render here has ever
exercised. `vehicles.vpp_pc` and `vehicles_preload.vpp_pc` contributed
**zero c/g pairs**: they contain no `.ccmesh_pc` at all.

```
vehicles.vpp_pc:  1749 .ccar_pc   744 .gcar_pc   744 .cvtf_pc
                   544 .cpeg_pc   480 .gpeg_pc   372 .str2_pc
```

**Vehicle geometry is `.ccar_pc`/`.gcar_pc`**, a separate carrier with no
reader in this project (`spec-vehicle-geometry.md` covers it). So codes
100/101 are unreachable through the `.ccmesh_pc` path, and rendering a
vehicle is not breadth work at all — it needs a new format library. Flagged
rather than started: that is a new line of work, not a continuation of this
one.

#### 3. Material count at "outer sub-header +0x0C" — NOT reproduced

Relayed from Team A: the material count is a `u16` at *outer sub-header
`+0x0C`*, equal to `1 + max(materialId)` in 428/428. Every relayed claim
gets verified here before adoption (§9.15 is why), and **this one did not
reproduce.**

Reading `+0x0C` of the `0x70` header — the same header whose `+0x04` is the
group count, which is what "outer sub-header" most naturally means here —
gives **0 / 549**, with the field reading **zero on every mesh**.

Rather than guess a second offset, I searched for it, using `1 +
max(materialId)` as an oracle computed purely from the draw ranges:

* every `u16` offset from −0x80 to +0x100 around the Mesh sub-block;
* **multi-material meshes only** — 272 of 549 have a single material, so
  their oracle value is `1`, and a `u16` reading `1` is everywhere in a
  header. Including them floors every offset near 50% and buries the
  signal. *(The uncorrected scan's "best" offset was 54.6% against a ~46%
  chance floor — the same wrong-denominator trap spec §8.2 records for its
  own vertex-bound check.)*

Corrected, the best offset in the window is **+208 at 36.8% of 277**. No
offset comes close to the population agreement the claim describes.

**This does not make the claim wrong.** It makes it unlocatable from the
spec text: "outer sub-header" is not pinned to a base, and the field is not
within ±256 bytes of the Mesh sub-block. The useful finding for Team A is
that an independent implementer, holding the same document, cannot find the
field — which is a documentation defect whether or not the offset is right.
**Not wired into any reader**; the material-id range check continues to come
from the draw ranges themselves, which needs no such field.

### 9.22 The material binding, found — and why my search missed it
