§9.21 recorded a failure to reproduce the material-count field. The claim
was right; **my reading of "outer sub-header" was wrong, and so was the
window I searched.**

"Outer sub-header" is the **`0x424BD00D` geometry sub-header**, not the Mesh
block's `0x70` header. It sits *before* the Mesh sub-block — past the
material block and its 16-byte pad — which is why scanning ±256 bytes
around the Mesh block could never have found it. This reader already tracks
that exact position as `GeometryBlock::offset()`, so verifying it here
cross-checks their derivation rather than re-implementing it:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Magic `0x424BD00D` at `GeometryBlock::offset()` | **549 / 549** |
| `u16(+0x0C) == 1 + max(materialId)` | **549 / 549** |
| Control, `+0x0E` instead — all meshes | 272 / 549 |
| Control, `+0x0E` — **multi-material only** | **0 / 277** |
| Real field — multi-material only | **277 / 277** |

**The control is the part worth reading twice.** The neighbouring `u16`
matches 272 times across the whole population and **zero** times once
single-material meshes are removed — because those 272 *are* the
single-material meshes, whose oracle value is `1`. Same denominator effect I
flagged in §9.21, now visible as a clean separation: the real field is
277/277 exactly where the control is 0/277. **That is what a pinned offset
looks like**, and neither number means much without the other.

*Lesson for my own search, not theirs:* an oracle-driven offset scan is only
as good as its window. I bounded ±256 bytes around the structure I already
knew, which quietly assumed the field was near it. The field was in the
parent structure. **A scan that finds nothing has ruled out its window, not
the hypothesis** — and I should have said "not in this window" rather than
letting "not reproduced" carry the weight it did in §9.21's heading.

#### The binding itself — textures are not indexed at all

Every refuted hypothesis in §9.18 shared one assumption: that `materialId`
selects a texture *by position*. It does not. Each per-material record holds
a run of **12-byte entries**:

| Offset | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `+0x00` | `u32` **byte offset** into the mixed-case name blob at `subheader + 0x88` — not the lowercase list in the material block |
| `+0x04` | `u32` sampler/parameter name hash |
| `+0x08` | `u32` slot index, sequential from 0 |

Slot 0 is diffuse (`_d`/`_dp`, 1261/1266), slot 1 normal (`_n`, 1266/1266,
constant hash `0x2808EB90`), slot 2 the surface-type material
(`Cloth_Matte`, `Skin_Ca`, `Metal`…, constant hash `0xDFE71DA8` in
1251/1264).

**This retroactively explains §9.18's counter-example.** `brad`'s 5 materials
against 8 texture names, with a `_d`/`_n` pair shared across two materials,
looked like an irregularity that killed every slice-based reading. It is the
format working normally: materials share a diffuse and normal pair and
differ in their slot-2 surface type. The thing that refuted the simple
readings was the same thing the real structure predicts.

**Implementer caveat, carried forward:** the run's start offset *within* the
record varies between meshes (`+0x64`, `+0x04`, `+0x74`, `+0x54`, …) — it
must be located by its own constraint (first position where slot indices
read 0,1,2,… consecutively *and* every name offset lands on a real string
start), not hardcoded. If a material ever renders with an obviously wrong
texture, **suspect the run-location heuristic first, not the entry layout.**

#### 9.22.1 REQUIRED FIX to the run-location heuristic — read before implementing

Team A found a defect in that heuristic before anything here was built on
it. **Accept a located run only if `run length ≥ 2` AND the parameter hash
is non-zero. If either fails, report NO BINDING** — do not return whatever
the search picked.

The evidence, and why the original number was hollow: across 10 archives
**3,954 / 3,954** material records "find a run", which looks conclusive and
is not. Split by run length, it is two different populations:

| Run length | Positions tying for best | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| ≥ 2 | exactly one, **1,285 / 1,285** | unambiguous |
| == 1 | **six or more, in all 300 cases** | no information at all |

The 300 single-entry cases were being resolved by picking arbitrarily among
six-plus equally valid candidates. They also carry parameter hash
`0x00000000` in 290/300 — where a real slot carries a real constant (slot 1
is always `0x2808EB90`) — and resolve to `missing.tga`,
`flat-normalmap_n.tga`, `normal_blank_n.tga`. **They are placeholder/LOD
meshes with no real binding to find**, not meshes a reader failed on.

**This is precisely the failure §9.18 refused to risk.** Without the guard,
those 300 would have bound an arbitrary neighbouring string — a wrong but
real-looking texture — and rendered a plausible character that is silently
incorrect. The check that would normally catch a rendering bug, *looking at
it*, is the one check blind to this. The guard converts it into a visible
"no binding", which is the whole point.

**Not yet verified here**, because nothing has been implemented to verify:
this reader adopts relayed claims only when code depends on them (§9.15,
§9.22). When texture binding is built, the run-location heuristic *and this
guard* get re-derived against the shipped archives first, and the
ambiguity count — how many positions tie — gets reported alongside the hit
rate, not instead of it.

**Status:** §9.18's blocker is lifted — `MeshDrawMode::Textured` can bind
real per-material textures instead of flat colours. Not yet implemented
here; the flat-colour path (§9.19) remains correct and still asserts only
what it can.

### 9.23 Turning the ambiguity lesson on this project's own search

§3's newest lesson — *a match rate without an ambiguity count is not a
measurement* — arrived from Team A's run-location defect (§9.22.1). A
lesson filed as something that happened to someone else is an anecdote, so
it was pointed at the nearest place this project does the same thing.

`sr3mesh` locates the draw-group array **by search** (§9.10), and
`mesh_block.h` asserted the invariants were *"strong enough that a wrong
offset cannot pass."* Reading the loop: it `break`s on the **first**
candidate that validates and never counts the rest. **That claim had never
been measured** — "we always find one" is silent on whether the one found
is the only one, which is exactly the shape that let 300 placeholder
records be resolved by arbitrary choice in §9.22.1.

`tools/validation/validate_groupsearch.cpp` replicates the search
independently — it does not call `MeshBlock`, so it cannot inherit the
reader's behaviour — and counts every candidate satisfying all invariants
rather than stopping at the first.

| Surviving candidates | Meshes |
|---|---|
| **exactly 1** | **549 / 549** |
| 2 or more | **0** |

**The claim holds, and is now evidence rather than confidence.** The header
comment has been rewritten to say which it is and to name the harness.

Worth being clear about what this did and did not change: **no bug was
found.** The reader was correct the whole time. What changed is that a
load-bearing assumption — first-match is safe — moved from asserted to
measured, at the cost of one harness. That is the right trade whenever a
structure is located by search rather than computed, and there are other
such places in this project (the pre-header offsets, §9.7; the material
count scan, §9.22) whose survivor counts have never been reported either.

*The honest footnote:* my own material-count scan in §9.21 reached the
right conclusion — that I had not found the field — only because its output
happened to be shaped as a ranked list of candidates, so the absence of a
clear winner was visible. That was the output's shape saving the
conclusion, not a check designed in. The discipline was not actually in
place; it is now, at least here.

### 9.24 Real per-material textures — §9.18's blocker closed, on screen

`sr3geometry::MaterialBindings` (`include/sr3geometry/material_binding.h`,
`src/material_binding.cpp`) resolves a draw range's material id to its
actual textures, and `MeshRenderer::drawTextured` binds one per range.
`sr3_viewer mesh … --mode textured` now renders shipped characters with
their real materials.

**Verified before any of it was written** — §9.22.1 required exactly that,
via `tools/validation/validate_material_binding.cpp` over 549 meshes:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Runs found == declared material count | **546 / 546**, delta histogram is a single `+0` bucket |
| Meshes with no run passing the guard | 3 — placeholder, correctly **no binding** |
| Resolved names also in the material block's independently parsed list | **6,064 / 6,064** |
| Slot 1 parameter hash `0x2808EB90` | 1,831 / 1,834 |
| Slot 0 name ends `_d`/`_dp` (multi-material meshes) | 1,544 / 1,565 |

The cross-check is the load-bearing one. The mixed-case names come from a
blob at `subheader + 0x88` reached by byte offset; the material block's
lowercase list is parsed by a **different reader from a different part of
the file**. Complete agreement across 6,064 lookups is not something a
wrong base offset or a mis-sized entry could produce.

**A denominator effect, for the third time in one session.** Slot 0's
`_d`/`_dp` rate reads **84.8%** over the whole population and **98.7%**
over multi-material meshes — because single-material placeholder meshes
bind `missing.tga` and score 4.1%. Team A quoted 99.6%; my first figure
looked like a discrepancy with their work and was two populations in one
average. Checking the split before reporting it is now reflex, and it has
paid three times (§9.21 chance floor, §9.22 control, here).

#### What the pictures show

`brad`: 5 materials over 8 texture names — a black suit, white shirt, tie,
an ID badge on the lapel, sunglasses, skin-toned hands. `nightblade`: 7
materials — red coat, grey armour, two crossed blades, strapped boots, belt
pouches. Every texture on the surface it belongs to.

This also settles §9.19's remaining question the same way §9.20 settled the
LOD one: the flat-colour render *showed* the partition was sensible; the
textured render shows the **binding** is, and the two agree — the garment
boundaries the colours found are exactly where the textures change.

#### Two deliberate refusals in the implementation

1. **A material whose texture fails to resolve renders in its flat material
   colour, never in a neighbouring material's texture.** Substituting the
   nearest available map would produce a finished-looking character that is
   quietly wrong — the exact failure *looking at the render* cannot catch.
   A coloured patch says plainly that something is missing.
2. **`MaterialBindings::parse` accepts only when the run count equals the
   declared material count.** A partial or over-long match means the search
   latched onto something that is not the per-material array, and binding
   most of a character correctly is worse than binding none of it, because
   it looks like success.

`MaterialBindings::located() == false` is a normal outcome, not an error:
placeholder and LOD meshes genuinely have no per-material binding. The
reader reports that rather than inventing one.

### 9.25 `sr3vehicle` — `.ccar_pc`, and a pre-existing gap it exposed

`include/sr3vehicle/vehicle.h`, `src/vehicle.cpp`. Deliberately a **small**
library, because `spec-vehicle-geometry.md` §1's central claim is that
`.ccar_pc` is not a new mesh format — it is an assembly container that
embeds the `.ccmesh_pc` chain this project already reads and adds a named
part hierarchy. So this reads the outer header and the part array and hands
everything else to the existing readers.

Validated against the spec's own published figures
(`tools/validation/validate_vehicle.cpp`):

| Measure | Result | Spec |
|---|---|---|
| `.ccar_pc` parsed | **372 / 372**, 0 failures | 393 exist |
| Parts | 9,536 | 9,951 |
| Part count range | 3 … 41 | 2 … 43 |
| Morph present / absent | 315 / 57 | 326 / 67 |
| `.gcar_pc` morph offset ≥ `.ccar_pc` size | **315 / 315** | all 326 |
| Transform row-major signature | **9,536 / 9,536** | 9,951/9,951 |
| …column-major **control** | 1,627 / 9,536 | 1,694 |
| Parent `-1` or `< count` | **9,536 / 9,536** | 9,951/9,951 |

372 of 393 because the remaining pairs live in archives not scanned here;
every proportion tracks (parts, morph split, type histogram, and the
column-major control at 17.1% against the spec's 17.0%).

**The cross-format check is the one that matters.** The `.gcar_pc`'s leading
`u32` must equal the embedded Mesh sub-block's check value — two structures
located independently in two different files. **205 / 205 exact.** Nothing
in either decoding refers to the other, and the vehicle header's `+0x04`
was not used to find the check value.

#### What this needed from `sr3geometry`, and why

Vehicles have **no material block at all** (absent 393/393), and
`GeometryBlock::parse` locates the `0x424BD00D` sub-header by searching near
`roundUp16(material block end)` — with no material block, there is nothing
to anchor to. `.ccar_pc` states the offset outright at header `+0x04`, so
`GeometryBlock::parseAt(content, subheaderOffset)` was added: the same walk,
entered at a stated position, throwing if the magic is not actually there.
`parse()` now locates and delegates, so there is one walk, not two.

#### The gap this exposed — NOT a vehicle problem

The embedded mesh parses in **205 / 372**. All 167 failures are a *single*
kind, and it is not vehicle-specific:

> *computed array layout did not land on a Mesh sub-block version-9 marker
> after the six arrays — the BlobA length field or the array alignment rules
> may not hold for this file*

The same error accounted for all 9 failures in §9.21's sweep of
`items.vpp_pc`. **This is a pre-existing `sr3geometry` six-array-walk
limitation that vehicles merely exposed at scale** (45% of vehicles against
75% of the items that hit it). The vehicle reader itself parses 372/372
with every invariant exact; nothing about the failures is in the `.ccar_pc`
layer.

**That makes the six-array walk the highest-value next target in this
project** — it now blocks roughly half of all vehicle geometry, and the
spec's own note that arrays 5/6's gate widths are unconfirmed is the
obvious place to start.

#### Deliberately not done

* **Materials.** The shared material block is absent in every vehicle, so
  there is no name list to bind (§7 leaves the source HYPOTHESIS/OPEN).
  Vehicles therefore cannot be textured the way §9.24 textures a character,
  and the reader says so rather than binding something plausible.
* **Bone binding.** Part transforms are relative to `.rig_pc` bones, matched
  by name hash, but the rig is referenced from a global vehicle-info table
  *not present in this file* — so the caller must supply it. `sr3rig` is a
  hard dependency of vehicle rendering.
* **The four hardcoded vehicles.** `truck_2dr_garbage01`, `sp_backhoe01`,
  `truck_2dr_tow01` and `car_2dr_muscle04` get flag `0x8000` set on specific
  hinged parts by the engine *constructor*, not by the file (§5). That is
  behaviour, not data, so `Vehicle::specialCaseNote()` reports it and
  applies nothing — a faithful reader and the engine genuinely differ here,
  and hiding that inside the parser would misrepresent the file.
* **Part-type names** for the rare enum values. Types 5, 7, 9–13, 15, 16,
  19–21, 26 occur at most 92 times each and the spec leaves them OPEN;
  `partTypeName()` returns `nullptr` for them rather than inventing labels.

### 9.26 The six-array walk bug — found, and two wrong answers on the way

§9.25 flagged the walk as the highest-value target: 167/372 vehicles and 9
items meshes failing to reach the Mesh sub-block. **Fixed. 372/372 vehicles,
561/561 characters and items, zero parse failures.**

#### The tool that made it tractable

An **independent oracle**: the Mesh check value equals the paired
`.gcar_pc`'s leading word, so the true sub-block can be located using *no
array arithmetic at all*. Searching for `u32(+0x00)==9 AND u32(+0x04)==gcar
leading word` found it in **372/372 with exactly one candidate each** — zero
ambiguity, so every failure had a known ground truth to diff against.

Also measured, and worth recording as a dead end others need not re-explore:
**a c-file-only search is not a viable fallback.** Version-9 alone gives
6–24 candidates per vehicle; adding "c-length fits the file and ≥ 0x80"
still leaves 1–13, unique in only 15 of 372. `GeometryBlock` cannot locate
the sub-block without the paired file. The arithmetic had to be fixed, not
routed around.

#### Wrong answer 1 — mine

The residual was a clean ±8 with all four array counts at zero, and ten
failing samples fitted `align8(blobEnd + 1)` *exactly*. Scored on the whole
population it got **185/372 — worse than the 205/372 it was replacing.**

Ten perfect fits, refuted. Same shape as Team A's keyframe model that
reproduced two files exactly, including a reversal symmetry, and still died
at scale.

#### Wrong answer 2 — a version split that wasn't

Every failing sample printed geometry version 42, which looked like the
discriminator. Measuring the **passing** set too: v42 205 passing, v42 167
failing. All 372 are v42. *A property shared by every failure is not a cause
unless the successes lack it* — and a list of failures can never show that.

#### Wrong answer 3 — Team A's first diagnosis

They reported the cause as the sub-header derivation, with "should take you
from 205/372 to 372/372". That entry offset — `u32(file + 0x04)` — was
already what `parseAt` used for every number reported. The **failure
signature** settled it: `parseAt` throws distinguishable errors for a bad
magic versus a bad walk, and all 167 were the walk, **zero** were the magic.
Redirected with that evidence; they re-tested against the oracle and agreed.

#### The actual bug

BlobA's content begins **one byte past the next 16-boundary** — a leading
NUL, a convention already recorded elsewhere in this format family — and the
declared length counts from there. That part the reader had right, via
`kBlobAContentPad`. What it had wrong was **pre-aligning the result to 16**:

```
was:  arraySpaceStart = roundUp16(blobDataStart + blobALength)
now:  arraySpaceStart =           blobDataStart + blobALength
```

`layOutArrays` *already* 16-aligns every populated array and already returns
`roundUp8(pos)` for the trailer. The extra rounding was redundant for
populated arrays and actively wrong when there were none — it rounded the
cursor past the 8-aligned landing site.

**Why it hid for so long, and why it was never vehicle-specific.** The walk
re-aligns before every array it actually visits, so the error is absorbed by
the first populated array. Vehicles have arrays 1–4 *entirely empty*, so
nothing re-aligns between the blob and the Mesh block and the error reaches
the landing site untouched. Vehicles are simply the one population that
cannot hide it — which is why the same bug also accounted for all 9
`items.vpp_pc` failures in §9.21, and why §9.25's instinct that a 45%-vs-rare
split was suspicious was right.

#### A test that was testing the reader, not the format

The fix broke three assertions in `synthetic_ccmesh_test.cpp`, and **the
test was wrong**. It asserted that with arrays 1–3 empty, all four arrays
report the *same* offset — which silently also assumed the array space began
16-aligned. It did, because the reader pre-aligned it. The assertion was
encoding the bug.

Its real intent — "no empty array consumes an alignment step" — is preserved
and now stated as the invariant that actually holds: empties share the
cursor, and the populated array sits **one** 16-alignment past it, not
three. This is §9.16's fixture lesson arriving in a new place: *a test
assertion can inherit the reader's convention just as a fixture can*, and
when a fix breaks a test the first question is which of the two encodes the
format.

#### Result

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Vehicle embedded mesh | 205 / 372 | **372 / 372** |
| Vehicle cross-reference check | 205 / 205 | **372 / 372** |
| Characters + items parse failures | 9 | **0** |
| Synthetic suites | 14 / 14 | **14 / 14** |

Textured character rendering is unchanged and still correct — checked
rather than assumed, since this touched the block every mesh flows through.

### 9.27 The slot index is not the role — a bug in my own API

§9.24 recorded "slot 0 diffuse, slot 1 normal, slot 2 surface" and
`MaterialBinding::diffuse()` was keyed on `slot == 0`. **That was an
over-generalization from character data, and on vehicles it returns the
wrong texture.** Team A flagged it; measured here before changing anything
(`tools/validation/validate_binding_roles.cpp`, characters and vehicles
tabulated separately as hash × slot).

| Parameter hash | Characters | Vehicles | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0x2808EB90` | slot 1 (**1,831**), slot 0 (2) | **slot 0** | **DIFFERENT** |
| `0x69B48F91` | slot 0 (978), slot 1 (2) | slot 0, slot 1 | same |
| `0xE848C9CA` | slot 2 | slot 2 | same |

**`0x2808EB90` is slot 1 on characters 1,831 times and slot 0 on
vehicles.** The slot index is only position-within-material; the role
travels with the hash. A `diffuse()` reading slot 0 would have handed the
renderer a **normal map** on vehicles — decoding to olive, looking like a
shading bug rather than a binding bug. Exactly the silently-plausible class
this reader exists to refuse, and it was mine.

**Fixed by keying on the hash**, with the confirmed constants measured
rather than assumed:

* `0x2808EB90` → normal map: names a `_n` texture in **1,833/1,833**
  character entries and 36/36 of the vehicle entries carrying it;
* `0x03B65AF7` → colour: `_d`/`_dp` in **854/854**;
* `0x69B48F91` → colour: `_d`/`_dp` in 701/980, the remainder placeholder
  meshes binding `missing.tga`.

`diffuse()` now returns **null** when a material carries none of the known
colour samplers, instead of falling back to slot 0. Vehicles legitimately
return null: their colour samplers are not among these, and vehicle paint
is believed to come from the `.cvtf_pc` customisation catalogue at runtime
rather than the model file — still a HYPOTHESIS (spec §7), so nothing is
invented for it.

**Character rendering is byte-identical after the change** — the same five
materials resolve to the same textures on `brad`. Hash-keying agrees with
slot-keying everywhere slot-keying was right, and refuses where it was
wrong. 14/14 suites green; the binding validator still reports 546/546 and
6,064/6,064.

#### Two premises in the relay that the measurement did not support

1. **"Vehicles have no material block at all"** — mine, in §9.25. Wrong as
   stated. Vehicles lack the material-*reference* block (the lowercase name
   list at file+0) but **do** carry the same mixed-case name blob at
   sub-header `+0x88`. Corrected.
2. **"The binding rule applies unchanged and finds runs on all 372
   vehicles"** — relayed, and **not what this reader does: 3 / 372** (now
   **1 / 372** after §9.34's name-start tightening removed two false
   acceptances). Not a
   defect. `MaterialBindings::parse` accepts only when the run count equals
   the declared material count, and vehicles report `materialCount` 36
   against 11–32 runs. That is open item #1 in the relay itself — the
   material↔run association is *not pinned* for vehicles — so the guard is
   refusing precisely the case nobody can yet attribute. **369 vehicles
   correctly report no binding rather than 11–32 runs that cannot be tied
   to a material.**

   *Sharpened by a later retraction (§9.28):* the "36 materials" figure was
   wrong semantics on a right field. Sub-header `+0x0C` is exactly
   `1 + max(materialId)` on `.ccmesh_pc`, but on vehicles it is only an
   **upper bound** — a vehicle declares a material set sized for the whole
   multi-part asset, larger than any single embedded mesh uses, and max id
   is strictly less than it in 86/86. So the equality the guard tests can
   **never** hold on a vehicle. That makes the refusal structural rather
   than a near-miss, and confirms the guard should NOT be relaxed to a
   bound: a bound would admit exactly the unattributable runs it exists to
   reject.

The second one is worth keeping as a pattern: *a guard doing its job looks
identical to a feature failing to work*, and only the reason distinguishes
them. Here the reason is documented open, so `located() == false` is the
honest answer and loosening the guard to raise the number would be
manufacturing a result.

### 9.28 The draw-range material field is packed 16:16

Relayed from Team A: the vehicle draw-range field at record `+0x00` is two
16-bit values, not one u32 —

```
materialId   = field & 0xFFFF
submeshIndex = field >> 16
```

— with the suggestion to mask **unconditionally** rather than branch per
format, *explicitly offered as a safety argument rather than a
measurement*: they had not checked whether the packing exists on
`.ccmesh_pc`.

That distinction was the whole reason to measure it. `sr3mesh` reads this
field as a plain u32, and §9.19's material partition plus §9.24's texture
binding are both built on it. If any character mesh carried non-zero high
bits, shipped behaviour was wrong.
`tools/validation/validate_materialid_packing.cpp`:

| Population | Ranges | Non-zero high half | Max raw | Max low | Max high |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Characters | 6,402 | **0** | 6 | 6 | 0 |
| Vehicles | 87,012 | **77,886** | 917,541 | 50 | 14 |

**Characters: zero, in every range.** So the earlier plain-u32 reading was
never wrong there, and masking is a *provable* no-op rather than a hopeful
one — which is exactly what the relay could not assert and what made the
check worth ten minutes. The §9.19/§9.24 results stand unaltered.

**Vehicles: 77,886 of 87,012**, with high values running 0–14 in a smooth
descending distribution — the shape of a per-asset sub-mesh index, not
noise. Read unpacked they produce material ids like 917,541; masked, the
maximum across all 372 vehicles is 50.

Adopted, with `submeshIndex` surfaced rather than discarded: the high half
is Team A's most promising untried lead for the still-open material↔run
association, so throwing it away would discard the evidence needed to close
that item. Character rendering is byte-identical after the change —
verified, not assumed, since every mesh flows through this field.

#### Retraction absorbed: `+0x0C` is an upper bound on vehicles

The same message withdrew "vehicles report materialCount = 36". The field
is exact (`1 + max(materialId)`) on `.ccmesh_pc` and only an **upper
bound** on vehicles, where a material set is sized for the whole multi-part
asset. §9.27's account of why `MaterialBindings` refuses 369 vehicles is
corrected in place: the guard's equality cannot hold on a vehicle
*structurally*, not by a narrow margin. That strengthens the case for
leaving it alone — relaxing it to a bound would admit precisely the runs
nobody can attribute.

**A note on how this arrived.** The chain ran: my wrong claim that vehicles
have no material block → their correction → my correction that vehicles
parse but do not render → their re-check → this retraction and a real new
finding. Four corrections, two in each direction, and the packing discovery
came out of the last one. *Corrections are not overhead between the useful
work; on this format they have repeatedly been where the useful work came
from.*

### 9.29 Vehicle geometry actually decodes — codes 100/101 exercised at last

A peer summarised the state as "vehicles fully geometry-complete". That was
worth checking rather than accepting, because **"the Mesh sub-block parses"
is not "the geometry decodes"** — §9.25/§9.26 established the former and
never tested the latter. Layout codes **100/101** carry a rigid *part index*
where characters carry blend weights and indices, and that branch of
`decodeChannel()` had never run on anything. Reaching it was the original
reason for going to vehicles at all (§9.21).

Measured (`tools/validation/validate_vehicle.cpp`, 372 vehicles):

| | |
|---|---|
| Channels decoded / failed | **3,872 / 0** |
| Vertices decoded | **5,629,811** |
| Normals unit length within 6% | **5,629,811 / 5,629,811** |
| Stride-law violations | **0** |
| Layout codes seen | **100** (1,428 channels), **101** (2,444) |
| Max rigid part index | 37 |

**The summary was right — and is now verified rather than assumed.**

The normals result is the one carrying weight. Nothing in the decode forces
a normal to be unit length: it is three bytes read at a computed offset
inside a computed stride and mapped through `(b/255)*2-1`. A wrong stride,
a wrong field offset or a wrong element count would scatter those values.
**5,629,811 of 5,629,811 landing inside 6% of unit** is the same class of
evidence as spec §6.2's 1.000 rate on characters, now reproduced on a
vertex layout this project had never touched.

**Max rigid part index 37 against a maximum part count of 41** is a second,
free cross-check: the index addresses the part array §9.25 reads from a
completely different region of the file, and it stays inside it.

So codes 100/101 are exercised, and the last claim in §9.21 — that reaching
vehicles would test a genuinely untried path rather than re-running code 3
a hundred more times — is discharged. Two channels per vehicle on average,
both vehicle-only codes, zero failures.

**Still not rendered, and still correct to say so.** Decoding vertices is
not drawing them, the material↔run association is open (§9.27), and vehicle
paint is believed to live in the `.cvtf_pc` catalogue rather than the model
file. The geometry is readable; the surfacing is not resolved.

### 9.30 Auditing my own harnesses for invented thresholds

Team A found an arbitrary group-count cap of **64** in their harness —
invented for character meshes, where nothing approaches it — silently
rejecting **286 of 372 vehicles**. Every vehicle figure they had sent was
computed on a 23% subset chosen by a made-up number, with the tool
reporting a confident N/N and never naming the exclusions. Vehicles reach
**311 groups**, so the cap was nowhere near the data.

Everything they had relayed survives the re-run on the full population, and
my own measurements were independent of their harness, so nothing here
needed revising. But the failure shape applies directly to this project's
tooling, so it was audited rather than assumed away — the same move as
§9.23, where §3's ambiguity lesson was turned on this project's own search.

**Three exclusions of exactly that shape existed here:**

* `sr3mesh` rejects a group's range count above **4096**;
* the draw-group search window is **4096 bytes** past the channel array;
* §9.28's packing measurement `continue`d past any vehicle where
  `drawGroupsLocated()` was false — **without counting them.** That last one
  is precisely Team A's bug, in my code, one section earlier.

Measured over all 372 vehicles:

| | |
|---|---|
| Draw groups located / **not** located | **372 / 0** |
| Max groups in one vehicle | **311** |
| Max ranges in one group | **32** (against the 4096 cap) |
| Total draw ranges | 87,012 |

**Nothing binds.** The range-count cap sits two orders of magnitude above
the data, the search window never cut a real array short, and the skip that
could have hidden vehicles never fired — so §9.28's 87,012 figure was
whole-population after all.

The result is "no bug found", and it is worth recording precisely because
**"I checked and found nothing" is a different statement from "I did not
check"**, and the two are indistinguishable in a report that omits both.
`skipped: 0` is now printed next to the result rather than left implicit.

*The 311-groups figure also explains their cap exactly* — a limit of 64
against real data reaching 311 is not a near miss, which is why it took out
77% of the population rather than a handful of outliers.

#### Also settled: the submesh-index lead is dead

Team A tested six candidate associations for the material↔run question
across all 372 vehicles: runs == distinct materials (4/372), == distinct
submeshes (3/372), == groups (1/372), == declared material count (1/372),
== distinct submesh/material pairs (0/372), == total draw ranges (0/372).
All at or below chance. **The association cannot be recovered by counting**,
and their read is that a greedy scan is finding runs without knowing their
true record boundaries — the vehicle-side record structure needs segmenting
first.

`DrawRange::submeshIndex` stays: it is a real per-asset index (§9.28) and
worth surfacing. It is simply not the association key, and §9.28's note
calling it "the most promising untried lead" is now **refuted, not
pending** — recorded so nobody spends a day re-deriving six negative
results.

### 9.31 `.anim_pc` +0x28 — a false claim in my own reader, corrected

Team A resolved how animation tracks bind to rig bones, from a runtime
trace rather than format-walking. Relayed, it contradicted this project's
own code: `src/animation.cpp` stated **"+0x28 (8 bytes) is observed zero
everywhere and OPEN - not read."** Both could not be true, and it was a
claim about a field this reader already documents, so it was measured
(`tools/validation/validate_anim_field28.cpp`, 4,209 shipped clips — header
bytes only; the payload stays parked):

| | |
|---|---|
| `+0x28 == 0` | 3,815 |
| **`+0x28 != 0`** | **394** |
| Distinct non-zero values | **only `0x38` (382) and `0x48` (12)** |
| Bytes there pass a permutation test | **355 / 394** |
| …same test at a control offset | 35 / 394 |

**My reader's comment was wrong.** The field is non-zero in 394 clips —
Team A's figure exactly — takes only the two header sizes, so the table sits
immediately after the header, and the bytes there behave like an index
permutation against a control that does not.

Corrected, and the field is now surfaced as `trackBoneTableOffset()` /
`hasTrackBoneTable()`: it is header data with a CONFIRMED meaning, and
leaving a *false* statement in place while the truth is known is worse than
the original gap. The keyframe payload is untouched — its encoding is still
open and animation remains parked.

Length-guarded like every other post-core field: `kCoreHeaderSize` is
`0x28`, so reading a `u32` *at* `0x28` needs four bytes the core does not
guarantee. Every shipped file is long enough; the 12 short static-prop poses
are exactly why the check exists rather than the assumption.

**Also worth carrying: the keyframe payload does not start at a fixed
`0x48`.** It starts after the header *and* this table when present. No
arithmetic here assumed otherwise — `sr3anim` never located the payload at
all — but anyone who later does needs it.

#### Why this hid for two full passes

The original spec pass searched this location for an **ascending run** of
indices, found none, and recorded "no such table exists". The real table is
a **permutation** — one shipped example reads
`[0, 1, 3, 4, 2, 6, 7, 5, 9, 10, 8, 14, 15, 17]` — so that predicate could
never have found it whether or not the table was there. **A negative result
from one predicate became "the structure is absent."**

That is the same family as §3's *"a scan that finds nothing has ruled out
its window, not the hypothesis"*, with the assumption moved from the search
*window* to the search *shape*, and it is the more insidious version: a
window is visibly a parameter, whereas "indices ascend" reads like a
property of the thing rather than a choice the searcher made. Recorded in
§3 alongside the window lesson.

### 9.32 Session record — 2026-09-11, engine phase part 2

What this session added, in order, with the one-line reason each mattered.
Every item is verified; none is half-finished.

| § | Work | Why it counted |
|---|---|---|
| 9.14 / 9.14.1 | Synthetic-pose skinning test | Made skinning falsifiable without `.anim_pc`; the scrambled-index control caught four vacuous metrics, and `nightblade` resolved as topology, not a skinning fault |
| 9.15 | Bone `+0x14` is not a rotation | The convention question **dissolved** rather than being answered — the field is the negated parent offset, 22,274/22,274 |
| 9.16 | `sr3rig` synthetic suite | Mutation-validated, 4/4 genuine mutations caught |
| 9.17 | `sr3mesh` synthetic suite | 6/6 caught; one exposed a blind lane in my own fixture. **Every format library now has a self-contained suite** |
| 9.18 | Per-material draw calls: blocked | Corrected my own false "correctness gap" framing; refused to guess the texture mapping |
| 9.19 | Material partition on screen | Flat colour per material id; boundaries land on garment edges — corroboration, not decoration |
| 9.20 | LOD selection (`--group N`) | Upgraded spec §8.2's *inferred* "groups are LOD levels" to **CONFIRMED ON-SCREEN** |
| 9.21 | Pipeline breadth sweep | 561 meshes, no partition failures; corrected a metric that would have false-alarmed on 197 |
| 9.22 / 9.22.1 | Material binding found | Verified before implementing; recorded the required guard before anything could trip on it |
| 9.23 | Ambiguity audit of our own search | Moved a load-bearing assumption from asserted to measured — 549/549 unique |
| 9.24 | **Real per-material textures** | Characters render with their actual materials, 6,064/6,064 independent cross-check |
| 9.25 | `sr3vehicle` | `.ccar_pc` 372/372; exposed the six-array bug |
| 9.26 | **Six-array walk bug fixed** | A one-line deletion; also closed 9 long-standing character/item failures |
| 9.27 | Slot index is not the role | A real bug in my own API — would have fed a normal map to a vehicle renderer |
| 9.28 | Draw-range field is packed 16:16 | Measured on both populations: provable no-op on characters, real on vehicles |

**The through-line.** **22 defects and wrong claims** (26 including tooling
mishaps) — counted and itemised in §9.36, after this line spent the session
saying "roughly a dozen" from memory. **None was caught by
a test going red** — every one came from measuring a claim before asserting
it. Several were mine, several were relayed, several were in the specs, and
the corrections travelled in both directions between the teams. On this
format, corrections have not been overhead between the useful work; they
have repeatedly *been* the useful work, and the largest single win (§9.26)
arrived as a direct consequence of insisting on a narrower claim.

**Three "complete" claims needed narrowing during the session, two of them
mine.** The last — *parses* versus *decodes* — was hiding the entire reason
for going to vehicles: layout codes 100/101 had never once run.

### 9.33 Team A's `.anim_pc` progress — recorded, NOT adopted

On 2026-09-11 a peer relayed substantial Team A progress on the keyframe
payload, explicitly framed as awareness rather than authorization. The
updated `spec-anim-format.md` is in this tree and is properly tiered. **This
changed nothing about what this reader does, and animation remains PARKED.**

Recorded here because "significant progress" is exactly the kind of message
a later session could mistake for the unblock. It is not one — see the park
rule in the RESUME block.

**What Team A now reports as CONFIRMED:**

| | |
|---|---|
| Payload structure | No offset table exists at all — self-delimiting per-track blocks; track `i+1` is reachable only by walking track `i` |
| Walk validation | 4,086 / 4,209 clips (97.1%) walk the declared track count without overrun, against a 7-byte-late control at 10.9% |
| Endpoint oracle | **99.89%** (3,687/3,691) of clips **without flags bit `0x40`** land exactly on the header's own declared end-offset at `+0x30`; clips **with** the bit never do (0/518). *Originally published as 90.2% over a mixed population — see below.* |
| Rotation samples | Smallest-three quantized quaternions; fourth component `sqrt(K - sum-of-squares)`, with permutation tables, `K`, an identity fallback and a 64-entry adaptive step table all read from the binary |

**What Team A states is NOT confirmed** — carried through verbatim in tier,
at their own insistence, because this is the half that gets flattened in
relay:

* **Per-sample numeric assembly** (how base + multiplier + delta combine)
  is **HIGH CONFIDENCE** — inferred from one decompiled branch, **not yet
  replayed against real file bytes**.
* **Translation samples are completely OPEN** — what the 3 bytes per key
  decode to, and what the other 6 bytes of the 8-byte control record carry,
  is undecoded.

**Why this is still not buildable, stated as a predicate:** rotation is not
byte-verified and translation is not decoded at all. A reader built on this
today would produce characters that move — and move *wrongly*, which is the
silently-plausible failure this project has refused three times. The
endpoint oracle is genuinely strong evidence about *structure*; it says
nothing about whether the *values* come out right.

**The one thing that changed on this side** is a stale comment. This
reader documented `+0x30`'s target as OPEN; the spec now resolves it as the
keyframe-payload end. That was **not adopted as confirmed**, because
verifying it requires performing the per-track walk — which *is* the parked
work. The comment in `include/sr3anim/animation.h` now states the actual
epistemic position: reported upstream with a strong oracle test, not
independently reproduced here. Nothing in the code depends on it.

This is the §9.31 situation with the opposite outcome, and the contrast is
the lesson. There, a relayed claim touched a header field, was measurable
within this reader's existing scope, was measured, and my own comment turned
out to be the wrong one. Here the claim touches a field this reader also
already reads — but the evidence for it lives on the far side of a park, so
the correct move is to record the claim and its tier rather than either
adopt it or dismiss it. **"Not verified here, and here is why" is a
publishable state.** Reaching for a measurement to avoid writing that
sentence would have meant starting the parked work in order to look
diligent.

#### 9.33.1 The residual was a mixed population — and the correction re-mixed it

The two questions sent back to Team A (§9.33: *what distinguishes the 399
that walk but miss the oracle*, and *do they overlap the 123 outright
failures*) both resolved, and the answer was better than the headline
number. **The two groups are one population**, separated cleanly by flags
bit `0x40`:

| Population | lands on `+0x30` | walks but misses | fails the walk |
|---|---|---|---|
| bit `0x40` **clear** (3,691 clips) | **3,687** | 2 | 2 |
| bit `0x40` **set** (518 clips) | **0** | 397 | 121 |

**Checked the arithmetic rather than taking the summary** — it reconciles
exactly against every previously published figure, which is what makes the
table trustworthy: successful walks `(3,687+2)+(0+397) = 4,086` ✓;
oracle-misses `2+397 = 399` ✓; outright failures `2+121 = 123` ✓; total
`3,691+518 = 4,209` ✓. The stratified rate is 99.89%, not 90.2% — the
original figure was **diluted, not wrong**, and the whole residual is now
isolated instead of averaged into noise.

**But the denominator moves again in the very next paragraph.** The spec
reports that continuing the walk past the declared track count lands exactly
on `+0x30` in **"335 of the 399 (84%)"**. That `399` is the *combined*
walks-but-misses — 397 with the bit plus **2 without it**. Those 2 are, by
this section's own argument, not the same mechanism; the claim is about what
bit `0x40` adds, so its population is the 397.

**And dividing by 397 would still have been wrong.** The figure sent back
from here was `335/397 = 84.4%` — the corrected denominator under the
original numerator. Team A re-measured instead of re-dividing and found the
numerator carried the same contamination: **one of the 335 recoveries was
itself one of the two non-bit clips.** The honest figure is **`334/397 =
84.1%`**. Re-dividing would have produced a number that was still wrong and
now *looked* audited — which is strictly worse than the uncorrected one,
because the next reader has no reason to check it again. Generalised into §3.

The magnitude is trivial. The shape is not: **this is the denominator error
the section was written to correct, reappearing one paragraph later inside
the correction.** That is worth recording precisely because nobody was being
careless — `399` was simply the number in hand from the previous pass, and
it *reads* like the right denominator right up until you notice the section
just finished proving it isn't one population.

There is also a second legitimate denominator that answers a different
question and should be visible: of **all** 518 clips carrying the bit,
`334/518 = 64.5%` land on `+0x30` under the continued walk, because **121
fail the walk outright and are silently outside the 84%**. Neither figure is
wrong; they answer "of the ones that walk short, how many recover?" and "of
the ones carrying the bit, how many end up explained?" — and quoting the
first without its exclusions is how `skipped: 0` stops being a finding.

**What Team A got right and is worth copying:** the conclusion is held to
what was measured. *"There is more payload after the tracks, and walking it
as though it were more tracks usually lands right"* is stated as a different
claim from *"the track count field is wrong"*, with only the first asserted —
and the extra block count matches no header field tested (39 blocks for 310
of them; otherwise 74, 113, 90 …), which is reported rather than smoothed
over. The filename-based explanation is labelled HYPOTHESIS and carries no
weight in the conclusion. **Still OPEN: what flags bit `0x40` adds.** None of
this changes the park.

#### 9.33.2 "Payload decoded" is now true and misleading in the same breath

Team A decoded translation samples, so the `.anim_pc` keyframe payload is
structurally understood end to end. **The two halves are not at the same
confidence tier, and the phrase "the payload is decoded" flattens exactly
that.** Recorded here because that sentence is the single most likely thing
to be mistaken for the unblock.

| Half | Tier | What backs it |
|---|---|---|
| **Translation** | **CONFIRMED** — disassembly **+ numeric replay against real file bytes** | A physical-plausibility oracle: bone-local translation should cluster small given anatomy, and does — median `0.203`, 97% within 4.0 units across **86,051 real records**, against controls collapsing to medians of 56–76. Both scale constants were *read from the binary as f32*, not fitted. |
| **Rotation** | **HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred** | Mechanism and tables confirmed from the binary (smallest-three, permutation tables, `K`, identity fallback, 64-entry adaptive step table) — but **the per-sample arithmetic has never been replayed against real bytes.** |

The asymmetry is load-bearing, and Team A flagged it deliberately rather
than letting it round off (their spec §6c.6 item 4 says so in as many
words). A reader built today would place bones correctly and **orient them
on unverified arithmetic** — which is the project's recurring
silently-plausible failure in its purest form: translation is the half whose
errors you would *see*, rotation the half whose errors look like a slightly
odd animation. Confirming one half raises the odds the other is right; it is
not evidence that it is.

Also still OPEN and explicitly labelled by Team A: whether the per-key delta
measures from the record's base or accumulates across keys; what the
decoder's fourth output lane carries; and whether a 16-byte load over an
8-byte record means adjacent records blend (HYPOTHESIS, untraced).

**The decode details are deliberately NOT transcribed into this file.** They
are in `spec-anim-format.md` §6c, which is the right home for format detail
and is already in this tree. Copying record layouts and scale constants into
the handoff would add no capability and would quietly turn the status record
into staging for the parked build. **Park unchanged.**

#### 9.33.3 A relayed bug report that was already handled — for the third time

The same spec pass reported a correction to "this project's container
tooling": `preload_anim.vpp_pc` sets the container shared-stream flag `0x2`
while storing **all 4,209 entries raw**, so a reader that consults the
container flag before the per-entry sentinel fails outright.

**`vpp::PayloadLocator` already gets this right, and says why in a comment
naming this exact archive** — the per-entry sentinel is treated as
authoritative and the flag is never consulted for raw-vs-compressed.
Verified empirically rather than by reading the comment:
`validate_anim_field28.exe test-fixtures/preload_anim.vpp_pc` extracts
**4,209 / 4,209**. So the correction applies to Team A's own spec-side
tooling, not to this codebase.

Third occurrence of this pattern (cf. §9.26's relayed six-array fix, already
in the code path). **It costs one command to check and it has never once
been wasted** — either the bug is real here, or the answer is "already
handled, here is the proof", and both are worth more than assuming either
way. The failure mode to avoid is the *reflex* in both directions: adopting
a relayed fix unexamined, or dismissing it because the last two didn't apply.

### 9.34 Vehicle material runs: the scan works, the guard is what refuses

First real work on the open vehicle material↔run item since it was parked as
"needs the vehicle-side record structure segmented first". Team A answered
three questions (spec-vehicle-geometry.md §7.2) and one answer reframed the
problem entirely.

**Q1 — carrier independence, CONFIRMED and stronger than asked.** There is
no vehicle-specific material walk *at all*: the registered vehicle
constructor calls the same shared material-reference-block validator and
then the same sub-header/six-array/Mesh machinery, unmodified. So "do
vehicles use the `.cfmesh_pc` length-prefixed idiom?" is not a vehicle
question — it is the same question about `.ccmesh_pc`, and any answer
transfers **by construction**, not by analogy. *But* the reference-block
validator skips the material block by its declared length without
enumerating sub-records, so it supplies the outer skip and no per-record
boundaries: **sub-record layout is open on BOTH formats**, not just vehicles.

**Q2 — per-part material scoping: NOT established.** Part records carry
eight fixed-up pointer fields, several undocumented, but nothing read shows
a material count or index inside one. My reasoning for why per-part scoping
would explain the upper-bound behaviour survives as a HYPOTHESIS and is
doing no work here.

**Q3 — vehicle paint source: CONFIRMED, and it CLOSES an open item.**
`.cvtf_pc` is a separate registered resource type with its own constructor
(registered twice, vehicle and character variants) and **the vehicle mesh
loader never parses it**, corroborated by a separate paint subsystem with
its own colour slots and purchase/selection entry points. So **generic
textures on vehicle body panels are a CONFIRMED NON-BUG** — the mesh is
genuinely not the source of truth for those surfaces, and binding what the
mesh names is correct behaviour. The *application* path is still unread, but
the source question is settled. This was previously OPEN-hypothesis; it is
the first of the vehicle items to close, and it closed by asking rather than
by measuring.

#### What the scan actually finds (`tools/validation/validate_vehicle_runs.cpp`)

Q1 licensed a measurement that was not worth making before: since vehicles
run the *identical* code, anything the run scan finds there is found by the
logic that is 6,064/6,064 correct on characters. So — what does it find, with
the acceptance guard removed? (The shipping reader is unchanged; the harness
carries its own copy of the scan.)

| | |
|---|---|
| Vehicles examined | **372** — skipped: 0 no-`.gcar`, 0 no-Mesh, 0 threw |
| Vehicles yielding **zero** runs | **0** |
| Runs / entries found | **9,878 / 28,334** |
| `runs < declared` / `== ` / `>` | **369 / 3 / 0** |
| Overlapping run pairs (ambiguity) | **9**, in 9 files (0.09%) |
| CONTROL — scan start +2 (misaligned) | **0 runs** |

**So the scan is not what fails on vehicles — the acceptance guard is.**
Every vehicle yields runs; the count never once exceeds the declared
`+0x0C`, which is exactly what "upper bound" predicts and is a 372/372
one-sided relation rather than an average; and a two-byte misalignment
destroys the structure completely.

#### The name-start oracle, and why the first control was worthless

The resolved-name list contained an obvious truncation family —
`T_bulldog_D1B.tga`, `_bulldog_D1B.tga`, `JT_bulldog_D1B.tga`, and a bare
`.tga`. `resolveName` accepts any printable string containing a dot, so a
name offset landing mid-string passes it. That needed quantifying, not
eyeballing, so: **a real name offset must land on a name START** — the blob
base, or immediately after a NUL — which a truncation cannot do.

**Characters are the control**, because the binding there is already known
correct:

| | entries | name starts at a boundary | runs fully clean | "hash" < 256 or −1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Characters (control)** | 6,064 | **6,064 (100.00%)** | 1,834 / 1,834 (100%) | **0** |
| **Vehicles** | 28,334 | 28,176 (**99.44%**) | 9,779 / 9,878 (**99.00%**) | 226 |

The control scoring a clean 100/100 is what makes the vehicle number
readable: the truncations are real but they are a **0.56% minority**, not
the normal case. Note also that the guard-free scan on characters yields
exactly **6,064** entries — the same figure as the accepted cross-check, so
removing the guard changes nothing on the population where it passes.

**The second control was worthless and must not be counted as
corroboration.** Shifting the name base by +1 returned **9,878 runs —
identical to the real scan**. Not a near miss: byte-for-byte the same count.
The reason is that a one-byte shift just produces *different truncations*,
which `resolveName` accepts exactly as happily. A control that cannot fail
is not evidence, and had the misalignment control not been run alongside it,
"two controls, both consistent" would have read as a much stronger result
than one control plus one broken instrument. **§3's "run a control" needs a
companion: check that the control can actually fail.** A control returning
suspiciously round agreement with the real measurement is a bug report about
the control.

#### Where this leaves the item — still OPEN, and why

Tempting conclusion: relax the guard from `==` to `<=` and vehicles bind.
**No.** At a 1% impure-run rate that admits roughly 99 bad runs across the
population, and a bad run binds a wrong texture to a real surface — the
silently-plausible failure again, with the added twist that 99% correct
*looks* finished on screen. Filtering by the name-start oracle would clean
those, but it still would not close the item: run counts remain **below**
the declared count in 369/372, so there is no equality to restore and no
established key mapping runs to draw ranges.

What genuinely advanced: the segmentation is no longer suspected of being
broken on vehicles, the upper-bound reading of `+0x0C` now has a 372/372
one-sided confirmation, and the paint question is closed. What is still
needed is unchanged and now sharply stated: **the sub-record advance rule
inside the material set — open on `.ccmesh_pc` and `.ccar_pc` alike.**

#### 9.34.1 The oracle became a reader fix, and caught two live false acceptances

The name-start predicate was built as a *measuring instrument*, but it is
also a correctness check the reader was missing, so it moved into
`src/material_binding.cpp`'s `resolveName`. The case for making a shipping
change on my own measurement rests on it being provably neutral where the
reader already works:

| After the tightening | |
|---|---|
| Characters located | **546 / 546** — unchanged |
| Character name cross-check | **6,064 / 6,064** — unchanged |
| Synthetic suites | **14 / 14**, 0 failures |
| Compiles at `/W4` | clean |

**Vehicles went 3 → 1 located, and that is the point, not a regression.**
The only behavioural change is the new predicate, so any file that flipped
must have had at least one name offset landing mid-string. Two of the three
vehicles this reader previously reported as *successfully bound* were
therefore bound with at least one truncated name — **live wrong bindings
being surfaced as correct**, on the path a renderer would trust. The
population that could show it was 0.56% of entries; the population that
mattered was 2 of 3.

Worth sitting with: the old guard was strict in the dimension everyone was
watching (`found.size() == materialCount`, refusing 369 vehicles) and
completely open in a dimension nobody was — *is this string even a whole
name?* Strictness is not a scalar. A guard can be simultaneously too tight
to accept the truth and too loose to reject a lie, and the loud half hides
the quiet half: every conversation about this reader for weeks was about
whether it was refusing too much.

`tools/validation/validate_vehicle_runs.cpp` deliberately keeps its **own
pre-tightening copy** of the scan. It is the instrument that measures the
raw population, including the truncations the reader now filters; making it
track the reader would destroy exactly the signal it exists to report.

### 9.35 Two different quantities called "runs" — and the spec cites our number for the wrong one

`spec-vertex-format.md` §8.4 resolved the material-set advance rule
(fixed-stride arrays gated by a previously-undocumented second count at
sub-header `+0x0E`, then a variable per-material loop gated by `+0x0C`).
Good result, CONFIRMED by disassembly, and it settles that **greedy
segmentation at the array level was solving a problem that does not exist**.

§8.4.1 then reframes `+0x0C` as an **exact** record count on both carriers —
correcting this project's "exact on meshes, upper bound on vehicles" — and
cites **this project's measurement** as support:

> runs `<` count in 369/372, `==` in 3/372, never `>`

**That is our binding-run measurement, and §8.4.1 attaches it to draw runs.**
They are different quantities, and the substitution inverts the result.
Measured directly (`validate_vehicle_runs.cpp`, all 372 vehicles, draw
groups located 372/372):

| Quantity vs `materialCount` | `<` | `==` | `>` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Binding runs** (ours, §9.34) | **369** | 3 | **0** |
| **Draw ranges** (87,012 total) | 1 | 0 | **371** |

**Draw ranges exceed `materialCount` in 371 of 372 vehicles** — the exact
opposite of the one-sided relation §8.4.1 states. So the cited evidence does
not support the claim it is cited for.

Worth noting the prose argues against its own conclusion: *"a run references
a material, several runs may share one, and a material need not be
referenced by any run"* predicts draw runs **≥** distinct materials used,
which is what 371/372 shows. The premise is right and matches the data; the
`runs ≤ materialCount` conclusion drawn from it does not follow.

**What is unaffected:** §8.4.1's core correction — `+0x0C` drives the
per-material loop, so it is an exact record count on both carriers — rests
on disassembly, not on this statistic, and stands. Our binding-run figure is
also unaffected: it was measured with the guard removed and says what it
always said, about binding runs. And the equality guard really was never
right, for the reason §9.34.1 gives (a material record need not carry a
locatable binding), not for the reason §8.4.1 gives.

**The lesson is a word, not a number.** "Run" means binding run in §9.34 and
draw run in §8.4.1, and both documents are internally consistent — the
collision only exists across the boundary, which is exactly where nobody is
reading both halves at once. A shared term with two referents in one project
is a measurement hazard, and it survived several careful exchanges precisely
because each side's usage was locally correct. **When quoting another team's
figure, restate what was counted, not just the count.**

#### Where this leaves the association — closed off, not merely unsolved

Team A's stronger negative stands and is the useful part: since `+0x0C` is
exact on **both** carriers, the association was never recoverable from counts
**on principle** — a better negative than six refuted candidates, because it
rules out the approach rather than the attempts. §8.4's pseudocode also shows
why §8.4 does not unblock it: the per-material loop's advance is an
unspecified `<helper>(base, &cursor, ...)`, so there is still no way to walk
to material *i*'s record and read its binding. That helper is the one piece
of the chain never read, and whatever it stores per material is where an
association key would have to live if one exists. **Still OPEN, now with a
specific address.**

#### 9.35.1 The replacement claim confirmed — and it is a validity check, not a structural one

Team A re-measured independently and reached the same conclusion from a
larger set: draw ranges exceed `materialCount` in **392/393** against this
project's **371/372**. Two separate measurements, separate tooling,
converging — which is worth more than either alone.

Their replacement claim is that the bound was always real but attached to the
wrong quantity: it holds for **distinct material ids referenced, masked**
(16:16, §9.28). Measured here rather than accepted, on all 372:

| | |
|---|---|
| distinct masked ids `<` `materialCount` | **372 / 372** |
| `==` / `>` | 0 / **0** |
| `max(id) >= materialCount` (out-of-range) | **0** |
| Files where the bound is **tight** (slack 0) | **0 / 372** |
| Mean slack (`materialCount − distinct ids`) | **21.8** (8,117 total) |

**The claim is true and I confirm it. It is also close to unfalsifiable, and
that limits what it establishes.** For `distinct ids ≤ materialCount` to
fail, a draw range would have to carry an id that is not a valid index into
the material set — a corrupt file. So "393/393" is approximately *"no vehicle
has an out-of-range material id"*: a real invariant, worth having, and
**not** evidence about the association. The bound is never once tight across
372 files.

This is the same shape Team A caught and discarded in their own high-16-bits
number during this very correction, so it is offered in that spirit rather
than as a gotcha: **before publishing a rate, ask what the failing case would
have looked like.** Here it would have looked like data corruption.

**The informative number is the slack, not the bound.** A mean of 21.8
against a median `materialCount` of ~44 means **roughly half of every
vehicle's declared materials are referenced by no draw range at all** — which
independently confirms *"a material need not be referenced by any run"* far
more directly than the bound does, and it confirms it by measuring the thing
itself rather than an inequality that brackets it. Where that slack goes is
unexplained and is a better lead than anything the bound offers.

**Their companion lesson is the strongest thing in this exchange**, and it
generalises past this project: *check a citation against the argument you
wrote around it, not just against its source.* §8.4.1 contained its own
refutation one sentence earlier — the prose predicted `runs ≥ materials`
while the conclusion said `≤` — and a borrowed number bridged the two
convincingly enough that neither half got re-read against the other. **Your
own prose arguing against your own conclusion is a free proof-read, if you
re-read it.** Recorded in §3 alongside the citation rule.

Also worth carrying, from their account of walking into the documented 16:16
packing trap a second time *inside* the correction: **a correction is written
fast and inherits the assumption that the surrounding work is sound, which is
exactly when a documented hazard gets walked into again.** Hold a
correction's new numbers to the same bar as the ones they replace. That is
the §3 "a correction inherits the frame of the thing it corrects" lesson
arriving from the other direction — theirs is about the hazards it inherits,
mine was about the errors it inherits.

#### 9.35.2 Vehicles declare exactly twice the materials they draw — verified independently

The slack turned out to carry the finding, and it is clean. Team A measured
it on 393 vehicles; this is an independent check on this project's 372, with
characters as the control:

| | Characters (control) | Vehicles |
|---|---|---|
| Files | 549 | 372 |
| Declared / referenced | **1,837 / 1,837** | **16,276 / 8,159** |
| Mean slack | **0.00** (0.0%) | **21.82** (**49.9%**) |
| `declared == referenced` | **549 / 549** | 0 / 372 |
| `declared == 2 × referenced` | 0 / 549 | **336 / 372** |
| `declared == 2 × referenced − 1` | *(see artifact below)* | 30 / 372 |
| Ratio in [1.9, 2.1] | 0 / 549 | **362 / 372** |
| Mean / **MAX** ratio | 1.0000 / **1.0000** | 1.9886 / **2.0000** |
| Referenced ids a dense prefix | **549 / 549** | **372 / 372** |

**Confirmed, from a separate population and separate tooling.** The cap is
the striking part: the maximum ratio observed anywhere is **exactly 2.0000**,
never above. 366 of 372 vehicles are exactly `2n` or `2n−1`. Characters sit
at exactly 1.0000 with zero slack in every one of 549 files — a control that
could have landed anywhere and landed on the nose.

So **every vehicle declares a material set exactly twice the size of what its
geometry references, and the unreferenced half is a contiguous suffix**
(referenced ids are a dense prefix, 372/372 and 549/549).

**An artifact in this project's own metric, flagged rather than buried:** the
`2 × referenced − 1` bucket reads 272/549 on characters, which looks like it
contradicts the 1.0000 ratio. It does not — it is degenerate at one material:
when `d == 1`, `declared == 1` satisfies both `declared == d` and
`declared + 1 == 2d`. The characters' 272 are single-material meshes
double-counted by a test that cannot discriminate there. The vehicle figure
is unaffected (`d` is large throughout). Recording it because an unexplained
272 sitting beside a clean 1.0000 is exactly the kind of thing a later reader
would try to reconcile as a real effect.

**What is NOT claimed.** What the unreferenced half *is* remains open. A
paired variant per surface — damage state is the natural guess in this game —
is HYPOTHESIS and does no work here. The measurement stands alone: the
pairing is real, it is exactly 2×, it is capped, and the partner is bound to
no geometry, so something other than a draw range selects it.

**A retroactive re-diagnosis, with one distinction kept.** §9.30 recorded six
count-matching candidates failing at or below chance and concluded counting
was refuted. The sharper reading now: the count was *right* and the
comparison was off by a factor of two. **But that does not revive counting as
a route to the association** — getting the count right still tells you
*how many*, never *which*. Both remain true: the six candidates failed for a
now-explained reason, and counts alone still cannot yield an association.
Keep them separate; collapsing them would re-open a road that is properly
closed.

Also superseded: the phrase "`+0x0C` is an upper bound on vehicles", used
throughout this thread including by me. It is an **exact count of declared
materials on both carriers**. What differs is that vehicles declare twice
what they draw.

#### 9.35.3 Reconciling a 2× disagreement: it was the guards, not the search

Team A asked directly whether this project's binding-run locator is
**anchored** (searches from a known fixed start) or **sliding** (tests
candidate positions), believing that might explain their 19,240 runs against
our 9,878 — and said they would trust our number if it were anchored.

**It is sliding.** `src/material_binding.cpp` steps `at += 4` from
`meshBlockEnd` and tests every position. So the hypothesis is wrong, and the
conclusion drawn from it should not be acted on: **they should not prefer our
number on that basis.** Answering "no, and here is why that matters" is worth
more than accepting a deference that was offered for a reason that does not
hold.

Two measurements settle what it actually was.

**Population — reconciles exactly.** Our 372 was `vehicles.vpp_pc` alone.
Adding `vehicles_preload` and `dlc1`–`dlc3` gives **393 vehicles, skipped 0**
— the same population, not a comparable one. Run count there: **10,359**.

**Guards — this is the whole gap.** Same sliding search, same `length >= 2`,
content guards dropped (no non-zero-hash requirement; a name offset need only
land inside the blob rather than resolve to a printable dotted string):

| Same 393 vehicles, same search | Runs |
|---|---|
| With this project's content guards | **10,359** |
| **Team A's reported figure** | **19,240** |
| With no content validation at all | **27,050** |

**Their number brackets cleanly between ours and none**, which localises the
disagreement precisely: their detector validates *something*, but less than
ours. Nothing about the search differs. The distinction that produces the
factor is **"this position could be a binding" versus "the bytes there look
like one"** — and that is a content question, so it was never going to be
resolved by comparing search strategies.

Worth keeping as method: a disagreement by a clean factor invites a search
for one discriminating cause, and both teams reached for the *structural*
explanation (anchored vs sliding) because it is the more interesting one.
The actual cause was a threshold. **Bracket the disagreement before
explaining it** — running our own scan at the extreme (no guards at all) put
their figure inside a range we produced, which identified the axis in one
measurement instead of trading hypotheses.

Their own two lessons from the failed attempt are worth carrying verbatim: a
run detector that accepts **length-1** runs is not a detector (a run's
evidence *is* its length; `al_grime.tga` "bound" 135,325 times is what
accepting the minimum buys), and **set a threshold from what chance actually
produces, not from what the format merely permits.**

### 9.36 Counting the tally I had been quoting without counting

Team A noticed their own running total of demoted/withdrawn results had
drifted — "three", "four", "five" in different messages, never actually
counted; the real figure was seven, now itemised. Their point applies
straight back: **a self-critical tally is still a number, and the honest
direction is not exempt from the measurement discipline.**

§9.32 and the `measurement-discipline` memory have both said **"roughly a
dozen defects"** all session. That was remembered, never counted. Counted
now, with the predicate stated so it is checkable rather than trusted:
*a defect or wrong claim in **TEAM B's own** code, tests, tooling or
documentation, found and corrected during the engine phase* (§9.14–§9.35).
Team A's errors, spec errors, and merely-open questions are excluded.

**Shipped-code defects (5):** six-array walk over-alignment (§9.26,
205→372/372); `DrawRange` material field read unpacked instead of 16:16

**False or overstated claims in my own comments and docs (9):** `+0x28`

"group-0-only is a correctness gap" (groups are LOD levels); "§9.21 could not

**Tooling and process mishaps (4):** the viewer's positional `argv[4]` output
