no-opping at exit 0.

**22 defects and wrong claims; 26 including tooling mishaps.** "Roughly a
dozen" understated it by more than half — and in the *flattering* direction,
which is precisely why nobody queried it.

#### The through-line, restated more precisely

The old phrasing — *"none was caught by a test going red"* — was itself
slightly overstated, and by the same mechanism. Accurately: **not one was
caught by the synthetic suites.** Several *were* surfaced by real-data
harnesses reporting a rate that looked wrong (the six-array walk showed up as
205/372, not as a failed assertion). Those are different mechanisms, and
collapsing them made the line pithier and less true. The useful version:
**a suite of assertions never found a defect here; a number that looked
wrong found many.** That is an argument for measuring rates on real
populations, not for distrusting tests.

Also worth carrying, from Team A's own count of it happening **twice in one
session**: *the right fact, in the right document, not reaching the tool that
needed it* — their scan not applying their own §8.4.2 hash rule written
earlier the same day, and the vehicle constructor address present in the
inventory but missing from the spec that needed it. **Writing a rule down and
implementing it are separate acts, and the gap between them is invisible from
either side alone.**

### 9.37 `.anim_pc` payload built — walk and translation confirmed; my rotation "refutation" was my own bug (see §9.37.1)

Unparked by the user directly. Built `sr3anim/payload.h` + `src/payload.cpp`
from `spec-anim-format.md` §6c, with `tools/validation/validate_anim_payload.cpp`
as the real-data replay. Three results, and they are at three different
tiers, which is the whole point.

#### 1. My first implementation was wrong, and the oracle said so immediately

Walk completed on **105 / 4,209** against the spec's published 97.1%. One
mis-transcription caused all of it: §6c.1 writes `align2(p+1)` and
`align4(p+3)`, which are the **C idioms** `(p+1) & ~1` and `(p+3) & ~3` —
i.e. *align `p` up*. I read them as "call an align function on `p+1`", which
applies the offset twice.

Rather than guess, `probe_anim_walk.cpp` scored **128 readings** of the walk
against the oracle the file itself declares (the cursor must land exactly on
header `+0x30`). Aligning up scored **88.78%** where every other reading
collapsed; only 2 variants cleared 50%, and they were the same reading. A
second round found the remaining residual: the payload starts **after the
track→bone table** when one is present. Final:

| | |
|---|---|
| Walk completes | **4,086 / 4,209 (97.1%)** — matches spec exactly |
| Walk fails | **123** — matches spec exactly |
| Lands on declared `+0x30`, flags `0x40` clear | **3,687** — matches spec exactly |
| Same, flags `0x40` set | **0 / 518** — matches spec exactly |

Stratified, the walk is **100.00% on every flags population** except `0x0C`
and `0x1C`, which are 0/2 each and are the entire 4-clip residual. That is a
better statement than "99.89%": the failure is a named 4-clip population, not
a smear.

#### 2. Translation — independently confirmed

86,051 control records, the spec's exact figure, reached independently.

| reading | median | p90 | ≤1.0 | ≤4.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **real alignment** | **0.232** | **2.40** | 77.8% | **96.5%** |
| control +1 | 81.4 | 400.0 | 1.1% | 2.1% |
| control +2 (field assignment) | 0.470 | **88.22** | 64.5% | 82.3% |
| control +3 | 60.0 | 400.6 | 0.6% | 2.2% |

The spec's +2 p90 is 88.2; mine is 88.22. **Translation is CONFIRMED and
holds up under an independent replay.**

**My first translation control was broken and I nearly reported it.** It
shifted the *sample* bytes — but a delta is divided by 4000 and contributes
at most 0.03 per axis, so shifting samples moved the answer ~1% and the
"control" returned 0.055 against the real 0.067. Near-identical, which is
exactly the tell recorded in §3 today. The control has to shift the
**record**, so the `i16` bases are misread.

#### 3. Rotation — the never-run replay, and it *appeared* to fail (IT DID NOT — see §9.37.1)

> **⚠ STALE LABEL, corrected 2026-09-12 and kept visible as the instructive
> failure.** This heading read *"and it FAILS"* for hours after the claim
> beneath it had been retracted in §9.37.1. The top-level §9.37 heading was
> fixed and the prose correction was written, but **this sub-heading was
> not**, so a reader skimming headings — which is how these documents are
> actually read — would have taken away precisely the refuted conclusion,
> and the stale label would have pointed them at the wrong evidence.
> Found by Team A's rule, applied to this file: **a correction must replace
> the LABEL, not merely add prose above or below it. Audit by label, not by
> prose** — the defect is a mismatch between two parts that each read fine
> in isolation. The measurements below are real; the conclusion drawn from
> them was wrong, and §9.37.1 explains why.

§6c.2 marks the numeric assembly `[HIGH CONFIDENCE — inferred]`, "read from
one decompiled branch and not replayed against file bytes". Replayed:

```
base <= 63, step <= 16, delta <= 127, scale = 8.6327e-05
  max stored component = (63 + 16*127) * scale = 0.1809
  max |vector part|    = sqrt(3) * 0.1809      = 0.3133
  MAX ROTATION ANGLE   = 2*asin(0.3133)        = 36.5 degrees
```

**No bone can rotate more than ~36° from identity, for any key in any clip.**
That is a ceiling in the arithmetic, not a property of the data — and over
**2,963,687 samples** the observed maximum is **35.52°**, sitting right
against it. Data pressing against a limit is what you see when the real
encoding extends past a limit your reading imposes. Median 5.59°, p99 25.6°.
Character animation needs ±180°.

**All three of my rotation oracles returned perfect scores, and all three
were vacuous — for the same reason that is itself the finding.** With every
stored component ≤ 0.181, the reconstructed one is always ≥ 0.950, so
smallest-three **cannot** fail (100.00% of 2.96M) and clamping **cannot**
occur (0.00%). Temporal continuity sat at 0.9978 against a cross-track
control of 0.9994 — the control *higher* than the real, because everything is
near identity.

Had I reported those three numbers as written, this would have read as a
triumphant confirmation: 100%, 0%, and near-perfect continuity. **The
strongest-looking result of the session was the emptiest.** What exposed it
was asking the question §3 now insists on — *what would the failing case have
looked like?* — and finding the answer was "arithmetically impossible".

`Payload::rotationsUsable()` returns **false** and the header says why. The
decode is kept because it is the evidence, and because the walk and control
records around it are confirmed.

**The park's stated reason was exactly right.** It was held because rotation
had never been replayed; the replay refutes it. A reader shipped this morning
would have produced characters translating correctly and rotating up to 36° —
stiff, but entirely plausible on screen.

#### 9.37.1 The refutation was wrong. The spec was right. Read this before §9.37.

**§9.37 claimed the spec's rotation assembly was REFUTED. That claim was
false, and the error was entirely mine.** It is left standing above rather
than edited away, because how a confident wrong result got that far is the
useful part.

**What was actually wrong.** The assembly is

```
component = (base * 64 + mult * delta) * 4 * SCALE
```

and this reader computed `(base + mult * delta) * SCALE` — **no `*64` on the
base, no `*4` overall.** That alone capped components at 0.181 and rotation
at 36.5°. Nothing else was wrong with it: base width was never the issue
(this reader read the full 6 bits throughout), and after correcting the
signed-base and packed-6-bit-delta details from the spec's new bit table,
**every intermediate matched Team A's worked example exactly** — base
`8, -1, -1`, mult `4, 4, 2`, delta `0, 6, -1`.

The spec states the achievable *extreme* — `(16×32 + 32×64) × 4 × SCALE =
0.884` — but never writes the expression. Solving that extreme against three
worked component values recovers it exactly on all three axes. **A stated
range is not a stated formula**, and the gap between them is where this went.

After the fix: max angle **180.00°**, median 34.40°, p90 83.69° — against
Team A's independent 180.00 / 31.16 / 80.40.

#### Why a wrong result looked like a strong one

All three rotation checks scored **perfectly**: smallest-three 100.00% of
2,963,687, clamping 0.00%, continuity 0.9978. Written up as measured, that
reads as overwhelming confirmation. **Every one of them was vacuous**, and
for a single reason: with components capped at 0.181 the reconstructed
component is always ≥ 0.950, so smallest-three *cannot* fail and clamping
*cannot* occur.

The one signal that something was wrong was in the numbers and I read it
backwards: **the continuity control scored HIGHER than the real reading**
(0.9994 vs 0.9978). §3 already says exact or inverted agreement between a
control and its measurement is a bug report about the control. I had written
that lesson this same day, applied it correctly to the *translation* control
minutes earlier — and then walked past the identical signal in the rotation
block, because by then the vacuity was pointing at a conclusion I found
interesting.

Post-fix the same three checks read **99.01%, 37 clamps, 0.9993 against a
control of 0.9614** — imperfect, discriminating, and therefore meaningful.
**A test that cannot fail and a test that passes look identical in a
results table.** The only way to tell them apart is to ask what the failing
case would have been, and I asked that question of the arithmetic ceiling
(correctly concluding ~36° was impossible for animation) without asking it
of my own three green checks.

#### What I should have done differently

The ceiling argument was sound *as far as it went*: 36° really is impossible
for character animation, so something was definitely wrong. **I then jumped
from "something is wrong" to "the spec is wrong", when my own implementation
was the far more likely culprit and the cheaper thing to re-check.** §3's
rule about relayed claims — verify before adopting — has an obvious mirror
that was not written down until now: **verify before REFUTING, and suspect
your own reading first.** A refutation is a claim like any other and deserves
the same bar; publishing one costs the other side real time, and Team A spent
theirs replicating a result that was never there.

Recorded in §3. Team A's handling is worth copying too: they measured before
accepting, withdrew their first hypothesis explicitly when it turned out to
be a guess made before they had numbers, and — having found the divergence
was mine — still fixed the two genuine defects in their own section that my
wrong implementation had surfaced.

#### 9.37.2 Rotation CONFIRMED, and a synthetic suite that catches the bug that got published

Two independently-written decoders now agree on real data — this project's
180.00 / 34.40 / 83.69 (max / median / p90 degrees) against Team A's
180.00 / 31.16 / 80.40. **The median gap is small, unexplained, and recorded
rather than smoothed over.** Rotation is CONFIRMED — disassembly plus two
empirical replays.

Team A hoisted the assembly to the top of §6c.2 after this project reported
it was effectively unfindable. Their framing of why is worth keeping:
**"present in the document" and "available to a reader" are different
claims.** The formula sat 85 lines below the description inside the
numeric-replay subsection, and stating the achievable extreme was not a
substitute — the factors 64 and 4 were visible without being placeable.

**New suite: `tests/synthetic_anim_payload_test.cpp`, 11 tests, 15th green
suite.** Fixtures built from the spec, never from the reader. Two of them use
an **external oracle** — Team A's worked key (control `88 BF 7F C4`, samples
`00 6F C0`, expected components `+0.176798 / −0.013812 / −0.022790`) — so the
assertion comes from an independently-written decoder rather than from a
restatement of this reader's own arithmetic.

**Mutation-tested, because a green suite proves nothing on its own.**
Restoring the exact published-and-retracted assembly — `(base + mult*delta) *
SCALE`, no `*64`, no `*4` — makes **6 checks fail across the two tests
written for it**. The build was verified to have succeeded separately before
reading that as a catch: a compile failure and a caught mutation both exit 1,
and §3 records a previous run where that confusion produced false negatives.

One test caught an error while being written: the expected extreme was
hand-computed as `−0.707160` from a rounded scale, against the true
`−0.70719329`. Worth noting *because* it is minor — the expectation was
written out independently rather than by printing what the reader returns and
pasting it back, which is the only version of this test that can fail.

#### An external correction worth recording: exact coincidence is WEAK evidence

Team A logged both of their predictions about this project's bug as wrong,
and the second one carries a lesson sharper than the first. They solved the
0.181 ceiling backwards to a 4-bit base and presented it as arithmetic rather
than as a guess — and the digit match was **coincidental**: `0.176798` is
just `8 × 64 × 4 × SCALE` for an unremarkable base value on the axis they
happened to pick.

**An exact numeric coincidence is weaker evidence than a matching average,
not stronger.** One matching number is a sample of size one; exactness is
persuasive in a way magnitude is not, while carrying no more information.
That is a direct companion to §3's *two aggregates agreeing is not a
relation* — the same error with the sample size reduced to one, and it feels
*more* convincing rather than less, which is what makes it dangerous.

They also turned this project's own rule back on themselves: they measured
before accepting (which is what surfaced the real spec defects), but then
guessed twice at the specific bug instead of publishing one named key's
intermediates — which should have been the first move, not the third. The
bracket beats the hypothesis, again.

**Same mistake in both directions on the same day:** this project walked past
its own control-agreement rule on rotation hours after applying it correctly
to translation; Team A walked past a lesson they had written that morning
against a displacement scan. Recorded because it argues that these rules
don't fail from being unknown — they fail from being unapplied at the moment
a wrong answer looks interesting.

### 9.38 Flags `0x40`: the extra payload is real, uniquely located, and unpredicted (SUPERSEDED — see §9.54: not "extra payload", a skipped layer-override table)

The last open piece of the `.anim_pc` payload, attacked from the data side
now that a verified walk exists (`tools/validation/probe_anim_flag40.cpp`).

| All 518 clips carrying the bit | |
|---|---|
| Land on `+0x30` walking the declared tracks | **0** — confirms the 0/518 |
| Land when the SAME walk continues past the declared count | **328** |
| Never land within +512 extra blocks | **190** |
| **Mean number of block counts that land** | **1.00** |

> **⚠ THE AMBIGUITY RESULT BELOW IS REFUTED — see §9.44.** A wrong start
> (+7 bytes) achieves the same "exactly one working count" in 333/518,
> marginally *more* than the real start's 328. Uniqueness was a property of
> a 512-wide search, not of the data. The paragraph is kept as written
> because "this was the new information" was the central claim and its
> failure is the instructive part. What survives §9.44 lists precisely.

**The ambiguity result is the new information.** Team A reported the landing
rate but not how many block counts land per clip. It is **exactly one, every
time**: no clip has two different continuations that both hit its declared
end. A self-terminating walk hitting a coincidental landing would not behave
that way, so this is a **location**, not a fit. That materially strengthens
the "there is more payload and it parses as more tracks" reading — while
still not establishing *what* the extra blocks are.

**Denominators, since the two teams' figures differ and both are right.**
Theirs is 334/397, over clips that walk short. Mine is **328/518**, over
*every* clip carrying the bit — which includes the ~121 that fail the walk
outright. Same phenomenon, conservative denominator; quoting 84% and 63.3%
as though they disagreed would be the §3 error again.

**The extra count is real but not predicted by anything in the header:**

> **⚠ REFUTED — see §9.46.** A search from a deliberately wrong start
> (+7 bytes) produces the identical clustering: **310 clips at a single
> value**, 42 instead of 39. The tight concentration was search geometry,
> not data. The table stands as published because the shape of its failure
> is instructive — the same 310 clips group under both readings, so they do
> share something real; the *number* simply never described it.

| extra blocks | clips |
|---|---|
| **39** | **310** |
| 2 | 3 |
| 113 / 90 / 4 | 2 each |
| 75, 74, 73, 61, 55, 47, 17, … | 1 each |

14 distinct values over 328 clips. Scored against every header field
available: `+0x0A` (track count) matches **1/328**, `+0x0B` (bone count)
**1/328** — chance. `bones − tracks` does not match either (the `auto_drv`
cluster is tracks 46, bones 69, extra 39, while `bones − tracks` is 23).
**So the count is not derivable from the header, on this population, by any
candidate tested.** Stated as the predicate: these fields do not predict it,
which is weaker and more accurate than "nothing does".

**What the clustering suggests, marked as HYPOTHESIS and doing no work
here.** 310 of 328 share `extra = 39`, and the named examples are all
vehicle-occupant clips — `auto_drv_ak_fire_*`, `auto_drv_ps_fire_*`,
`auto_ridel_*` — with an identical rig signature (46 tracks, 69 bones). That
is consistent with a second animated entity layered into the same clip, and
consistent with Team A's independent filename-based guess. It is also exactly
the kind of story that explains everything and predicts nothing, so it is
recorded and not used: a clip on the *same* rig signature
(`auto_ridel_ps_fire_wndright`, 46 tracks) has `extra = 74`, which the
layered-entity reading does not account for.

**Still OPEN, now with sharper edges:** what the extra blocks contain, why
the count is 39 for a large cluster and scattered elsewhere, and what
distinguishes the **190** clips that never land. That 190 is itself larger
than the ~121 that fail the walk outright, so roughly 69 clips walk short
*and* are not explained by continuation — a third sub-population nobody has
characterised, and the honest next target.

#### 9.38.1 The third population is turn-in-place animation — root motion, measured

Chased the sub-population §9.38 named, and it characterises cleanly. First,
a correction to my own arithmetic: I estimated it at **~69** by subtracting
Team A's outright-failure count from my landing count — **two teams'
populations in one subtraction**, the exact error §3 keeps recording. Measured
directly on one population it is **55**, with 135 outright failures.

Split the 190 non-landing clips by whether the *declared* walk completes:

> **⚠ THE TWO NUMBERS IN THIS TABLE ARE SUPERSEDED — see §9.40.** They were
> produced by a probe's private copy of the walk, which disagrees with the
> shipping reader on 14 clips. Correct figures: **121** outright failures and
> **69** in the third population. Kept visible rather than edited away, and
> marked *here* rather than only corrected downstream — a correction that
> lives only in a later section leaves the wrong number standing for anyone
> who reads this one first, which is the same defect as a stale confidence
> label (§3).

| flags `0x40` clips that never reach `+0x30` | ~~then~~ | **now (§9.40)** |
|---|---|---|
| Fail the declared-count walk outright | ~~135~~ | **121** |
| **Walk cleanly, but never reach `+0x30` at any count** | ~~55~~ | **69** ← the third population |

**Track count discriminates nothing** — 45 and 46 dominate all three groups
(landed, third, failures). Measured on all three rather than on the odd one
out, which is what makes "nothing" a result rather than an absence.

**Two independent measurements do discriminate, one on labels and one on
bytes:**

| | landed (328) | **third (55)** | failures (135) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Name contains `trn` | 1.5% | **81.8%** | 1.5% |
| Root rotation > 45° | 2.1% | **87.3%** | 8.9% |
| Median root rotation | 0.00° | **90.00°** | 0.00° |

The filename result alone would be a story about labels. The root-motion
angle at header `+0x0C` is a **format-level property read from bytes**, and
it agrees: a median of **exactly 90.00°** against 0.00° in both controls,
matching the `trn90_l` / `trn90_r` names precisely. Both controls sit at
baseline on both measures, so neither is picking up something merely common
in the archive.

**HYPOTHESIS, stated as one and doing no work in the conclusion:** a
turn-in-place clip needs the root's orientation *over time*, while `+0x0C`
records only the net delta — so these clips plausibly carry per-frame root
motion as extra payload that is **not more tracks**, which is exactly why
continuing the track walk never reaches their declared end. Untested.

**What this does NOT show, and it matters:** flags `0x40` is not simply "has
root motion". The 328 clips that *do* land also carry the bit and have a
median root rotation of **0.00°**. So the bit marks "extra payload" and there
are at least **two different kinds** of it — one that parses as further
track blocks, one that does not. That is a sharper statement of the open
question than §9.38 could make, and it narrows the target: the remaining
work is not "what does `0x40` add" but "what is the second kind of extra
payload, in clips whose root turns".

### 9.39 Delta mode resolved: the per-key delta measures FROM THE BASE

`spec-anim-format.md` §6c.6 item 1 was open with an explicit note that the
distinguishing test "has not been run": does a translation key's delta
measure from the control record's base, or accumulate across the run?

```
reading A (from base):  pos_k = base/64 + delta_k          / 4000
reading B (accumulate): pos_k = base/64 + sum(delta_0..k)  / 4000
```

**Discriminator: cross-run continuity.** A control record covers a run of
keys and the next record starts the next run. An animation does not teleport
because a record boundary falls between two consecutive keys, so the correct
reading should make run *i*'s last position and run *i+1*'s first position
nearly equal — and the wrong one should not. Both readings scored on the
same pairs, each against its own control (the gap to an **unrelated** run in
the same track, which says what "no continuity" looks like in this data).

`tools/validation/probe_anim_delta_mode.cpp`, 3,687 clips, 75,796 runs:

| run length | reading A | reading B | A/B |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | *identical by construction* | | 30,602 pairs, **zero information** |
| 2–4 | 0.0332 | 0.0599 | 1.8× |
| **5+** | **0.0137** | **0.1137** | **8.3×** |

| long runs (n = 13,017) | median gap | own control | separation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **reading A** | **0.0137** | 0.0923 | **6.76×** |
| reading B | 0.1137 | 0.2085 | 1.83× |

**Reading A wins, and the shape of the win is what makes it convincing.**
Not the margin alone — the **dose-response**. The two readings are
*identical* at run length 1, diverge mildly at 2–4, and diverge sharply at
5+, which is exactly what an accumulation error does and exactly what a
coincidence does not. Reading A also gets **better** as runs lengthen
(0.0332 → 0.0137) while B gets worse (0.0599 → 0.1137): longer runs mean
smoother motion, so a correct reading should improve, and an accumulating
error should compound. Reading B barely clears its own control at 1.83×.

**[CONFIRMED — empirical.]** Not disassembly-confirmed; this is one
independent line of evidence, well controlled, and should be labelled that
way rather than promoted.

#### The stratification was the whole result

The pooled figures were **7.34× (A) against 4.83× (B)** — a real but
unimpressive margin that would have supported "probably A, weakly". Stratified,
it is 6.76× against 1.83× with an 8.3× gap ratio.

The cause: **30,602 of 70,220 pairs — 43.6% — had run length 1, where the
two readings are arithmetically identical.** Those pairs cannot distinguish
anything, and they were dragging both columns toward each other. This is the
denominator lesson pointing the *other* way from usual: the familiar failure
is a mixed population inflating a result, and here a
zero-information stratum was **deflating** one. Same fix either way — find
out what is in the denominator before reading the rate — but worth recording
because the usual instinct, "a diluted number is an overstatement", would
have pointed away from the truth here.

**Still open in §6c.6:** the fourth decoder output lane, and whether a
16-byte load over an 8-byte record means adjacent records blend. The second
one is now more interesting, not less: inter-record blending is a *continuity*
mechanism, and continuity is exactly what this test just found to be strong
at record boundaries under reading A.

### 9.40 A census that answered someone else's question and broke my own number (SUPERSEDED — see §9.54: the whole split this section corrects is retired)

Team A flagged that this project's **518** and their spec's **522** looked
like the same population disagreeing, and — correctly — asked each side to
**re-derive independently with a stated predicate** rather than reconcile
arithmetically. Did that (`tools/validation/probe_anim_population.cpp`,
which deliberately references no external figure).

#### The 518/522 gap was never a disagreement

| predicate | count |
|---|---|
| `*.anim_pc` entries | 4,209 (0 extract failures, 0 parse rejects) |
| flags `0x40` **set** | **518** |
| flags `0x40` **clear** | 3,691 |
| within bit-set: walk / fail / land / miss | 397 / 121 / **0** / 397 |
| within bit-clear: walk / fail / land / miss | 3,689 / 2 / 3,687 / 2 |

**522 is a corpus-wide non-landing count** (399 miss + 123 fail, spanning
*both* strata); **518 is the bit-carrying population**. The 4-clip difference
is exactly the bit-clear residual (2 miss + 2 fail) that their own §6c.4
table already lists. Two correct numbers counting different things — the
same cross-boundary shape as §9.35, caught this time *before* either side
built on it.

#### The census broke my own split, and the way it broke is the lesson

It reported **121** outright failures where §9.38.1 had said 135. Chased it:
`probe_anim_flag40.cpp` was asking **its own private copy of the walk**
(`walkN`) whether the declared walk completes, while the census asked the
**shipping reader** (`sr3anim::Payload::walk`). They disagree on **14 clips**.
Corrected split, shipping reader as the authority:

> **⚠ OVERSTATED — see §9.45.** "Shipping reader as the authority" is a
> tie-break, not evidence. The cause of the disagreement is now known
> (`span == 0` translation control records) and **which behaviour is correct
> is OPEN** — the file's own endpoint oracle cannot decide it, and the
> association actually leans the other way. The true split is **bounded**:
> 121/69 if `span == 0` is legitimate, 135/55 if it signals a misparse.
> Neither is established. The table below reads as though 121/69 were
> settled; it is not.

| | was | **now** |
|---|---|---|
| land via continuation | 328 | **328** |
| outright failures | 135 | **121** |
| third population | 55 | **69** |

The third population's signal survives but weakens honestly: `trn` in the
name **65.2%** (was 81.8%) against 1.7% in failures; root rotation > 45°
**71.0%** (was 87.3%) against 9.1%; median root rotation still **exactly
90.00°**. The 14 clips that moved in are mostly *not* turns, which is why
the rates fell — and they fell in the direction that makes the result less
flattering, which is the direction that suggests it is real.

#### I "corrected" a right answer into a wrong one

§9.38.1 records me estimating the third population at **~69** by subtracting
Team A's failure count from mine, then rejecting that as "subtracting across
populations you did not both define" and re-measuring directly to get 55.
**The subtraction was right. The direct re-measurement was wrong.**

The rule is still correct — two counts over differently-defined sets cannot
be subtracted, and I had no way to know at the time that ours were
compatible. What the episode adds is the missing half: **"re-measure it
directly" only beats "infer it" if the direct measurement uses the
authoritative implementation.** Mine used a probe's private copy of
production logic, which is a *second implementation*, and second
implementations drift. I replaced an inference I couldn't validate with a
measurement I hadn't validated either, and felt more confident for it.

**The distinction that matters: a probe may carry its own copy of the logic
deliberately, and that is sometimes correct** — `validate_vehicle_runs.cpp`
keeps a pre-tightening copy on purpose, documented, precisely so it can
measure what the reader now filters (§9.34.1). The failure here was that
`walkN` was an *accidental* second implementation, assumed identical to the
reader and never checked. Deliberate divergence, documented, is a tool.
Undocumented divergence, assumed away, is a bug with two places to hide.

`probe_anim_flag40.cpp` now prints `walkN vs shipping reader disagree: 14`
on every run, marked **SHOULD BE 0**, so the discrepancy cannot quietly
return. Which 14, and why, is **OPEN** — the disagreement is recorded rather
than explained, because I have not measured the cause.

### 9.41 Two §6c.6 items probed: one narrowed, one genuinely undecided

#### 9.41.1 The fourth byte per translation key — four candidates refuted

Each translation key carries one byte beyond its three axis deltas, meaning
OPEN (§6c.6 item 2). Characterised over **465,547 keys from 3,687 clean
clips** (`tools/validation/probe_anim_fourth_byte.cpp`):

**What it is:** small, right-skewed, **unsigned** — median 2, mean 7.49,
71.5% of values in 1–7, only 3.4% zero, 96.6% positive under an `int8`
reading against 0.03% negative. Nothing like a balanced signed delta.

**What it is NOT — four candidates refuted, each against its own control:**

| candidate | result |
|---|---|
| constant within a control record's run | **46.95%** against a **47.71%** same-length-window control — ratio 0.984×, no separation at all |
| a scale/exponent selector for the three deltas | every correlation with delta magnitude \|r\| ≤ 0.03 over 465,547 samples; three exact-match forms all at 0.74–0.84%, i.e. noise |
| a forward frame/time index | correlation with track-local index is **−0.196** — the wrong sign |
| a countdown index | both restatements fail against their own shuffled controls (2.45% vs 2.04%; 7.15% vs 6.63%) |
| a slot number | **6.42%** of keys have byte > the track's key count |

**The one surviving signal, unexplained:** `byte == track-local index` in
**19.2%** of keys against a **2.02%** shuffled control. Real separation, no
identified functional form — neither ascending nor descending fits.

**The strongest correlations are structural, not per-key motion:** −0.337
with the track's total key count, −0.186 with the covering run's span. That
is the signature of a **per-key duration** — a densely-keyed track packs many
keys into a fixed clip length, so each gap is small. Being tested now with a
decisive oracle: every track in a clip spans the *same* animation, so under a
duration reading `sum(bytes)` must be nearly equal across tracks **within** a
clip and vary **between** clips.

**The agent flagged two of its own controls as uninformative** rather than
quoting them: a `dx`-based monotonicity control has a different marginal
distribution from the byte, and a half-rotation control reads ~0% for any
mostly-non-constant ordered sequence whether or not a trend exists. Reporting
a control you ran and then declining to count it is the behaviour §3 asks
for, and it is rarer than it should be.

#### 9.41.2 Inter-record blending — a real crossover, and still OPEN

§6c.6 item 3: a 16-byte load over an 8-byte record is consistent with
fetching two consecutive records to blend between them (HYPOTHESIS,
untraced). Tested with the same cross-run continuity oracle that settled
§9.39, over 70,220 adjacent run pairs:

| stratum | NOBLEND | BLEND | n |
|---|---|---|---|
| span 1 (**zero information** — `f`=0 makes the readings identical) | — | — | 30,602 (43.6%) |
| span 2–4 | 6.98× | **16.10×** | 26,601 |
| span 5+ | **8.00×** | 4.01× | 13,017 |

**The two informative strata point in opposite directions**, and this is not
noise. Three checks establish that:

* **Model divergence** — the two readings' own predictions differ by a
  comparable amount in both strata (median 0.037 at span 2–4, 0.042 at 5+),
  so neither stratum is one where the hypotheses agree anyway.
* **Smooth monotonic crossover** — BLEND's gap grows 0.0101 → 0.0308 from
  span 2 to span 10+, while NOBLEND's shrinks 0.0400 → 0.0091. A crossing
  near span 4, not a flip.
* **Base-difference control** — raw `|B1−B0|` shrinks only ~33% across that
  range, far too little to explain NOBLEND's 77% improvement as "long runs
  are static so their bases already agree".

**Recorded as still OPEN.** The directional lean, stated as a lean: a true
blend-toward-next-record decoder should get *better*, not 3× worse, as its
weight `f` approaches 1 at span 10+ — where the hypothesis makes its
strongest prediction. That argues against the specific linear `f = k/span`
mechanism, and is consistent with §9.39's independent finding that the delta
measures from the base. A plausible reading of BLEND's short-span win, **not
tested and doing no work here**: at span 2 the last key genuinely sits about
halfway to the next base in smooth motion, so BLEND fits the *animation*
rather than revealing the *storage*.

**Why this is a good outcome rather than a failure.** The §9.39 pattern was
diluted-then-decisive: every non-trivial stratum agreed and only the
zero-information one blurred the pooled figure. Here the non-trivial strata
genuinely disagree, and the pooled figure (9.89× vs 7.34×, favouring BLEND)
would have been published as a confirmation. **Stratification prevented a
wrong answer this time, having rescued a right one last time** — the same
discipline catching opposite errors.

### 9.42 The rigid-bone claim is REFUTED — and the reason resolves the cross-format null

§9.37's cross-format test (anim translations vs rig rest offsets) returned a
null, and stratifying by track→bone table (§agent work) left it confounded.
So the same physical claim was tested a second way, needing **no rig, no bone
mapping and no cross-format pairing** (`tools/validation/probe_anim_bone_rigidity.cpp`):
if a translation track is a bone's parent-relative position, the bone is
rigid, so `|t|` must be near-constant across that track's keys.

**It is not.** In the only stratum with power (5+ keys, **n = 10,122**):

| | median relSpread | real < control, per track |
|---|---|---|
| real track | **1.2687** | — |
| shuffled-axis control | **1.0572** | real wins only **32.3%** |
| cross-track control | 1.7458 | real wins 93.5% *(weak bar, 90% skipped)* |

The shuffled control takes each track's own keys and draws the three axes
from keys a third of the track apart — destroying the vector relationship
while preserving every per-axis distribution. **The real reading is
*looser* than that control.** If these were rigid-length vectors turning in
direction, decorrelating the axes should have inflated the spread. It did
the opposite.

The apparent tight cluster in short tracks (2–4 keys: ~65–70% below 0.25) is
**reproduced point-for-point by the same shuffled control**, so it is an
artifact of narrow per-axis marginals in short single-run tracks, not
evidence of rigidity.

#### The population accounting is the actual finding

| tracks seen (3,687 clean clips) | 166,297 |
|---|---|
| **zero translation keys** | **150,466 (90.5%)** |
| exactly one key (zero information) | 5,373 |
| usable for this test | **10,419 (6.3%)** |

**Nine tracks in ten carry no translation data at all.** That reframes
everything: translation is not stored per bone as a rest offset — it is
stored only for the bones that actually *translate*. Which means the bones
that have translation tracks are precisely the ones whose translation
**changes**, so of course their magnitude is not constant.

**So the physical claim was not merely unproven, it was misapplied.** I
assumed every bone's translation track restates its rigid parent offset;
in fact the format omits translation for the ~90% of bones that only rotate,
and stores it exactly where it varies. The cross-format null in §9.37 follows
directly — comparing an animated translation against a rest offset only makes
sense if the translation *is* the rest offset, and for the tracks that exist
it is not.

**What this does NOT touch:** the decode arithmetic
(`axis = base/64 + delta/4000`) stands — §9.39 confirmed it independently
through cross-run continuity at 6.76× against its control, and this result
says nothing about it. A wrong interpretation of a correctly decoded number
is a different defect from a wrong decode, and conflating them would repeat
§9.37.1 exactly.

**Implementation consequence, and it is load-bearing for rendering:** a
bone's local translation must come from the **rig's rest offset** when the
clip carries no translation track for it, and from the **animation** only
when it does. A renderer that expects a translation per bone per frame will
be wrong for 90% of bones.

#### The agent caught its own broken control

Worth recording because it is the behaviour §3 asks for and rarely gets: the
first shuffled control drew the three axes from *adjacent* keys, which
usually share a control record and therefore a base — a control that could
barely fail. It was identified as such, rebuilt to span a third of the track
so it crosses run boundaries, and re-run before any number was reported.
Had it shipped, the real reading would have "beaten" a control that was
nearly a copy of itself, and the rigidity claim would have been **confirmed
by a broken instrument** — the §9.34 name-base control failure exactly, one
step earlier in the pipeline.

#### 9.42.1 The double-meaning audit, run on this project's own work

Team A found a third instance of the same defect class this week — the word
**"lands"** doing double duty in their own spec: *"reaches the declared
`+0x30` endpoint"* (true for 0/518) and *"reaches it when the walk continues
past the declared count"* (true for 328/518). Same word, two predicates,
opposite answers. Their rule: **never write a bare noun that could mean two
things — say which kind, every time, including in table headers and variable
names.**

Ran it here. **This project had the identical defect, in the harness that
produced the numbers**, printing `land on +0x30 as declared` and `land with
MORE blocks` three lines apart. Relabelled to name the predicate every time:

```
  reach +0x30 at DECLARED count : 0     (expected 0)
  reach +0x30 by CONTINUING     : 328
  reach +0x30 at NO count <=+512: 190
```

**And re-reading those tables under the audit found something worse.**
§9.38.1 still carried **55 / 135** with nothing marking that §9.40 had
superseded them with **69 / 121**. The correction existed — one section
later — and the original table stood unmarked, so anyone reading §9.38.1
first took away the wrong numbers. Now marked in place with both values
shown.

That is the stale-label defect (§3) appearing for the **second time in this
file in one day**, and both times it was found by an audit aimed at something
else — the first at headings, this one at terminology. Neither was found by
re-reading the prose, because the prose was correct both times. **The
correction and the stale artifact each read fine in isolation; only
enumerating the artifacts separately from the text finds the mismatch.**

Worth stating as a working rule: **after correcting a number, grep for the
old value.** It is a five-second check, it does not depend on remembering
where the number was repeated, and both of today's instances would have been
caught by it immediately.

### 9.43 §6c.6 item 2 RESOLVED: the fourth byte is a per-key duration

The extra byte after each translation key's three axis deltas — OPEN since
the payload was decoded — is a **per-key duration**.

**The oracle: every track in a clip spans the same animation.** So if the
byte is a per-key duration, `sum(bytes)` over a track must be nearly equal
for *every* track in that clip, and must vary *between* clips. Measured
(`tools/validation/probe_anim_fourth_duration.cpp`), 2,950 clips with ≥2
qualifying tracks:

| | n | median relative spread | frac < 0.01 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **REAL — `sum(byte)`, within clip** | 2,950 | **0.0057** | **50.27%** |
| CONTROL 1 — `sum(byte)`, across clips | 2,950 | 0.3670 | 28.92% |
| CONTROL 2 — `sum(\|dx\|)`, within clip | 2,938 | 1.4041 | 0.14% |

**64× separation from the cross-clip control; 246× from the same-shape
control.** Half of all clips have every track's byte-sum agreeing to within
1%. **[CONFIRMED — empirical.]** Not disassembly-checked.

**Control 2 is the one that makes this a result.** It sums a *different
per-key byte* (`|dx|`) over the same tracks in the same way, so it holds
track length and summation structure fixed and varies only which byte is
summed. Without it, low within-clip spread could have been an artifact of
tracks in a clip having similar lengths. It scores 246× worse, so it isn't.

**What the total is NOT:** `sum(byte)` does not equal the track's rotation
key count — correlation **+0.04**, exact match 6.37% of 15,831 tracks. The
rotation control records' span sum equals `rotationKeys` exactly in
15,831/15,831 tracks, so that quantity carries no information beyond
`rotationKeys` and was checked for exactly that reason before being used.

#### How four refuted candidates led to the right one

§9.41.1 refuted "per-run constant", "delta scale selector", "forward index"
and "countdown index", each against its own control, and was written up as
*not* determining what the byte is. The answer came from the residue those
refutations left behind: the strongest surviving correlations were
**structural** — −0.337 with the track's key count, −0.186 with the run span
— and negative. A per-key duration predicts exactly that sign, because a
densely-keyed track packs more keys into a fixed clip length.

**The refutations were not wasted motion; they were the measurement.** Four
candidates eliminated with controls left a correlation pattern that only one
hypothesis explained, and that hypothesis then passed a sharp independent
oracle. Worth recording against the instinct that a probe reporting "I could
not determine this" has failed — §9.41.1's honest negative is what made
§9.43 possible one step later.

#### An unexplained signal, deliberately still open

`byte == the key's track-local index` in **19.2%** of keys against a 2.02%
shuffled control. The obvious deflation — that both quantities are small so
they coincide by chance — was tested by stratifying on index, and **it is
not that**: the ratio to control *widens* with index (4.9× at index 0–7,
29.5× at 8–31, **47×** at 32+) where a small-number coincidence would
converge toward the control. Real, above chance, and not the ascending or
countdown index already refuted. **[OPEN.]**

Now under test: whether `sum(byte)` per clip matches a header field, which
would both confirm the duration reading independently and identify a
currently-unidentified header quantity.

### 9.44 The ambiguity-1.00 result is REFUTED by its own missing control (RETRACTED — the control had the wrong anchor; see §9.52. §9.52's reinstatement is itself now SUPERSEDED — see §9.54: not ambiguity, a skipped table)

Team A cautioned that "exactly one block count works, never two" is only
evidence of a location if the candidate space is narrow — and that with a
wide space, a unique fit can be a property of the search. **They were right,
and the check they suggested destroys the result.**

The search tried **512 candidate block counts**. Running the identical
continuation search from a deliberately wrong start (+7 bytes, the
displacement the spec's own walk control uses):

| | clips finding a working count | mean working counts |
|---|---|---|
| **REAL start** | **328 / 518 (63.32%)** | 1.00 |
| **WRONG start (+7)** | **333 / 518 (64.29%)** | 1.00 |

**The wrong start does marginally better than the right one, with identical
ambiguity.** So:

* **"Ambiguity is exactly 1.00, therefore a location not a fit" — REFUTED.**
  Uniqueness was a property of the search. I reported it (§9.38) as *the*
  new information, and it was worth nothing.
* **"328 clips reach `+0x30` by continuing the walk" — UNSUPPORTED** as
  evidence that extra track blocks exist. A permissive search over 512
  candidates finds *some* count that lands for ~64% of these clips no matter
  where it starts.

**This applies equally to Team A's 334/397**, which used the same method —
flagged to them immediately, because it is their figure as much as mine and
neither of us ran this control.

#### What survives, stated precisely

Not everything falls, and the distinction matters:

* **The 121 outright walk failures survive** — determined by
  `Payload::walk`, not by the search.
* **The 69-clip third population survives, and is arguably strengthened.** It
  is defined by *absence*: these clips walk cleanly yet no count in 512
  produces a landing. A search that fires spuriously ~64% of the time finding
  **nothing** for 69 clips is a stronger negative than it looked before, not
  a weaker one.
* **The turn-in-place signature survives intact**, because its decisive
  measurement never touched the walk: root-motion rotation is read from the
  header quaternion at `+0x0C`. Median **90.00°** in the third population
  against **0.00°** in both other groups is independent of any search.
* **The 328 bucket survives only as a label**, meaning "a count was found",
  which we now know is a weak predicate.

#### Why this fits Team A's reframe rather than fighting it

They report from disassembly that **nothing in the stream setup ever tests
flags `0x40`** — the only place the bit is read is a runtime layer-blend
sampler gating a caller-supplied per-layer override. If the decoder never
uses the bit to locate anything in the file, then **there may be no
`0x40`-keyed extra-block structure to find at all** — and a search that
"works" from any starting offset is exactly what you would expect when there
is nothing real to lock onto.

Three payload models were refuted before this; the fourth explanation is that
the question was malformed. That is a better outcome than a fourth refuted
model.

#### The lesson, which is not the obvious one

The obvious reading is "I forgot a control". The sharper one: **I did run
controls — several, carefully — and reported an ambiguity count precisely
because §3 demands one.** The ambiguity count was itself the *response* to a
discipline. What I never asked was whether that count could distinguish
anything, and **a diligence measure adopted as a habit stops being a check
once you stop asking what its failing case looks like.** §3 already says a
control must be able to fail; it did not say that an *ambiguity count* is a
control and needs the same test. It does now.

### 9.45 The 14 disagreeing clips: cause found, correctness NOT decided

§9.40 recorded that two implementations of the same walk disagree on 14 of
518 clips, with the cause OPEN. Found it, and then found that knowing the
cause does not settle which side is right.

**Cause — unanimous, 14/14, byte-verified**
(`tools/validation/probe_anim_walk_divergence.cpp`): the probe's private
`walkN` returns failure the instant an 8-byte translation control record
reads `span == 0`; `sr3anim::Payload::walk` has no such check and advances to
the next record until the spans cover the track's keys. Both implementations
enter the divergent track at the **identical cursor** in every case, so the
split originates strictly inside that one loop. Direction is unanimous too:
all 14 are *reader says complete, probe says failed*; **0/14** go the other
way. The three other candidate causes scored **0/14** each, and
**cause-unknown is 0/14**.

**Which behaviour is CORRECT is a different question, and the file's own
oracle cannot answer it** (`tools/validation/probe_anim_span0.cpp`):

| | lands on `+0x30` | misses |
|---|---|---|
| contains a `span == 0` record | **0** | **14** |
| contains none | **3,687** | 385 |

25 such records exist in 87,410 (0.03%), in exactly 14 clips — **precisely
the 14 that disagree**, which independently confirms the cause analysis is
complete rather than partial.

**The oracle is silent by construction here.** It can only confirm the skip
(a clip containing `span == 0` that still lands would prove skipping right);
it cannot refute it, because a clip that misses could be missing for any
reason. No such clip exists, so: **OPEN.**

#### The association points the other way from where I assumed

I treated the shipping reader as the authority in §9.40 and corrected the
split to 121/69 on that basis. **That was a reasonable default and it is not
evidence.** "Authoritative" means *this is what the project ships*, not *this
is correct* — and the data now suggests the probe may have been right:

`span == 0` occurs in **0 of 3,687** landing clips and **14 of 399**
non-landing ones. A record declaring it covers no keys is exactly what you
would expect to read if the cursor had drifted into bytes that are not a
control record at all. On that reading `span == 0` is a **symptom of a
misparse**, not a legitimate padding record, and refusing it is the more
correct behaviour.

**So the split is bounded, not known:**

| | if `span == 0` is legitimate | if it signals a misparse |
|---|---|---|
| outright walk failures | **121** | **135** |
| third population | **69** | **55** |

Both §9.38.1's original figures and §9.40's correction are inside these
bounds. **Neither is established**, and §9.40's confident "corrected split,
shipping reader as the authority" overstated what had been shown.

**What this does not disturb:** the turn-in-place signature is measured on
the header's root-motion quaternion, which no walk touches — median 90.00°
against 0.00° in both other groups holds under either bound.

#### The lesson: an authority is a tie-break, not an oracle

Two implementations disagreeing is a *question*. Picking the shipping one
answers "which do we ship", and I let that stand in for "which is right"
because the shipping reader had been validated elsewhere — on a population
that, it turns out, **contains none of the disputed cases**. A validation
that never exercised the disputed behaviour confers no authority over it.

**Ask what population validated the authority before deferring to it.**
`Payload::walk` is confirmed against 3,687 landing clips, and not one of them
contains a `span == 0` record.

### 9.46 "extra = 39 in 310 clips" also falls — and how it falls is the informative part (RETRACTED — same wrong-anchor control; see §9.52. §9.52's reinstatement is itself now SUPERSEDED — see §9.54: "39" was the skipped table's size, not extra track blocks)

Team A's rule — **a region DEFINED BY the thing you are testing cannot test
that thing** — applied to the one §9.38 result not yet re-examined. The
extra-block histogram was published as a finding: *extra = 39 in 310 of 328
clips*. But the extra count is the **first working count of the same search**
that §9.44 showed works equally well from a wrong start. So: run the
histogram on the control too.

| extra blocks | REAL start | CONTROL (+7 bytes) |
|---|---|---|
| **39** | **310** | 0 |
| **42** | 0 | **310** |
| 90 | 2 | 2 |
| distinct values | 14 | 13 |

**The control clusters exactly as tightly — 310 clips at a single value —
just at 42 instead of 39.** Same population, same concentration, a number
shifted by three.

**So "extra = 39" is REFUTED as a finding about the data.** The tightness
was never evidence: a search that finds a fixed target will report whatever
block count reaches it from wherever it began, and starting seven bytes
earlier changes that count by a constant. The value carried no information
about the format.

#### What the control's *shape* still shows, stated carefully

The same **310 clips** cluster together under both readings. That
correspondence is not produced by the shift — it survived it. So those 310
clips genuinely share something (almost certainly a common rig and track
layout; they are the `auto_drv_*` / `auto_ridel_*` family at 46 tracks). What
is refuted is that the **number 39** describes anything. A real shared
property, measured by an instrument that cannot report it.

That distinction is worth keeping separate from the refutation, and equally
worth not over-reading: an unexplained grouping is not a finding either.

#### The §9.38 continuation analysis, now fully accounted

| claim | status |
|---|---|
| ambiguity exactly 1.00 ⇒ a location | **REINSTATED** (§9.52) — the "REFUTED" here used the wrong anchor; the correct anchor scores 37/383 (9.66%) vs 328/383 (85.64%) |
| 328 clips reach `+0x30` by continuing | **REINSTATED** (§9.52) as evidence of extra track blocks |
| extra = 39 in 310 clips | **REINSTATED** (§9.52) — the correct-anchor control does NOT cluster at 39 (0/37, spread over 27 distinct values) |
| 121–135 outright walk failures | **stands** (§9.45, still open on which bound) |
| 55–69-clip third population | **stands, strengthened** — defined by resisting even a permissive search |
| turn-in-place signature, median root rotation 90.00° | **stands, untouched** — measured on the header quaternion, no walk involved |

**This table itself was wrong between 2026-09-12's two documentation passes — see §9.52 for the full correction.** The "REFUTED"/"UNSUPPORTED" verdicts above are what this section originally concluded; they do not describe the current state of the evidence.

**Three of my published claims about `0x40` are gone, and the two that
survive are the ones that never depended on the search.** That is not a
coincidence: the search was the common instrument, and once it was shown to
fire from any starting point, everything reading off it fell together while
everything measured independently held.

**The general form, which is the part to carry:** when one instrument
underpins several findings, its failure is **correlated**, not
distributed — they do not fail one at a time as you check them, they were
all already wrong. So the cheapest audit after discrediting an instrument is
not to re-test each conclusion, but to **list everything that read off it**
and treat the whole list as suspect until individually re-established.

### 9.47 Header `+0x06` identified: it is the clip's total duration

`spec-anim-format.md` §2 has carried `+0x06` as **[HYPOTHESIS]** — *"a u16
count, plausibly a frame or key count, but see §6 — the arithmetic does not
support the obvious reading."* It is the total duration, and two
independently-derived measurements now confirm each other.

**Measurement 1 (§9.43):** the extra byte per translation key is a per-key
duration, established by an oracle the format supplies — every track in a
clip spans the same animation, so `sum(bytes)` per track must agree across
that clip's tracks. It does: within-clip relative spread median **0.0057**,
against **64×** (cross-clip) and **246×** (same-shape) controls.

**Measurement 2 (here):** that per-clip total `S` **equals `+0x06` exactly**.

| | exact match | shuffled-S control |
|---|---|---|
| `+0x06` == S | **40.98%** (n=2,950) | **0.10%** — ~400× |
| stratified: clips whose tracks agree on S to ≤1% | **81.46%** (n=1,483) | — |
| stratified: clips whose tracks disagree | **0.07%** (n=1,467) | — |

Every near-control — track count, bone count, file size, declared payload
end — sits at chance against its own shuffle, which is what says the test is
working rather than merely agreeable. No `S/2`, `S+1` or `S−1` transform
matched at all, so this is not an off-by-one or a half-rate.

**The stratification is what makes it conclusive.** `S` is a median across
tracks and is only trustworthy where those tracks agree; the misses
concentrate almost perfectly in the clips where `S` is a known-bad estimate
(0.07% vs 81.46%). A wrong candidate would miss uniformly across both strata.

#### The two measurements confirm each other, and neither assumed the other

§9.43 established the byte is a duration **without reference to any header
field** — purely from tracks within a clip agreeing. §9.47 identified `+0x06`
**without reference to the duration reading** — purely by exact match against
a shuffled control. Each would stand if the other were withdrawn, and
together they close a field that has been HYPOTHESIS since the header was
first tabulated.

#### The §6 objection is answered, not overridden

Spec §6 refuted `payload ≈ +0x06 × tracks × bytes_per_key` — median 0.55
bytes per frame-track, "half a byte per key, which cannot be a literal
uncompressed key". **That refutation stands and does not conflict with this
one.** It refuted the payload being a *uniform array indexed by frame*; it
never refuted `+0x06` being the frame count. Keys are sparse and each holds
for a variable number of frames — which is exactly why a frames × tracks
array over-counts by roughly 2× (median 2.214 bytes per key is the mean gap
between keys). **The arithmetic that killed the uniform model is the same
arithmetic that predicts this one.**

#### A caveat with a testable prediction attached

The spec records `+0x06` ranging **2–1099**; measured `S` reaches **2016**
(median 240, p90 946). Those cannot always be equal, and the ~19% residual in
the tight stratum is unexplained. **Prediction, untested:** the mismatches
should concentrate in clips where `S > 1099`, because a `u16` field holding a
value the spec never observed above 1099 cannot represent them. If instead
the residual is spread evenly across the `S` range, something else is wrong
and this identification needs revisiting. Recorded as a prediction rather
than a result, so it can falsify rather than decorate.

**Tier: [CONFIRMED — empirical]** for `S == +0x06`, on two independent
lines with controls. Not disassembly-checked, and the *unit* remains
unidentified — 240 median is consistent with e.g. eight seconds at 30 Hz, but
nothing here establishes a rate and that arithmetic is offered only to show
the magnitude is not absurd.

### 9.48 `span == 0` resolved: it is a misparse signature, and my probe was right

§9.45 left the 14 disputed clips genuinely undecided, bounded at 121/69 or
135/55, because the endpoint oracle could only ever confirm the skip and had
returned silent. Team A proposed a **two-sided** test: the two readings make
opposite, symmetric predictions about the bytes *following* a `span == 0`
record — legitimate padding leaves the cursor correct, so the successor
should look like a real control record; a drifted cursor should produce
bytes that do not.

They also applied this project's own lesson to their proposal before making
it: **validate the plausibility profile before trusting it.** That gate was
made mandatory and it passed:

| profile validation (n = 86,051 clean records) | acceptance |
|---|---|
| baseline, real records | **94.39%** |
| misaligned +1 / +3 / +5 | **0.00%** |
| misaligned +2 (lands on `i16` boundaries — the "least bad" control) | 25.90% |

Bounds derived from data: span ∈ [1, 65], bases ∈ roughly [−200, 264]. Note
**the lower span bound is 1 — no clean record anywhere has `span == 0`.**

#### Per-clip verdict, n = 14

| verdict | clips |
|---|---|
| **DRIFT** (≥1 successor with span 12,682–65,099) | **11** |
| CLEAN (≥1 accepted, zero drift) | 3 |
| unscorable | 0 |

**Three clips have BOTH** an accepted successor and a drift successor —
`npc_head_blank`, `_fear`, `_sneer`: track 0's `span == 0` is followed by a
plausible record, track 2's drifts into a span above 33,000. One drift
invalidates a walk, so they are DRIFT.

#### The CLEAN bucket is a selection effect, not evidence

The three CLEAN clips (`npc_head_pain_b`, `_sad`, `_smile`) **have no track-2
translation data at all.** They were examined on two successors each, one of
which was tautological. They are not clean because `span == 0` is legitimate
there — **they never present an opportunity to drift.** Their sibling clips,
same family, same track 0 pattern, *do* drift the moment a second track
exists.

So the honest statement is not "11 drift, 3 are fine" but **"11 of 14
demonstrably drift; the other 3 lack the data to tell, and their siblings
suggest they would."**

#### The instrument's own tautology, caught before it could inflate the result

8 of the 25 successors are themselves `span == 0` records — which a profile
built from a population containing **zero** such records can never accept.
Their rejection carries no information. Counted as evidence they would have
pushed "reject" from 11 to 19 and made the case look far stronger than it is.
This was caught by the agent running the test, not by the design.

#### Consequence: the shipping reader is changed

`sr3anim::Payload::walk` now **refuses a `span == 0` translation control
record** rather than skipping past it. Justification, in the shape §9.34.1
used for the name-start check:

* **Zero effect on the known-good population** — `span == 0` occurs in 0 of
  3,687 clips that land on their declared endpoint. This cannot break
  anything that currently works.
* **It stops reporting success on walks that demonstrably drift.** Reporting
  `walkComplete()` for a cursor that has left the record stream is a false
  claim of success, which is worse than a conservative failure — and all 14
  fail to reach `+0x30` under either reading, so nothing is lost.
* **The disagreement disappears** because the reader now agrees with the
  probe, which the evidence says was right.

**And §9.40's reasoning is now doubly wrong**, which is worth stating
plainly: I preferred the shipping reader as "the authority" and corrected
121/69 on that basis. The authority was not merely unvalidated on the
disputed construct (§9.45) — **it was wrong about it.** Split, with the
reader corrected: **135 failures / 55 third population**, with 3 clips
resting on a lean rather than a proof.

#### 9.48.1 The arc, and one dependency the turn finding still carries

With the reader corrected, `walkN vs shipping reader disagree: 0` and the
split returns to **135 / 55** — which was §9.38.1's original figure. The
round trip is worth recording because each step was defensible on what was
known at the time:

| step | figure | basis |
|---|---|---|
| §9.38.1 | 135 / 55 | a probe that rejected `span == 0` |
| §9.40 | 121 / 69 | "the shipping reader is the authority" |
| §9.45 | bounded, undecided | the authority was never validated on this construct |
| §9.48 | **135 / 55** | the successor test: 11 of 14 demonstrably drift |

**The original number was right and the correction was wrong** — but the
correction was not carelessness, it was deference to an authority whose
validation population contained none of the disputed cases. The fix was not
"trust probes over readers"; it was **asking what validated the authority.**

#### The dependency, stated rather than buried

The turn-in-place signature is measured on the header quaternion and is
untouched by any walk. **But the GROUPS it compares are not.** The 55-clip
population is defined as *walks cleanly yet no block count in 512 reaches
`+0x30`* — and that predicate uses the continuation search §9.44 discredited.

Pooling honestly: of 383 bit-set clips that walk, 328 "reach by continuing"
(median root rotation **0.00°**) and 55 do not (median **90.00°**). Compare
all 383 against the 135 failures instead and the signal washes out, because
the 328 dominate. **So the finding does depend on that split existing.**

What that leaves is defensible but narrower than "turn clips are the third
population":

* the predicate *resists a permissive continuation search* is **reproducible
  and well-defined**, even though the search itself proves nothing about
  file structure;
* clips satisfying it have a root-motion profile — median **90.00°** against
  **0.00°** — that is measured entirely independently, from the header;
* two independently-obtained properties correlating at 87.3% is meaningful
  **whatever the first one turns out to mean.**

So: **a real correlation between a reproducible predicate and an independent
header property. Not an explanation.** The causal story — that turn clips
carry layered root orientation and that is why they resist the walk — remains
HYPOTHESIS, and Team A's disassembly finding (nothing in stream setup tests
flags `0x40`) makes the *layering* half of it more likely and the
*file-structure* half less.

#### 9.47.1 The `+0x06` caveat was REFUTED, and the residue is a second effect

§9.47 predicted that the ~19% of tight-stratum clips where `+0x06 != S`
would be **the same set** as clips where `S > 1099` (a `u16` field never
observed above 1099 cannot hold a larger total). Team A asked for this
verified as **sets, not counts**. It was, and the prediction fails:

| tight stratum, n = 1,483 | `+0x06 == S` | `+0x06 != S` |
|---|---|---|
| **S ≤ 1099** | 1,208 | **271** |
| **S > 1099** | 0 | **4** |

**All 4 of the `S > 1099` clips mismatch — that half of the prediction
holds exactly — but they are 4 of 275 mismatches.** The remaining **271**
(18.3% of the `S ≤ 1099` row) mismatch where the ceiling explanation
predicts none. Observed max `+0x06` is 1099 in both strata; max `S` is 1,540
tight / 2,016 overall.

**Set-verification is what caught this.** Two sets of "similar size" would
have looked like agreement; 271 against 4 is not a near-miss, it is a
different phenomenon. Counting alone would have confirmed a wrong story.

**So `+0x06 == S` is real but incomplete**, and §9.47's tier was overstated:
81.46% in the tight stratum against a 0.10% shuffled control is a strong
effect that is **not** universal, and the ~19% shortfall has a cause that is
not the ceiling.

#### The residue has structure, and it is not noise

For the 271, `+0x06` is **consistently smaller** than `S`, and identical
`(S, +0x06)` pairs recur across near-duplicate clip names — three
`*_bs_sd_t_run*` clips all at `S=56, +0x06=14`; four `*sprnt` clips all at
`S=105, +0x06=14`. Reproducible, therefore a real second effect.

**A pattern I thought I saw here did not survive checking my own arithmetic,
and it is corrected in place rather than quietly fixed.** My first pass read
`S / +0x06` off six of the ~20 printed examples as `4, 4.5, 3.5, 5.5, 7.5, 8`
and called that "multiples of one half". Recomputing all 20 explicitly:

| S | +0x06 | S / +0x06 |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | 4 | 1.5 |
| 56 | 14 | 4.0 |
| 71 | 15 | **4.733** |
| 72 | 16 | 4.5 |
| 84 | 24 | 3.5 |
| 105 | 14 | 7.5 |
| 110 | 20 | 5.5 |
| 120 | 15 | 8.0 |

**7 of 8 distinct pairs are exact half-integers; `brute_grap_entr_a`
(71/15) is not.** I had picked six values that fit and left out the two that
did not, without noticing — one absent because I never listed it, one
because I mis-stated the set. That is the small-sample-fit trap this
project has already logged twice today, caught this time before publication
rather than after only because the arithmetic was worth re-running before
committing to a sentence with "multiples" in it.

**So: a mostly-clean half-integer pattern with at least one real
exception, from 8 distinct pairs out of 271 — not a rule.** The
mismatching clips are overwhelmingly locomotion — `run`, `sprnt`,
`jbike_hover`. **HYPOTHESIS, untested and doing no work here:** these are
looping clips where `+0x06` records one cycle while `S` sums the whole
stored sequence, which a half-integer ratio would fit but a 4.733 does not
without a further wrinkle (an odd cycle count, most likely). Recorded so it
can be tested, explicitly not adopted.

**Tier for `+0x06 == S`, corrected: [CONFIRMED — empirical] for the 81%
where it holds, with a REPRODUCIBLE 19% exception whose mechanism is OPEN.**
Not "confirmed with a caveat" — the exception is a finding in its own right.

### 9.49 Team A's "weaker hit-predicate" hypothesis tested directly — refuted, in the informative direction (the gap this section chases is fully explained — see §9.54)

Team A proposed two candidate causes for why their continuation search
separates cleanly under a shift control (334/397 real vs 37/397 at +7, then
54/397 at −5) while mine does not (328/518 vs 333/518): a different anchor
being shifted, or a **weaker hit-predicate** — theirs counting "the walk
merely completes for some count" where this file has always required
"lands exactly on `+0x30`". They named the weak-predicate guess as the more
likely of the two and asked to check it before testing anything more
elaborate.

**Tested directly, on the same shifted (+7) runs, no new measurement
needed** (`probe_anim_flag40.cpp`):

| wrong-start (+7) hit predicate | rate |
|---|---|
| **STRICT** — lands exactly on `+0x30` (what this file has always scored) | 333 / 518 (**64.29%**) |
| **WEAK** — walk merely completes, any of 512 counts | 390 / 518 (**75.29%**) |

**Refuted, and the direction matters.** If their `334/397` used the weak
predicate, their shift result should land somewhere near this file's weak
reading (75.29%) or at least not fall below its strict one (64.29%). Instead
they report **9.32%** — *lower than either of my two readings, not higher*.
A weaker predicate cannot produce a *more* discriminating control; it can
only saturate faster. Guess #2 predicts the wrong sign.

**What this does establish:** neither of my own predicate variants is the
source of the disagreement — both saturate under shift here, so the choice
between them was never what made my search look non-discriminating. Their
search is doing something this one is not, and it is not merely "counting a
looser event." Their remaining hypothesis — a different anchor being
shifted (the declared endpoint, the track-block base, or the count origin,
rather than the payload start) — is untouched by this result and is now the
better-supported of the two, since the alternative just failed a direct
test.

**Also worth recording plainly:** their real-start rate (334/397 = 84.13%)
is meaningfully higher than this file's real-start rate (328/518 = 63.32%)
on a claimed-identical predicate and design. That gap needs the same
explanation as the shift gap, and probably has the same cause — whatever
anchor difference produces one likely produces the other, since both are
comparing the same search under nominally the same rule and getting
different numbers.

**Team A's own new lesson deserves recording as-is, because it named
something this project has not yet stated as sharply:** *a reconciliation
that leaves everyone correct deserves MORE suspicion than one that doesn't,
because it is the appealing kind and should be checked against the primary
source first, not last.* Their width-difference hypothesis felt tidy and
was wrong; this project's own instinct to test rather than accept the
tidier explanation is what caught it being wrong on the *next* guess too.

### 9.50 Tangent handedness is CONFIRMED on characters/items, NOT on vehicles

Team A flagged their tangent-handedness finding as directly actionable if
this project's renderer relies on it. It doesn't yet — `bitangent()` is
implemented but unused — so this was a header claim to verify before it
became a live defect, not an active one to fix in a hurry.

Verified independently (`tools/validation/probe_tangent_handedness.cpp`,
shipping readers only, never pooled across carriers):

| carrier | N (vertices) | extreme (0 or 255) | intermediate (1..254) |
|---|---|---|---|
| characters/items, `characters.vpp_pc` | 1,773,566 | **100.0000%** | 0.0000% |
| characters/items, `customize_item.vpp_pc` | 1,573,411 | **100.0000%** | 0.0000% |
| **vehicles**, `vehicles.vpp_pc` | 3,277,372 | **17.9837%** | **82.0163%** |

**Characters/items: the header's claim holds exactly.** 1,803 meshes across
two independent archives, **zero** intermediate values anywhere.

**Vehicles: it does not.** Team A's relayed 17.94% reproduces almost
exactly (measured 17.9837%). 82% of vehicle `tangentW` bytes spread smoothly
across 1–254 — 254 distinct values, peaking near the byte-range **midpoint**
(127/128), not at either extreme. Every vehicle mesh has a tangent channel
present (0/372 missing); the byte is there, it simply is not a two-valued
sign for the large majority of vertices.

**A genuine gap in the population, found and closed rather than left
silent:** `items.vpp_pc` contributed **zero** `.ccmesh_pc` pairs — verified
by direct inspection, not assumed a probe bug. Its packs hold either texture
sets with no mesh at all, or a different static-mesh format
(`.csmesh_pc`/`.gsmesh_pc`), out of scope here. `customize_item.vpp_pc`
substituted as a second characters/items source specifically to confirm
the 100% figure wasn't an artifact of having only one archive, and it
reproduced exactly.

**Header and accessor corrected to say what is actually known**
(`include/sr3mesh/mesh_block.h`): the handedness-sign comment on `tangentW`
and the `bitangent()` accessor both now scope the claim to
characters/items and state the vehicle figure explicitly, rather than
asserting a carrier-independent rule the data does not support. **Nothing
in this project currently calls `bitangent()` on a vehicle mesh, and
nothing should until the vehicle encoding is re-derived** — nine bones in
ten had no translation track (§9.42); this is the same shape of trap for a
different channel.
