| 9.56–9.56.1 | Animation stage 2 (real `.anim_pc` playback) built; full-skeleton rendering fragmented severely; root-caused via a new multi-bone regression suite plus a falsified alternative hypothesis (camera bones) to a real mesh-topology property, not a pipeline bug; a real `cmake` build-graph gap found and fixed along the way | Pipeline proven correct via permanent regression, not re-assertion; visual result explained rather than hidden or wrongly blamed on the code |
| 9.56.2 | Tested whether the fragmentation was `brad`-specific — it is NOT: reproduces on a distinct mesh (`angel`) with a calm walk cycle, less severe but still present on a larger-scale character (`brute_flamethrower`), confirmed by a new cross-mesh pre-check tool and by looking at every render | Broadens §9.56.1's finding into something more significant: a general property of this game's shared humanoid convention, no clean render achieved on anything tried yet |

**The through-line, stated once rather than per-section:** almost every
correction this session came from measuring a claim that looked rigorous —
an ambiguity count, an "authoritative" reader, a plausibility profile, a
shift control — and asking, one step later than it should have been asked,
whether that measurement could actually fail. The ones that couldn't were
wrong every time they were checked.

### 9.52 The 9.44/9.46 shift-control anchor dispute is RESOLVED — my control was wrong, not the finding it refuted (the methodology lesson stands; what was being measured is now fully explained, not just reinstated — see §9.54)

§9.44 and §9.46 (this session, above) published "REFUTED" against the
ambiguity-1.00 continuation result and the extra=39 clustering, both on the
strength of a shift control that found comparable hit rates from a
deliberately wrong start. Team A ran their own harness's identical-by-design
control on their 397-clip subset and got a completely different shape — real
334/397 (84.1%) vs shifted 37/397 (9.3%), a sharp drop, not a flat one. Both
sides had two guesses for the gap (candidate-space width, hit-predicate
strictness); both were tested and refuted (§9.49). The dispute was left
genuinely open at session-end, flagged in the RESUME block with an explicit
instruction not to resolve it by more reasoning — diff the two
implementations, or measure which anchor moves.

**Team A handed over their harness's exact predicate, read from source, not
prose.** That made the diff immediate:

| | this file's control (§9.44/§9.46) | Team A's control |
|---|---|---|
| shift applied to | **the payload START** — before any of the declared `tc` blocks are walked | **`end_of_declared_walk`** — the cursor position AFTER a correct, unshifted walk of the declared `tc` blocks |
| what gets walked from the shifted point | all `n` blocks (`tc+1..tc+512`), so the "declared" portion is corrupted too | only the `N` **additional** blocks (`1..512`) past a verified-correct declared walk |
| hit condition | exact match on `+0x30` | same — already confirmed identical in §9.49 |

**These are different perturbations.** Mine corrupts the walk from block
zero; theirs perturbs only the continuation, holding the real declared
portion intact. I had never noticed the difference because "shift the
control by 7 bytes" reads as one operation until you ask *shifted from
where*.

#### Rebuilt with Team A's exact anchor, on my own 518-clip population

`tools/validation/probe_anim_flag40.cpp` now runs both controls side by
side. Team A's anchor, implemented with my own independent decoder and run
on my own population:

| | REAL (unshifted) | Team A's anchor, shifted +7 |
|---|---|---|
| clips with a valid `declaredEnd` to test | 383 | 383 |
| found a working count | **328 (85.64%)** | **37 (9.66%)** |

Compare to Team A's own code, run at my exact 518-clip scope (relayed
after I'd already built the above independently): real 334 (64.48%),
shifted 41 (7.92%) — **the shifted counts land within four of each other
(37 vs 41) using two independently-written walkers**, and the small
real-count gap (328 vs 334, matching the already-known ~6-clip residual) is
unrelated to the anchor question. Two different implementations, anchored
the same way, agree. The version anchored my original way does not agree
with either.

**The extra-block histogram, retested the same way:** under Team A's
anchor, the 37 control hits scatter across **27 distinct values with none
dominant** (vs my original wrong-anchor control's 310-clip pile at exactly
42). Under the correct anchor there is no clustering to explain away —
which means the real search's **310 clips at extra=39** was never explained
by search geometry in the first place.

**The desync rate, Team A's proposed fast diagnostic, confirms the
mechanism directly:** of the 512 candidate block-counts tried per clip, the
fraction that complete in-bounds at all (before even checking whether they
land on target):

| | completion rate |
|---|---|
| REAL start | 15,694 / 265,216 (5.92%) |
| CTL-A — payload-start shift (this file's original, wrong anchor) | 16,617 / 265,216 (**6.27%, indistinguishable from REAL**) |
| CTL-B — Team A's exact anchor | 4,000 / 196,096 (**2.04%, roughly a third of REAL**) |

This is the causal mechanism, not just a correlated observation: my wrong
anchor completes (stays in-bounds) about as often as the real walk, so a
512-wide search over it has ample chances to coincidentally land on the
fixed target — which is exactly why it found "hits" at nearly the real
rate. Team A's correctly-anchored shift genuinely desyncs — completing a
third as often — so its search mostly finds nothing, which is the
signature of a real structural dependency on the exact byte offset, not
search-geometry noise.

#### What this reverses

* **§9.44's "ambiguity exactly 1.00 ⇒ REFUTED" is itself retracted.** The
  original §9.38 finding — that the continuation search lands uniquely, and
  that uniqueness means something — is **REINSTATED**, on a
  correctly-anchored control, confirmed by three independent lines
  (hit-rate, histogram shape, desync rate) and by an independently-coded
  second walker.
* **§9.46's "extra = 39 in 310 clips ⇒ REFUTED" is itself retracted.** The
  clustering is **REINSTATED** as a real, currently-unexplained shared
  property of those 310 clips (still the `auto_drv_*`/`auto_ridel_*` family
  at 46 tracks; still no header field predicts it — see §9.38's original
  predictor table).
* **What does NOT reverse:** §9.45's `span == 0` question was resolved
  independently in §9.48 via a different oracle (the two-sided successor
  test) and never depended on this shift control at all — it stands as
  fixed. The 121–135/55–69 population bounds and the turn-in-place
  signature (§9.44's "what survives" list) were never in question either,
  since none of them read off the shift control.

#### The lesson, and why it is not the same lesson as §9.37.1 or §3's existing control rule

§3 already carries "a control must be able to fail" and "verify before
refuting, suspect your own reading first" (from §9.37.1's rotation bug).
This is a third, adjacent failure mode: **the control itself was
under-specified code, and two people implementing "the same" control from
one sentence of description built genuinely different operations.** Both
of us had a control. Both controls could fail (and one of them did, on
cue — Team A's). The bug was not "no control" and not "an unfalsifiable
control" — it was that **"shift the search by 7 bytes" does not specify an
anchor**, and I picked one (payload start) that silently changed what was
being tested, then treated the result as informative about the real
question. **When a control is described in prose across a team boundary,
the anchor point is exactly the kind of detail prose drops and source code
cannot** — this is the same species of failure as the earlier "restate what
was COUNTED" citation-boundary lesson in `measurement-discipline.md`, one
level down: there it was a borrowed *number* stripped of its definition,
here it was a borrowed *control* stripped of its anchor. Both were caught
the same way — by going to the source and diffing, not by reasoning about
the prose harder.

### 9.53 Animation playback, stage 1: hierarchical CPU skinning library — CONFIRMED, not yet rendered

Immediately after the user confirmed the project's goal directly as **full
recomp** ("yes. full recomp. work autonomously" — see the RESUME block),
this session's first concrete step toward the next milestone (animation
playback) was built: the CPU math for posing a skinned character, as a
reusable library, proven to reproduce the project's existing confirmed
skinning result exactly rather than trusted on the strength of its own
derivation.

**Why this needed doing at all.** `sr3render/mesh_renderer.h`'s own header
comment says the interactive renderer does not skin — "blend
weights/indices decoded but unused." What HAD been confirmed
(`validate_pose.cpp`, synthetic single-joint-rotation test with a
scrambled-index control) was narrower than it looked at a glance: a rigid
rotation of one bone's whole subtree about that bone's own rest position,
which sidesteps the general hierarchical case (many bones, each with its
own local rotation, composed down the tree) entirely — by design, since
the bind pose has no rotation to get wrong (`sr3rig/rig.h`, confirmed on
the full population, 20,564/20,564 + 1,710/1,710).

**The derivation, worked out by hand and checked before any code was
written** (bones ordered parent-before-child, which `Rig::parse` already
enforces on the full population):

```
d_i     = restPosition_i - restPosition_parent(i)      (root: d_i = restPosition_i)
World_i = World_parent(i) * T(d_i) * Rot(R_i)          (root: World_i = T(d_i) * Rot(R_i))
Skin_i  = World_i * T(-restPosition_i)                 (= Pose_i * InverseBind_i)
```

At `R_i = identity` for every bone this telescopes to `World_i =
T(restPosition_i)` exactly, so `Skin_i = Identity` — bind pose, mesh
unchanged, matching `rig.h`'s design goal. Setting only one bone's `R_i`
to a rotation and leaving every other bone's `R_i` at identity was checked
by hand to reduce, for every descendant of that bone, to exactly
`validate_pose.cpp`'s confirmed special case — translations commute, so
the per-descendant pivot cancels out to the *same* pivot point for the
whole subtree, which is precisely what that harness's own comment already
claimed and had confirmed empirically.

**Built via a background Sonnet-5 agent** (per the "use as much parallelism
as helps" standing instruction), briefed with the derivation above and
told explicitly to re-check it rather than trust it, to extract — not
duplicate — `validate_pose.cpp`'s existing confirmed math rather than
write a second implementation of it (this project's own §3 rule: "a probe
that carries its own copy of production logic is a SECOND IMPLEMENTATION,
and second implementations drift"), and to prove parity numerically rather
than claim it.

**What exists now**, all independently re-verified by re-running it myself
after the agent reported done, not taken on the agent's word:

* `include/sr3rig/pose.h` + `src/pose.cpp` — `Mat3x4`/`Rotation3` affine
  math, `computeSkinningMatrices()` (the derivation above, one forward
  pass, throws on a parent-after-child violation), `skinVertexPosition()`/
  `skinVertices()` (the CPU blend-weight loop, same edge-case handling as
  `validate_pose.cpp`'s original — 255/non-positive-weight lane skip,
  out-of-range-index drop-and-count, near-zero-total-weight passthrough,
  otherwise renormalize). `rigToMeshSpace()` surfaces the confirmed
  `(x,-y,-z)` convention (§9.13) in one place instead of re-typing it.
* `tools/validation/validate_pose.cpp` **refactored in place** to call the
  library instead of its own hand-rolled math — confirmed by re-reading the
  file, not just the agent's claim.
* `tests/synthetic_pose_test.cpp` (new) — hand-computed expected values on
  a 4-bone synthetic skeleton, no game data, covering bind-pose identity,
  the shared-pivot induction step, parent-ordering rejection, and all the
  vertex-skinning edge cases. New 16th synthetic suite, `sr3rigpose_tests`.

**Regression numbers, re-run independently on real `characters.vpp_pc`
data** (not just quoted from the agent):

| mesh | bones/verts | HIERARCHICAL vs DIRECT (max vertex delta) | BIND-POSE vs identity (max, tol 1e-5) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `brad` | 68 / 5,044 | 1.194e-07 | 2.407e-07 |
| `brute_flamethrower` | 68 / 5,777 | 4.771e-07 | 2.421e-07 |
| `nightblade` | 94 / 6,768 | 2.385e-07 | 2.403e-07 |

"HIERARCHICAL vs DIRECT" compares the new general library path (one bone's
`R_i` set, all others identity) against the original hand-authored
"rotate about the joint" construction from the existing confirmed test,
both feeding the same vertex-skinning code — this is the regression check
that matters, and it matches to within ordinary float non-associativity,
not "looks similar." All 16 synthetic suites pass, re-run myself, not
copied from the report.

**What this is not.** No DirectX/rendering code was touched — nothing is
visually confirmed, because there is nothing on screen to look at yet.
This is CPU math only. **Two things remain before "animation playback" is
real:** (1b) wire this into the live renderer so an arbitrary pose can
actually be seen — turning the still-accurate "renderer doesn't skin"
comment in `mesh_renderer.h` into something to remove; (2) feed real
`.anim_pc` decoded rotations through `computeSkinningMatrices()` over time.
For (2), the agent flagged one real open point worth carrying forward
rather than assuming away: `.anim_pc` rotations are presumably rig-space
quaternions, and if the rest positions fed to `computeSkinningMatrices()`
are in mesh space (as this project's harnesses use), those rotations will
need conjugating by the same `(x,-y,-z)` transform first — untested,
because no per-bone animated rotation has been fed through this code yet.

**Tier: [CONFIRMED — empirical]** for the library reproducing the existing
confirmed test to ~1e-7 on real data, re-verified independently. **[OPEN]**
for whether the rig-space-vs-mesh-space rotation question above needs
handling before stage 2. Stage 1b (does this actually render) followed
immediately — see §9.53.1.

#### 9.53.1 Stage 1b: wired into the live renderer, screenshotted, visually verified by a human read — not just a subagent's word

A second background agent wired the stage-1 library into `MeshRenderer`
(a new optional `overridePositions` parameter on `upload()`) and added a
`sr3_viewer pose` command that renders the same hand-authored test pose
used above, headlessly, to PNG (`sr3_viewer` already had a `--out file.png`
capture path from earlier in the project). It reported clean numbers —
bind-pose renders pixel-identical to the pre-existing unposed `mesh`
command (0–2 differing pixels out of 648,000), bounding box growing only
in the geometrically expected direction — but explicitly could not judge
whether the posed image **looks like** a correctly bent limb, and said so
rather than claiming it. I looked at all six PNGs myself before writing
anything here.

**First read was alarming and turned out to be a already-known artifact,
not a new bug.** All three posed renders (`brad`, `brute_flamethrower`,
`nightblade`) show the arm bending cleanly and plausibly at the shoulder —
but also a long fan of thin, wildly-stretched triangles sweeping away from
the hip/waist area, which at a glance looks like a serious skinning
defect. **It isn't one — it's the M4/M5 "near-degenerate rest edge"
artifact this project already diagnosed and named at §9.14, now visible in
a picture for the first time instead of only as a number:**

* Re-ran `validate_pose.exe` myself (not trusting the render alone) and
  got, for `brad`: max edge stretch **328.28x, identical between the real
  run and the deliberately-scrambled control**. That exact number and that
  exact "identical in both arms" signature is §9.14's own smoking gun for
  "this statistic describes a near-zero-length rest edge, not the pose" —
  reproduced today bit-for-bit, not merely similar.
* §9.14 already named M4/M5 **void as stated** for this reason and
  identified **M3b (largest connected component of the moved set)** as the
  one metric that actually discriminates real skinning from garbage — and
  it does, clearly, in this run too: coherence 67.3% (`brad`) / 74.9%
  (`brute_flamethrower`) real vs 19.1% / 17.3% scrambled. (`nightblade`
  reproduces §9.14's already-flagged weak/unexplained 7.0% vs 3.5% case —
  a pre-existing open item, not new.)
* The rotated subtree includes bone `l-handprop` in all three meshes (a
  weapon/prop attachment point), and the bind-pose renders show
  swords/straps stitched close to the body — exactly where near-zero-rest-
  length seam edges would be expected. The fan artifact sits at that same
  location in every posed image. Consistent with, not proof of, that being
  the specific edges involved.

**So: the arm bends correctly (confirmed both numerically via M3b and
visually), and the fan artifact is the same already-understood
near-degenerate-edge phenomenon this project documented before this
session, seen for the first time rather than newly introduced.** Nothing
in stage 1 or 1b needed fixing on this evidence. It would need addressing
cosmetically before this is presentable as an actual animation (real
per-frame rotation will hit the same edges every frame), but that is a
rendering-polish item for later, not a defect in the skinning math or its
wiring.

**What remains before "animation playback" is real:** stage 2 —
`.anim_pc` decoded rotations, sampled over time, fed through
`computeSkinningMatrices()` in place of today's one hand-authored test
rotation, with the rig-space-vs-mesh-space rotation question from §9.53
checked against real data rather than assumed.

### 9.54 Flags `0x40` is FULLY CLOSED — §9.38 through §9.52's entire "third population" thread was a walk started one small table too early

**Every section from §9.38 to §9.52 that discusses flags `0x40` — the
328/135/55 split, the continuation search, "ambiguity exactly 1.00", "extra
= 39 in 310 clips", the shift-control anchor saga — is now SUPERSEDED, not
by a better inference from file bytes, but by an actual disassembly-level
answer neither side had:** there is a small **layer-override table**
(count table, value table, tail table) that the runtime builds fresh from
the clip's own bytes and inserts *before* the ordinary per-track keyframe
walk, if and only if flags bit `0x40` is set. The walk this project (and
Team A) ran all session started at `p0` (this project's own long-confirmed
`payload_start()`) for every clip regardless of the bit — correct for the
3,691 bit-clear clips, and **one small table too early** for every single
one of the 518 bit-set clips.

**Source: Team A traced two independent disassembly sites** —
`FUN_004c21a0` (the runtime layer-blend sampler, already known from the
prior pass) tests bit `0x40` to decide whether to *consult* a per-track
override array; a second function, `FUN_004c1190` (raw instruction `TEST
AL,0x40` at `0x004c11a0`), tests the *same* bit to decide whether to
*build* that array in the first place — parsing it directly out of the
clip's own resident file bytes, at exactly `clip + payload_start(clip)`,
re-parsed fresh on every call rather than cached or externally supplied.
Full trace in `spec-anim-format.md` §10, now synced (118,406 bytes,
verified byte count matches what was reported).

**The formula, read from the spec and implemented independently — never
from the game binary, and never by transcribing Team A's harness:**

```
p0 = payload_start(clip)                        (this project's own function, unchanged)
count_table:  tc entries, byte or u16 (flags bit 0x80) -- how many override
              values that track has
sum = total of all tc entries
align to 4 bytes
value_table:  sum * 4 bytes  (one f32-sized override value each)
tail_table:   sum * 1 or sum * 2 bytes (flags bit 0x02)
p1 = the cursor after all three
```

Then: walk exactly `tc` blocks from `p1` (the **unmodified**, already-
confirmed per-track walker) and check landing on `u32(+0x30)`.

**Independent replay, this project's own reader, `tools/validation/
probe_anim_layer_override_skip.cpp` (new), against the same 518/3,691-clip
population used throughout this thread — every number below reproduces
Team A's reported figures exactly, computed from the spec's prose alone:**

| Run | Population | Land exactly on `+0x30` |
|---|---|---|
| **REAL: walk from `p1`** | bit `0x40` set, n=518 | **518 / 518 — 100.00%** |
| Sanity: bit `0x40` clear, walk from `p0` (unchanged) | n=3,691 | **3,687 / 3,691 — 99.89%** (unchanged, as it must be) |
| Control A: shift `p1` by **+7** | bit `0x40` set, n=518 | **2 / 518 — 0.39%** |
| Control B: shift `p1` by **-5** | bit `0x40` set, n=518 | **0 / 518 — 0.00%** |
| Control C: apply the same formula, wrongly, to bit-`0x40`-clear clips | n=3,691 | **1 / 3,691 — 0.03%** (collapsed from the 99.89% baseline) |

Also confirmed on this population: flags bit `0x80` (wide index table) and
bit `0x02` (wide tail table) are both clear in all 518/518 cases — same as
reported; the wide-width branches remain unexercised by any file in hand
and are disassembly-only, unconfirmed for correctness, exactly as flagged.

**What this retires, precisely, and why it isn't a failure of this
session's method:**

* **§9.38's 328/135/55 split, the "third population," and every number
  downstream of it (§9.40, §9.44, §9.45, §9.46, §9.48/§9.48.1, §9.49,
  §9.52)** described real, correctly-measured properties of a walk started
  from the wrong cursor. There is no third population: every one of the
  518 bit-set clips lands cleanly once the walk starts from the right
  place. **"Extra = 39 in 310 clips" (§9.38, reinstated in §9.52) was never
  extra track blocks** — it was the continuation search, run from `p0`,
  coincidentally re-landing on target after enough blocks to cross
  whatever the skipped table's byte-length happened to be for that rig
  shape. The number described the missing table's size in "block-sized
  units," not a real structural feature.
* **§9.52's anchor-dispute resolution is NOT wrong and does not need
  retracting** — my shift control really was perturbing the wrong point
  (payload start instead of end-of-declared-walk), and Team A's really was
  the more discriminating design. That lesson stands. What it was
  discriminating turns out to have been a coincidental byte-alignment
  artifact of the missing table, not real extra payload — the control was
  sound; the thing both controls were probing no longer needs probing,
  because it has a direct answer now.
* **The turn-in-place root-rotation signature (median 90.00° vs 0.00°,
  §9.38.1) is untouched** — it was always read from the header quaternion,
  never from any walk, and remains real regardless of this section.

**The lesson, and it is a different one from anything else this session
surfaced:** every finding in this thread — mine and Team A's alike — was
built from the same kind of evidence, file bytes and inference from them,
however carefully controlled. **A file-side inference, however rigorously
controlled, cannot rule out an explanation that requires information the
file alone does not contain** (here: which runtime function reads which
bit, and what it does before that read). No amount of additional file-side
measurement this session could have found the layer-override table,
because the table's *presence* is inferable from bytes but its *reason for
being there* is not. This is the flip side of "verify before adopting a
disassembly claim" (this project's standing rule all session): disassembly
access is not just another data source to cross-check against file-side
inference, it can answer questions file-side inference is structurally
unable to. Neither side should have been expected to find this without it,
and the correct response to a whole thread being superseded this way is
not to have measured harder — it's the outcome that made all the
measuring worth doing, since a wrong explanation this well-controlled
needed exactly this kind of evidence to dislodge, not more of the same
kind that produced it.

**Tier: [CONFIRMED — disassembly + empirical]**, independently reproduced
end-to-end on this project's own reader, from the spec's prose alone.

* Mesh-block validation on non-empty `.gzn_pc` pairs: originally
  **932/1,001 (93.1%)** against the spec's **1,002/1,002 (100%)** — see
  §9.55.1 for what's now confirmed vs. still open.
* **0/2,596** validated blocks reported as inline-mode, against the spec
  §7.3 sample's ~23% estimate — **genuinely OPEN, not confirmed either
  way (corrected 2026-09-12, see §9.55.1's update)**: my "0/14,920, not a
  parser limitation" conclusion was premature — it never checked whether
  §7.3's ~23% was produced by a comparable full-validation test.

**The terrain-format/zone-data-format tension flagged above is
RESOLVED, cleanly, neither document was wrong:** Team A traced it —
`spec-terrain-format.md`'s single-file sample read `0x80002233`/
`0x80002237` as file-specific "magic" values, but both share the upper
16 bits `0x8000`, which is exactly `spec-zone-data-format.md`'s
population-wide top-level-record shape; the sample simply saw its first
two top-level records before anyone had the 790-id population view. I
verified this myself directly against `spec-terrain-format.md`'s own
text (§3: "own distinct magic, `0x80002233`... a second occurrence of a
near-identical magic value, `0x80002237`") — matches exactly. Bonus: the
terrain sample's `"Region<003>"` string (also independently verified,
same section) is a real, cross-referenced lead for whenever the
record-interior question is unparked, not chased further now.

**Tier: [CONFIRMED — empirical]** for the header and the parts of the
geometry chain independently spot-checked here. **[OPEN]** for what
§9.55.1 leaves open, and for the entire main
object-stream body, which remains exactly as unconfirmed as the spec
itself says it is.

#### 9.55.1 The three gaps, re-diagnosed: one was this project's own harness bug, one is refuted-and-narrowed, one is confirmed genuine

**Gap 1 (46-file extraction gap): the original number was itself wrong,
and the real cause was a bug in `validate_zone.cpp`, not in the shipped
reader.** `entryBytes()`/`walk()`'s `.czn_pc` loop had no per-entry
exception guard, only one frame up around the whole nested-container
recursion — so when a single `.gzn_pc` sibling's declared Raw payload
range exceeded its containing `.str2_pc`'s own size (`Container::
rawEntryBytes()` throwing `FormatError`, as it should), the exception
silently aborted **every remaining sibling in that container**, losing
whole groups of otherwise-fine files as collateral damage, not just the
one bad one. Fixed in a new diagnostic harness
(`tools/validation/diag_zone_gaps.cpp`) with a per-stem `try/catch`,
**re-run by me independently on the `dlc1-3` archives and reproduced
exactly**: 93/93 `.czn_pc` entries now visited (vs. partial coverage
before), **37 real per-entry failures** (not 46), all confined to
`dlc1/dlc2/dlc3.vpp_pc` — matching the report's claim of zero in the
city archives, which I did not re-run given their ~13-minute scan cost,
but the dlc-only figure alone already accounts for the full corrected
total (37 of 37). **Exact predicate, handed to Team A**: `.czn_pc` entries
whose paired `.gzn_pc` is `PayloadKind::Raw` with `dataOffset +
uncompressedSize` exceeding the containing `.str2_pc`'s total size — 37
files across 10 named `.str2_pc` containers, itemized list available.
**Fixed directly in `tools/validation/validate_zone.cpp` itself** (the
same per-stem `try/catch`, not just the diagnostic copy) and confirmed:
`.czn_pc` found on the `dlc1-3` archives went from 47 (silently
undercounted by the cascade bug) to **56 — exactly `93 - 37`**, matching
the corrected gap precisely.

**Gap 2 (93.1% vs 100%): Team A's specific hypothesis refuted with clean
numbers (both sides agreed the arithmetic didn't support it); the real
driver is identified, the root cause of that driver is still OPEN.** With
gap 1's extraction bug fixed, the population is exactly **1,002 non-empty
pairs** (matching the spec's own denominator precisely), 932 validate, 70
don't. Across all 1,002 — pass and fail alike — **every single entry**
decodes via the shared-stream-recovery path, never the `OkUnconfirmedContent`
mechanism Team A's hypothesis named (0 occurrences of it, or of plain
`Ok`, anywhere) — that specific mechanism is ruled out, not just
unconfirmed. Of the 70 failures: **52 (74%) have no g-backed-flagged
anchor candidate findable in the `.czn_pc` content at all**, 5 (7%) have a
candidate with no matching check-value in the `.gzn_pc`, 13 (19%) have a
match that `MeshBlock::parse` still rejects. Why the anchor signature is
simply absent for those 52 is the real open question now — **narrowed
from "unreconciled 93.1% vs 100%" to a specific, much smaller unresolved
question, and then RESOLVED — see §9.55.2, which also surfaced a much
bigger new open item along the way.**

**Gap 3 (0% vs ~23% inline): NOT resolved — corrected 2026-09-12 after
Team A pushed back, and they were right to.** I originally wrote this up
as "confirmed genuine absence, not a parser limitation": Team A's
explanation for their OWN tool (`mesh_scan.py` structurally cannot see
inline blocks) is correct for their tool and doesn't excuse this reader's
result, since `zone_geometry.cpp` explicitly attempts inline parsing —
true as far as it goes, but I stopped one step short. **What I measured is
real and stands**: scanned the full population for the same signature
regardless of any `.gzn_pc` pairing (inline blocks need none) and found
**14,920 candidates by raw signature (29.4% — actually higher than the
spec's 23% estimate, so the raw signature rate isn't the discrepancy)**,
of which 53.9% fail immediately on their own declared check value and the
remaining 2.7% all fail later on absurdly small declared segment lengths
with zero index count — **0 of 14,920 pass this reader's full
`MeshBlock::parse` validation.** That part is solid.

**What I got wrong: treating that as a refutation of the spec's ~23%
figure without checking what the ~23% actually measured.** Team A went
back to their own §7.3 methodology rather than just compare numbers, and
found their figure came from a check defined as matching the `.gzn_pc`'s
own tag from the start — **not** a full-parse validation the way this
reader's 0/14,920 is. Neither `mesh_scan.py` nor that original check has
ever run a full-replay validation on the inline population specifically.
**0% and ~23% may not be measuring the same predicate at all**, in which
case there is no real contradiction to explain — but confirming that
needs someone to read the original extraction script's exact test logic,
which neither side has done yet. Team A logged this as genuinely
OPEN/UNKNOWN rather than accept a plausible-sounding reconciliation
without checking it — precisely because doing that is close to the same
mistake already made once on this exact discrepancy.

**CLOSED, 2026-09-13 — Team A found the actual explanation, and it fully
reconciles rather than partially explains.** They explicitly tested and
**refuted** the tempting idea that this was the same header-displacement
class of bug as gap 2 or the 21,634-anchor mystery (80% of the
non-closing inline candidates sit at an alignment where no header-offset
dispute ever existed — a genuinely different defect, checked rather than
assumed). The real cause: a second, separate bug in their own §7.3
harness — it landed on the **length field** instead of the **flags byte**
when classifying inline vs. g-backed. Corrected estimate: **0.74%**
inline, not ~23% — small enough that this reader finding 0 inline blocks
in its own scan is no longer in tension with their figure at all. **This
gap is CLOSED clean on both sides**, not merely narrowed — my own earlier
"confirmed genuine absence" was still premature (right conclusion, wrong
justification at the time), but the gap itself no longer exists once both
sides' actual measurement methods are accounted for.

**Test suites**: all 18 (17 zone-era plus the animation bug-hunt's
`sr3rigmultibonepose_tests`, added by a different parallel agent) pass,
confirmed by direct rerun.

#### 9.55.2 Gap 2 RESOLVED: the 52 files have a real anchor, mis-bucketed by a 4-byte header-displacement bug — and a much bigger question found alongside it

**The premise of the 52-file bucket was wrong, not just unexplained.** The
`u32==9` anchor is **not absent** from those files. All 52 contain a valid,
4-aligned anchor whose check value opens a real, well-formed Mesh g-segment
in the paired `.gzn_pc`. They were mis-bucketed because **for these
specific blocks the real header begins at `anchor + 0x14`, not `anchor +
0x10`** (`sr3mesh::kHeaderStart`) — a zero filler word occupies
`+0x10..+0x13`, and `zone_geometry.cpp` reads its flags byte out of that
filler, gets `0x00`, concludes "inline", and routes the block down a path
that then correctly fails (there's no valid inline block there either).
**"0 g-backed-flagged candidates" described the flags byte, not the
anchor's presence** — that distinction is the whole finding.

**Independently re-verified by me, byte-for-byte, not taken on the
report's word**: extracted `sr3_city~sdlc2_gis_o!^dlc2_go` (the exact
example cited) via a new dump tool and read the raw bytes myself —
`czn+0xdc`=`09 00 00 00` (version 9), `+0xe0`=check value `0xE0006BDD`,
`+0xe4`=cLength 236, `+0xe8`=gLength 388, `+0xec`=`00 00 00 00` (the
filler the reader misreads), `+0xf0`=`01 00 00 00` (the real flags byte).
Cross-checked the `.gzn_pc`: its first 4 bytes are `dd 6b 00 e0`, matching
the declared check value exactly, and its trailing bookend at byte 384
(=`gLength`-4) matches again. Every claimed byte matched exactly.

**Confirmed via two independent oracles that never share an assumption**,
across all 24,477 anchors satisfying the confirmed anchor signature
(4-aligned `u32==9`, next word ≥0x10000, matching a 16-aligned check-value
occurrence in the `.gzn_pc` — §7.3's own criteria): a full-walk-closure
test, and a completely separate declared-offset field inside each channel
record that `mesh_block.cpp` parses but never uses for cursor advancement
(so it can referee without circularity). Both agree exactly: **2,596
anchors close at displacement `0x10`** (matching `locate()`'s current
output number-for-number), **247 close at `0x14`**, **zero disagree
between the two oracles, zero are ambiguous** (no anchor closes at more
than one displacement). All 52 of the gap-2 files have at least one
`0x14`-displaced anchor; 46 of 52 have every anchor at `0x14`.

**This is a diagnostic-only finding, not yet a shipped-code fix.** Making
`kHeaderStart` per-block rather than a fixed constant would touch every
format sharing `sr3mesh::MeshBlock::parse` (trees, foliage, vehicles,
characters, not just zones) — a real design decision, not a safe silent
patch, and correctly left as OPEN rather than made unilaterally.

**A much bigger, separate question surfaced alongside this one — SOLVED by
Team A, 2026-09-13, after being flagged here as this reader's next task.**
Of the full 24,477-anchor population, 21,634 (88%) closed at neither
displacement tested (`0x10` nor `0x14`), and I characterized 98.3% of
those as independently passing a strong self-check (the `.czn_pc`'s own
bookend word matching the declared check value) at "a ~2⁻³² per-trial
coincidence rate." **That stated rate was wrong by six orders of
magnitude — corrected 2026-09-13**: Team A measured the real empirical
false-positive rate directly (200 random 4-aligned trials per zone,
`zg2_candidate_reality.py` test D7) at **6.98%**, not ~2⁻³², because real
file content is full of hash/length-shaped records that coincidentally
satisfy the check's shape — the theoretical astronomically-small rate
assumed uniform-random content, which file bytes are not. **The underlying
conclusion survives regardless** (a ~14x separation over the 6.98%
background rate is still informative), but the load-bearing evidence for
"these are real, unwalked blocks" is Team A's own g-side bookend + exact
replay (controls firing at 0.13%, 0%, 0%, 0.21%), not this self-check,
which measured its own confidence wrong. **Root cause of the 88% gap,
found and confirmed by Team A**: `.gzn_pc` is a **contiguous CHAIN of
segments**, each shaped `[u32 tag][payload][u32 copy of tag]`, each
starting exactly where the previous ended — **only segment 0 is
16-aligned; every later segment is 4-aligned at wherever the running total
lands**, and the declared g-length encodes each segment's own alignment
residue. This reader's `ZoneGeometry::locate()` builds its g-file index at
a hardcoded 16-byte stride (`src/zone_geometry.cpp`, `for (size_t pos = 0;
pos + 4 <= gsize; pos += 16)`) — the identical bug class Team A found in
their own `mesh_scan.py`. **Corrected population, confirmed at 4/2/1-byte
alignment all landing on the same figure**: 2,843 → **38,152** blocks
(13.4x), 97.64% of 39,073 candidates, real firing controls throughout
(wrong-zone: 0.13%; length perturbed −4/+16/−16: 0%; +4: 0.21%).
Cross-carrier consequences, confirmed by Team A: `.clmesh_pc` 12,628→29,908
(1.83x), trees 15→25 (1.67x); characters/props/vehicles unaffected
(1.00x) — those carriers are single-segment, not chains. Full mechanism,
the byte-level worked example, and the corrected-count table: Team A's
synced `spec-zone-data-format.md` §10.4/§10.5.

New read-only diagnostic harnesses (not wired into CMake, matching
convention): `tools/validation/diag_zone_gap52b.cpp`,
`diag_zone_preheader.cpp`, `dump_zone_pair.cpp` (the byte-extraction tool
used for the independent re-verification above).

#### 9.55.3 `ZoneGeometry::locate()` FIXED — 38,152/38,152, exact match to the corrected target, independently re-verified

A background agent fixed the chain-walk bug, and found (and fixed) **two
further real bugs beyond the original scope**, both confirmed necessary —
without them the chain walk finds the right offsets and then every
non-16-aligned segment throws on the exact-length contract, zero net gain.

**Bug A: `sr3mesh::MeshBlock::parse()` aligned SEGMENT-relative, not
absolute, despite this project's own belief (stated in the dispatch brief,
itself now corrected) that it already aligned absolutely.** Every carrier
built so far starts 16-aligned, so segment-relative and absolute alignment
coincide — the bug had never been exercised until a genuinely
non-16-aligned start existed. **Bug B**: the fixed `kHeaderStart = 0x10`
constant drops every anchor at 4 (mod 8) — the exact, already-CONFIRMED-
but-deliberately-unfixed §9.55.2 header-displacement finding, load-bearing
here because those anchors are a real fraction of the chain.

**Both fixed as additive, default-preserving parameters** —
`MeshBlock::parse()` gained optional `gSegmentOffset`/`headerDisplacement`
parameters (default `0`/`kHeaderStart`, so all ~30 other call sites are
byte-for-byte unchanged) — and **regression-proved, not assumed**:
`validate_vehicle.exe`/`validate_mesh.exe` output confirmed unchanged
before and after. **I independently re-ran both myself**: vehicles
372/372, 5,629,811 vertices, 5,629,811/5,629,811 unit normals — matches
the pre-existing documented figures exactly.

**The chain rule itself was independently re-verified by the agent before
any shipped code was touched** — extracted a real zone (`sr3_city~s0715`)
byte-by-byte, found all 12 real g-backed segments by exhaustive search
(not by assuming the chain), and confirmed they tile the `.gzn_pc`
**purely additively, to the exact 557,224-byte EOF, zero gap** — extending
Team A's 6-row worked example to the full 12 segments, all matching.

**Corrected population, independently re-run by me on the fast subset**:

| | reported (agent) | independently re-run (me) |
|---|---|---|
| dlc1+dlc2+dlc3 blocks | 549 (was 79) | **549** — exact match |
| full 10-archive total | **38,152** (was 2,843, 13.42x) | not re-run (city archives ~1-8 min each); dlc subset matches exactly |
| files with ≥1 block | 1,002/1,002 | consistent with dlc-subset figures |

**38,152 is an EXACT match to the spec's own corrected target**, not just
"close." A second, independent structural test the agent added
(`tools/validation/validate_zone_chain.cpp`, mutation-tested) confirms
it's the right *set*, not just the right count: 1,002/1,002 files tile
their `.gzn_pc` to EOF exactly, with a firing control (length perturbed
+4 → only 21/1,002, 2.1%); 580 multi-block files carrying 37,730 blocks
and a 37,035/115/0 successor-placement split — both matching
`spec-zone-data-format.md` §10.5's own independently-published figures
exactly.

Existing `tests/synthetic_zone_test.cpp` had encoded the now-refuted
segment-relative-alignment behavior in two places — both rewritten (not
just extended) with the correct absolute-grid construction; four new
chain-specific cases added, mutation-tested (reverting either fix fails
exactly 6 checks, and a padding-specific case still passes in both
reverted states — the correct discrimination, not a blanket failure).

**All 19 synthetic suites pass — reconfirmed by me with a fresh rerun,
not taken from the report.**

**Tier: [CONFIRMED — empirical, independently re-verified]** for the
chain-walk fix, the exact 38,152 population match (dlc subset
independently reproduced by me), and the two shared-code bug fixes'
zero-regression claim (vehicles/characters independently re-run by me).
`ZoneGeometry::locate()` is no longer the open item it was three sections
ago — the natural next zone-reader task is now the main `.czn_pc`
object-stream body itself, still `[HYPOTHESIS]` and still parked on
Team A's side pending their own user.

**Tier: [CONFIRMED — empirical, independently re-verified byte-for-byte]**
for the 52-file `0x14`-displacement diagnosis. **[OPEN]** — whether/how to
fix the shipped reader (a per-format design decision, not this finding's
