### 9.56 Animation playback, stage 2: real `.anim_pc` timeline sampling built — the fragmentation is root-caused (§9.56.1): a real mesh property, not a code bug

**This is a status report on an unresolved problem, not a completed
milestone.** Built by a background agent: `include/sr3anim/sample.h`/
`sample.cpp` (real keyframe timeline sampling — hemisphere-corrected slerp
for rotation, confirmed cumulative per-key durations for translation) and
`include/sr3rig/animated_pose.h`/`animated_pose.cpp` (a caller-side bridge
onto stage 1's `pose.h`, which remains unmodified — layers animated
translation deltas onto `computeSkinningMatrices()` and does the
rig→mesh-space conjugation once, at the end, exactly as §9.53 described).
Wired into `sr3_viewer animpose`.

**What checks out, verified by me looking at the actual images:**

* Bind pose renders correctly.
* The rig-space/single-final-conjugation approach from §9.53 needed no
  correction — proven algebraically identical (not approximate) to
  per-item mesh-space conversion, since conjugation distributes over a
  matrix product whenever the conjugating transform is its own inverse
  (true here). The one open question §9.53 flagged is closed.
* Hemisphere-corrected slerp (`src/sample.cpp`'s `slerp()`) is correctly
  implemented — dot-product sign check and renegotiation before
  interpolating, the standard fix for the classic "quaternion long-way-
  round" bug. Read directly, not merely trusted from the report.
* **Isolating a single real, decoded joint** (holding every other bone at
  bind-pose identity) — tested on `l-thigh` and on the spine chain —
  **renders a clean, recognizable, plausible pose** each time, matching
  stage 1b's quality (only the same already-documented near-degenerate-
  edge cosmetic artifact, §9.14/§9.53.1, nothing worse). I looked at both.
* Bone-length preservation passed for every rotation-only bone pair; the
  one real deviation (bone `l-handprop`) is fully attributable to that
  bone's own small, confirmed translation key (0.0845 units) — expected,
  not a bug.

**What does NOT check out:** rendering the SAME clip with all ~48-49 bones
animated **simultaneously**, as real playback requires, produces a
severely fragmented, exploded, non-recognizable result — much worse than
any single-attachment-point artifact this project has seen before. I
looked at multiple frames myself; this is not a subtle judgment call.

**What has been ruled out, precisely, rather than guessed at:**

* Not a rotation-handedness/sign bug — negating the sampled quaternions
  produces an equally fragmented result in a different posture, not a
  clean one (if handedness were flipped, negating should have fixed it).
* Not the classic hemisphere/slerp bug — the code already guards against
  it, confirmed by reading it.
* Not (solely) the known near-degenerate-edge cosmetic artifact — that
  artifact is a small, localized fin at one attachment point (§9.53.1);
  this is whole-body fragmentation.
* Not a translation double-counting bug in the general case — the one
  case with a real, checkable translation delta (`l-handprop`) passed the
  bone-length check exactly.

**What has NOT been ruled out, and is the honest state of things: no
confirmed test in this project — not stage 1's regression check, not
`synthetic_pose_test.cpp`, not this task's own isolation tests — has ever
exercised `computeSkinningMatrices()` with MORE THAN ONE simultaneous
non-identity bone rotation.** Every confirmatory test to date, including
today's, rotates exactly one bone (or one bone's whole rigid subtree) at a
time. A real clip animates dozens of bones at once — genuinely new
territory for this code, not just a bigger version of what was already
tested. The composition formula itself (§9.53's derivation) is general and
gives no principled reason to expect a many-bone-specific bug, but "no
reason to expect one" is not the same as "tested and confirmed absent" —
exactly the distinction this project's own methodology exists to enforce,
so it is not being smoothed over here just because the timing is
inconvenient.

**Next step, precisely scoped, before any more rendering work on this:** a
synthetic (no game data, no DirectX) test with 2-3 chained bones each
given a real, independent, non-identity rotation simultaneously, checked
against a hand-computed expected result — isolating whether the defect is
in `computeSkinningMatrices`'s general composition, in
`computeAnimatedSkinningMatrices`'s translation-layering when combined
with multiple real rotations, or in the decoded rotation values themselves
for specific tracks in this specific clip (checkable by dumping and
sanity-checking every track's reconstructed quaternions — unit norm,
plausible angle — for the one clip already in hand, `auto_entrl_extct_
shot.anim_pc` against `brad.rig_pc`).

**Tier: [CONFIRMED]** for everything in the "checks out" list above. Full
resolution of the multi-bone case: §9.56.1.

#### 9.56.1 Root-caused: the pipeline is correct; the fragmentation is a real mesh-topology property, first exposed because nothing had ever animated both hands at once before

**Bottom line: `computeSkinningMatrices()`, `computeAnimatedSkinningMatrices()`,
and `sampleClipAtTime()` are now proven correct for the general multi-bone
case, by a permanent regression test, not just re-asserted.** A follow-up
agent wrote hand-derived synthetic tests with 2-3 simultaneous, different,
non-identity rotations across a branching skeleton — the exact case §9.56
identified as never tested — matching hand-computed expected world
positions to `1e-5`/`1e-4`. This is now `tests/synthetic_multibone_pose_test.cpp`,
the **18th synthetic suite** (`sr3rigmultibonepose_tests`), re-run by me
directly: **18/18 green.**

**The actual dominant cause of the fragmentation: `brad.ccmesh_pc` has
near-degenerate rest-pose mesh edges connecting vertices weighted to
kinematically unrelated bones** — the worst pairs connect left-hand
geometry (`l-finger1`) to right-hand geometry (`r-hand`), **4-19mm apart in
the bind pose**. Full-skeleton real playback is the first scenario in this
project's history where both hands move independently at once — every
prior confirmatory test (stage 1, 1b, and this stage's own isolation
checks) froze everything but one bone or subtree. These near-zero rest
edges stretch to **~1.1-1.2 absolute units (175x-291x)** — more than half
the character's own height — which is the same *class* of artifact already
documented at §9.14/§9.53.1 (a near-zero rest edge across a bone boundary),
a *different instance* of it, at a scale nothing before could have
triggered.

**A secondary hypothesis (bones 46-49, camera/camtarget/camfov/camdof — real
named bones per `spec-rig-format.md` §5/§8.1, driven by a real scripted
camera path in this "entrance/extraction shot" clip) was tested directly
and found insufficient alone**: rendering with those bones frozen (a new
`--exclude-camera-bones` diagnostic flag on `sr3_viewer animpose`) still
produces a severely fragmented image. **I re-ran this render myself**
(`sr3_viewer animpose ... --exclude-camera-bones`) and confirmed it
independently — the large sail-shaped spike persists with camera bones
excluded, exactly as reported. Camera bones inflate the bounding box
further but are not the dominant driver.

**A genuine, separate build-system gap was found and fixed along the
way**: `sr3anim`'s CMake target was missing `src/payload.cpp`/`sample.cpp`,
`sr3rig`'s was missing `src/animated_pose.cpp`, and `sr3_viewer` was never
linked against `sr3anim` at all — meaning a real `cmake --build` would
never have built stage 2's `animpose` command since it was added; it only
ever existed via ad-hoc `cl.exe` invocations. Fixed additively, confirmed
present in `CMakeLists.txt` directly by me (lines 150-156, 289-295,
369-374).

**What this means for stage 2's status: the pipeline is CONFIRMED correct.
The visual result is dominated by a real, pre-existing mesh/rig property,
not a defect in the code.** Whether that property is specific to `brad`
or general across characters was left untested here — answered, and
broadened, in §9.56.2.

**Tier: [CONFIRMED]** — the skinning/sampling pipeline, for the general
multi-bone case, via a new permanent regression suite. **[CONFIRMED, real]**
— the fragmentation's cause is a mesh-topology property, not a pipeline
bug, verified by two independent falsification attempts (camera-bone
exclusion, re-rendered and inspected by me) rather than accepted as the
first plausible story. **[OPEN, broadened by §9.56.2]** — how general the
property is, and how the original engine handles this class of seam.

#### 9.56.2 Broadened: NOT brad-specific — a general property of this game's shared humanoid rig/mesh convention, severity scales with character size

**Correction to §9.56.1's framing, checked directly rather than assumed:**
a follow-up agent tested whether a different mesh, a calmer non-cinematic
clip, or both would render cleanly. **Neither did, on any combination
tried.** I looked at the actual PNGs myself before accepting this.

* **`angel`** (a distinct, independently-modeled mesh, confirmed genuinely
  T-pose-matched to its own rig) animated with `pml1_um_walk.anim_pc` (an
  ordinary walk cycle, not brad's cinematic "shot" clip) — **still
  fragments severely.** I viewed `angel_walk_t2_frac0.66.png` directly: legs
  and lower torso stay plausible, the upper body/arm/head region explodes
  into large sail shapes, the same failure shape as brad's original render.
  This rules out "it was brad's specific mesh" and "it was that specific
  cinematic clip" as the explanation simultaneously.
* **`brute_flamethrower`** — same base skeleton topology as brad/reggies/
  angel (bones 0-45 numerically identical rest positions across all four,
  confirmed via `dump_rig_bones`) but scaled ~1.8x — fragments **much less
  severely** (I viewed `brute_walk_t2_frac0.66.png`: a recognizable running
  stride, legs and torso intact) **but not cleanly**: one persistent,
  prominent fin near the shoulder/hand region survives in every sampled
  frame, confirmed visually, not just by a bone-length number.
* A cheap bind-pose-only pre-check (new: `tools/validation/
  precheck_topology.cpp` — bone-hop distance from the rig's parent tree,
  grid-binned vertex proximity, flags close pairs whose primary bones are
  far apart in the hierarchy or on opposite left/right sides) found the
  same class of near-zero-clearance cross-limb pairs on **every** mesh
  tested (`brad`, `reggies`, `angel`, `joleen`, `nightblade`,
  `brute_flamethrower`) — thousands of flagged pairs each, and
  `brute_flamethrower`'s much lower count (2,873 vs 14,000-34,000 for the
  standard-scale meshes) lines up exactly with its larger scale and its
  much cleaner (though still not clean) render. **Two distinct mechanisms
  identified**, both present on every mesh checked: true opposite-hand
  proximity (`l-finger1`/`r-hand`-class, ~10 hops apart in the hierarchy),
  and a smaller, closer one at weapon-attachment marker bones sitting
  millimeters from their own sibling fingers (`l-handprop` near
  `l-finger4`/`l-thumb1`, 2-3 hops apart — the same *class* already named
  in §9.53.1, just far more visually prominent under real full-body motion
  than in that earlier single-joint isolation test).
* **Side finding — RETRACTED IN FULL, SEE §9.58 (2026-09-13, later the same
  day). Do not act on the paragraph below; it is kept verbatim as the record
  of what was claimed.** Both of its halves were measured directly and are
  wrong: the shipped humanoid rig is an **A-pose** (33.58° arm droop,
  identical on `brad`/`angel`/`joleen`/`reggies`), not a T-pose, and
  `reggies.ccmesh_pc`'s stored vertices sit in that same A-pose — its
  outermost arm vertex matches `brad`'s and `joleen`'s to 4.1 mm in X and
  7.2 mm in Y, and its mesh↔rig droop gap (4.19°) is at the population
  median over 275 mesh/rig pairs (3.95°). §9.58 also corrects "bones 0-45
  numerically identical" below to bones **1-44**: `reggies`'s bone 0 `root`
  and bone 45 `spinebend` genuinely do differ from everyone else's — the one
  real, isolated `reggies` anomaly, and it is in the rig, not the mesh.
  Original text follows.
* **Side finding, independently confirmed visually (2026-09-13, not just
  from bounding-box numbers)**: rendered `reggies.ccmesh_pc` plain (`sr3_viewer
  mesh`, no skinning applied — this is the mesh's own stored vertex
  positions) and it is unambiguously in an arms-down, relaxed stance —
  bounds 1.386 (X) × 1.644 (Y), width visibly less than height, nothing
  like brad/angel's arms-extended T-pose. `reggies.rig_pc`'s own rest
  positions are the same T-pose as brad's (bones 0-45 numerically
  identical across brad/reggies/angel, per §9.56.2's earlier check). **So
  the mesh's own rest vertices are NOT at the rig's bind pose** — meaning
  even the "identity rotation = bind pose = unchanged mesh" assumption
  this whole pipeline relies on does not hold for this specific character,
  independent of the near-degenerate-seam question. **Checked whether this
  is systemic (2026-09-13): rendered `joleen.ccmesh_pc` and
  `sophia.ccmesh_pc` the same way — both are ordinary T-poses, arms
  extended outward, no anomaly.** So this is an **isolated property of
  `reggies`'s specific asset data**, not a mesh/rig pose-convention split
  across a family of characters. Mechanism still genuinely unknown: wrong
  rig pairing, a missing pose-correction step specific to this one asset,
  or something else — narrowed to "not systemic," not explained further.

**Corrected conclusion:** this is **not** a `brad`-specific defect. It is
a property of this game's **shared standard-scale humanoid rig/mesh
convention** — near-degenerate rest-pose clearances between the two hands,
and between weapon-attachment marker bones and their own sibling fingers —
whose visual severity scales inversely with character size, and which no
test before this session's animation work had ever been positioned to
find (every earlier confirmatory test moved at most one bone/subtree at a
time). **This is a more significant, more general finding than §9.56.1's
original framing, and is being flagged as such rather than treated as
closed.** No clean full-skeleton render has yet been produced on any
mesh/clip combination tried.

**Tier: [CONFIRMED — empirical, cross-mesh]** that the fragmentation
generalizes and scales inversely with character size. **[OPEN]** — whether
ANY mesh/clip pairing in this game renders cleanly under this pipeline;
how the shipped, presumably-polished game avoids this being visible in
normal play (extra smoothing, dual-quaternion skinning, a weight-painting
convention this project hasn't identified, or something else entirely) —
recorded as the honest open question, not guessed at.

#### 9.56.3 The "does the game ever pose characters this way" question, answered directly from file data: yes, routinely — this is not a rare edge case

Team A's disassembly investigation into how the runtime avoids visible
seams was explicit going in that a legitimate answer might be "the shipped
game never poses characters into configurations that trigger this."
**Measured directly from real shipped data whether that's true, rather
than waiting on disassembly to answer it, and it is NOT true — real clips
push these joints through large rotations routinely, not as a rare edge
case.**

New harness, `tools/validation/probe_seam_rotation_range.cpp`: resolved
the risky bones by name on `brad.rig_pc` (`r-hand` [22], `l-finger1` [23],
`l-handprop` [27], `l-finger4` [26], `l-thumb1` [28]), then scanned every
`.anim_pc` clip in `preload_anim.vpp_pc` (4,209 clips, 4,072 with a
complete walk) for tracks mapped to those bones, and computed each
track's own maximum rotation angle (degrees, from the reconstructed
quaternion's `w` component, same `2*acos(|w|)*180/pi` formula this project
already uses for root-motion angle) reached anywhere in the clip:

| bone | clips touching it | min | median | p90 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `r-hand` [22] | 3,496 | 0.1° | **58.6°** | 101.9° | 179.1° |
| `l-finger1` [23] | 3,345 | 0.4° | **33.6°** | 84.6° | 163.2° |
| `l-handprop` [27] | 2,964 | 0.2° | **108.1°** | 176.8° | 180.0° |
| `l-finger4` [26] | 3,377 | 0.0° | **42.4°** | 81.7° | 177.3° |
| `l-thumb1` [28] | 3,411 | 0.0° | **31.8°** | 55.0° | 179.4° |

**Nearly every clip in the shipped population touches these bones
(2,964-3,496 of 4,072 walkable clips), and the median rotation reached is
already 32-108 degrees — with the 90th percentile at 55-177 degrees and
maxima approaching a full 180° reversal for every one of the five risky
bones.** These are not small, incidental wiggles; they are large,
routine joint rotations, exactly the magnitude of motion the earlier
175x-291x stretch measurements (§9.56.1/§9.56.2) were driven by. The test
clips tried so far (`auto_entrl_extct_shot`, `pml1_um_walk`,
`gangf_rpg_run_stand`) were not unusually extreme selections — if
anything, the population as a whole reaches equally large or larger
rotations as a matter of routine.

**Said plainly, not softened: the honest answer to "does the game ever
pose characters this way" is yes, constantly.** This makes Team A's
disassembly trail (does the runtime use a different skinning technique,
or a post-skin correction this project hasn't identified) more important,
not less — the "never triggered in practice" explanation is now
directly contradicted by file-side measurement, on the population that
matters (real shipped clips, not a synthetic worst case). Whatever the
shipped game does to avoid a visibly torn character during ordinary
gameplay, it has to actually handle this range of motion, not merely
avoid it.

**Caveat, stated precisely rather than glossed over**: this measures each
track's own isolated rotation angle relative to its bind-pose orientation,
not the full composed multi-bone transform or the resulting vertex-pair
stretch directly — a large isolated angle is consistent with, not
mathematically identical to, the stretch already measured, since the
final result also depends on ancestor bones' rotations and any
translation deltas. Given the already-confirmed correctness of the full
pipeline (§9.56.1) and how directly these angles line up with the
already-observed failure magnitude, this is treated as strong corroborating
evidence, not treated as itself a second independent proof of the exact
stretch ratio at every sampled moment.

**Tier: [CONFIRMED — empirical]** that real shipped clips routinely reach
rotation magnitudes at the risky bones consistent with triggering the
observed seam stretch. **[OPEN]**, more urgently than before: what the
shipped engine actually does about it.

#### 9.56.4 Team A's skinning trace closed: GPU vertex shader confirmed, every alternative technique refuted, genuinely no explanation found — plus a decisive follow-up measurement on this side

**Team A's disassembly trace reached its natural end, not a dead end from
giving up.** The skinning consumer is confirmed: a specific function
builds the D3D9 vertex declaration and calls `CreateVertexDeclaration`
directly, verified three independent ways (a usage-index table's
structure, 17/17 correct D3D9 byte sizes on a second table, a byte-exact
terminator constant). The actual blend arithmetic lives inside GPU shader
bytecode in a mode-a container under the entry-0-only disassembly
boundary this project has hit before with shaders — a complete answer to
*where* the skinning happens, at the point where *what it does* stops
being reachable by static disassembly.

**Three alternative seam-avoidance techniques were tested against real
evidence and refuted, not merely left unconfirmed:**
* Dual-quaternion skinning — ruled out by the palette element's byte size
  and fallback shape.
* A CPU smoothing pass — ruled out because the CPU never holds a skinned
  vertex position at all (the GPU consumes raw bind-space data + weights
  directly).
* A hard minimum-weight-floor convention (i.e. "small minority weights
  across a limb boundary get dropped/floored, so a seam like this can't
  actually manifest") — ruled out empirically: 1,683 of 11,343 vertices
  (14.8%) carry real minority weights across limb boundaries.
* Their own strongest working hypothesis going in (a flags-bit-1 remap)
  was killed three separate ways, including a shuffled control beating
  its own hit rate — they deliberately tried to break their best idea
  rather than let it stand unconfirmed, the same discipline this project
  has leaned on all session.

**Bottom line, stated as plainly as they gave it: no seam-avoidance
mechanism was found. They did not reach for "the game never triggers
this" as a soft landing** — they cited this project's own §9.56.3
rotation-population figures directly and marked that explanation
unavailable. **This is genuinely open on both sides**, not resolved by
either team.

**Meta-finding, their own record, checked against mine**: a previously-cited
fact on their side ("zero D3D9 vertex-shader-related COM vtable calls")
was itself wrong — a disassembly scan blind spot that missed the call
form the compiler actually emits. They corrected it in place. **Checked
whether this project ever cited or relied on that same claim anywhere in
`HANDOFF.md` — it does not appear (grepped directly, zero matches)**,
so nothing here needed correcting, but the check was made rather than
assumed clean.

**Team A's proposed decisive next step, run here and independently
confirmed rather than left as a suggestion**: the published 175x-291x
stretch RATIOS are computed against 4-19mm bind-pose gaps — a tiny
denominator inflates any ratio, real defect or not. The real question is
whether the ABSOLUTE displacement is itself anomalous. New harness,
`tools/validation/probe_seam_absolute_displacement.cpp`, reusing the
CONFIRMED pose pipeline exactly as `sr3_viewer animpose` calls it (no
second implementation of the math) — for every real mesh edge (from the
actual triangle list, not hand-picked pairs), classified same-limb vs
cross-limb by rig-hierarchy hop distance (same convention as
`precheck_topology.cpp`), reports **absolute** `|posed - rest|` edge
length in metres:

| | n | median | p90 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| cross-limb, near-degenerate (<5cm rest), frac=1.0 (worst frame) | 536 | **0.184 m** | 0.791 m | 3.109 m |
| ordinary same-limb (2-30cm rest), frac=1.0 | 4,443 | **0.008 m** | 0.126 m | 2.939 m |
| cross-limb, near-degenerate, frac=0.5 (mid-clip, cross-check) | 536 | **0.154 m** | 0.736 m | 2.921 m |
| ordinary same-limb, frac=0.5 | 4,443 | **0.006 m** | 0.130 m | 2.899 m |

**The maxima-convergence (~2.9-3.1 m in BOTH groups) was flagged as a
second, unexplained mystery rather than folded into the main conclusion —
and it is now closed, cleanly, 2026-09-13, following Team A's own
suggested test.** Their hypothesis: meaningful whole-body root motion
between sampled frames would inherit into every vertex's world position,
same-limb included, producing exactly this signature. **The literal
hypothesis was wrong — the skeletal root itself barely moves (0.096-0.315
m across the frames checked) — but the underlying mechanism was right, one
level over:** this clip drives the non-skeletal "camera-shot" helper bones
(`camera`, `camtarget` — real named bones in the same array, confirmed
§9.56.1/spec-rig-format.md §5/§8.1) through **enormous** scripted motion
(camera: 5.75 m, camtarget: 3.99 m bind-to-posed displacement), and while
those bones were already excluded from *dominant-bone classification* in
this measurement, they were **not** excluded from the actual skinning
computation — so any vertex carrying even a small **minority** blend-weight
lane on `camera`/`camtarget` (invisible to a dominant-bone-only check) got
dragged by meters regardless of what its real, legitimate dominant bone
was. Corrected by zeroing those four bones' rotation/translation in the
pose computation itself, not just the classification step, and re-measured:

| | n | median | p90 | max |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| cross-limb, near-degenerate, frac=1.0, camera-bones excluded from computation | 536 | 0.170 m | 0.753 m | **1.208 m** |
| ordinary same-limb, frac=1.0, camera-bones excluded from computation | 4,443 | 0.008 m | 0.106 m | **0.513 m** |
| cross-limb, near-degenerate, frac=0.5, camera-bones excluded from computation | 536 | 0.157 m | 0.720 m | **1.077 m** |
| ordinary same-limb, frac=0.5, camera-bones excluded from computation | 4,443 | 0.006 m | 0.113 m | **0.554 m** |

**The mystery collapses exactly as the test predicted — same-limb max
drops from ~2.9 m to ~0.5 m (an ~82% reduction), and the cross-limb group
is now cleanly elevated at every single percentile, including the max**
(1.08-1.21 m vs 0.51-0.55 m, roughly 2.2-2.4x — no longer converging).
Confirmed the worst same-limb pair BEFORE the fix was two vertices whose
*dominant* bone was the same ordinary body bone (`spinebend`/`spinebend`)
— exactly the shape a minority-weight leak from an unrelated, wildly-moving
bone produces: a pair that looks perfectly ordinary by dominant-bone
classification, dragged apart by a lane the classification never saw.

**Net, now fully clean: the cross-limb seam is real, substantially
elevated motion at every level of the distribution — median, 90th
percentile, and maximum — compared to ordinary same-limb joint
articulation under the identical real clip.** Not a ratio artifact (the
median/p90 gap already ruled that out); not contaminated by an unrelated
confound at the tail either, now that the actual mechanism behind that
confound (minority-weight leakage from the scripted camera-rig bones, a
real and now-understood phenomenon in its own right, distinct from the
seam question) has been found and removed.

**Tier: [CONFIRMED — empirical]** that cross-limb absolute displacement is
genuinely, substantially elevated versus ordinary same-limb displacement
under real clips, at every percentile, not just the median/p90 — the
maxima-convergence confound is identified, explained, and removed, not
merely set aside. **[CONFIRMED — empirical]** as a related side-finding:
per-vertex minority blend weight on the camera-rig helper bones
contaminates ordinary body-vertex motion measurements unless those bones
are excluded from the pose computation itself, not just from dominant-bone
classification — worth remembering for any future measurement on this
mesh/clip. **[OPEN]**: what the shipped engine actually does about the
(now unconfounded) cross-limb case, since no technique has been found on
either side to explain it away.

### 9.57 First audio reader — `sr3audio`, the `_media.bnk_pc` (VWSBPC) wrapper directory, genuinely new format territory

Built after checking both of Team A's newly-closed specs directly rather
than taking "ready" on faith (`spec-audio-format.md`, `spec-lua-bindings.md`)
and picking the one that's actually a file format with bytes to parse.
Reads the wrapper's **directory structure only** — magic, header fields, a
16-byte-record chain-walk — never Wwise/Vorbis audio internals, which stay
explicitly out of scope exactly as the spec itself draws that line.

**What exists**: `include/sr3audio/media_bank.h`/`media_bank.cpp`
(`MediaBank`: header parse + `walk(totalEntrySize)`, the caller-supplied
oracle from the outer `.vpp_pc` container, per the confirmed chain rule
`offset[i+1] = offset[i] + round_up(size[i] + extra[i], 0x800)`);
`include/sr3audio/wwise_bank_id.h`/`.cpp` (reads only the public Wwise
`BKHD` header's first 16 bytes, for the SoundBankID cross-reference — no
Wwise chunk internals touched). `tests/synthetic_media_bank_test.cpp` (19
tests, **19th synthetic suite, `sr3audio_tests`**, mutation-tested against
three deliberate bugs — dropping `extra` from the chain, removing the
zero-advance guard, hardcoding the anchor to `0x800` — all three caught;
one test case had to be rebuilt because its first version didn't actually
discriminate the bug it was meant to catch, caught and fixed before
trusting the suite). `tools/validation/validate_media_bank.cpp` +
`diag_media_bank_first_offset.cpp` (the diagnostic that separated the
anchor question from the chain-walk question — see below).

**Independently re-verified by me, not taken on the report** — reran
`validate_media_bank.exe` myself against all four real archives
(`sounds.vpp_pc`, `sounds_common.vpp_pc`, `voices.vpp_pc`,
`cutscene_sounds.vpp_pc`) and reproduced every headline number exactly:
**536/536 `_media.bnk_pc` entries walked cleanly, 89,631 total records
(122/53/275/86 per archive, matching the spec's own breakdown exactly),
260/260 in-archive cross-reference matches plus the 1/1 cross-archive
`interface` pair, 19/19 synthetic suites green** (also confirmed by direct
rerun).

**Two real corrections to Team A's own just-closed spec, both found by
this reader's independent replay, both worth sending back to them —
the spec's CORE structure is untouched, both are secondary
characterizations:**

1. **"Record 0's offset is always `0x800`" (§4.2) is false — true on
   278/536 files, not "always."** The rule that holds 536/536: `offset[0]
   = round_up(0x20 + recordCount*16, 0x800)` — the first block boundary
   after the header **and** the record table, not a fixed constant; `0x800`
   is just the common case where the table happens to fit in one block. A
   strict generalization, not a rival claim — it predicts `0x800` correctly
   on all 278 files where that's actually true. **Caught the same way this
   project's own §3 warns about**: the reader's first draft folded the
   anchor assumption and the chain-walk into one predicate (seed the
   cursor at `0x800`, then check the chain), so 258 files failed at record
   0 before the chain rule ever got tested — a 278/536 result that looked
   like a refutation of the CHAIN rule when it was actually only testing
   the ANCHOR assumption. Separated the two questions with a dedicated
   diagnostic before concluding anything; `walk()` now reads `offset[0]`
   from the table itself rather than assuming it.
2. **§4.2/§4.3's `extra`-field frequency claim is inverted.** Spec:
   "zero in the overwhelming majority of records," naive model (drops
   `extra`) clean on 530/536, broken on exactly 6. **Measured: 82,261 of
   89,631 records (91.8%) have `extra != 0`, across 281 of 536 files; the
   naive model is clean on only 255/536, wrong on 281** — independently
   reproduced by me, digit for digit, on my own rerun. Internally
   consistent (255+281=536, and the naive-clean set is exactly the
   no-`extra` set) — this isn't noise, the earlier pass and this one are
   reading the same field, just characterizing its frequency oppositely.
   **What the spec got right and this reproduces exactly**: `extra` is a
   real, additive, load-bearing field, not padding — the underlying
   §4.3 finding stands; only the "530/6" frequency split is wrong. Field
   assignment (`+0x04`=`extra`, `+0x08`=`size`) independently confirmed via
   value-distribution shape (extra: 8 distinct values, all block-aligned;
   size: 27,189 distinct values, high-cardinality, almost never
   block-aligned) rather than assumed from the spec's own labeling.

Both corrections are recorded in the reader's own header comments with
the evidence inline, not silently absorbed — worth relaying to Team A so
`spec-audio-format.md` can be corrected the same way this project's own
specs get corrected when a replay disagrees with the original pass.

**Tier: [CONFIRMED — empirical]** for the wrapper's directory structure,
independently re-verified end to end. **[OPEN]**: everything the spec
itself leaves open (`+0x14`, `+0x1C`, the record `tag` field, the `+0x08`
constant's role) — surfaced raw, not guessed at.

### 9.58 §9.56.2's `reggies` "mesh is not at the rig's bind pose" side-finding is RETRACTED — both halves of it were wrong, and the shipped humanoid rig is an A-pose, not a T-pose

**What §9.56.2 claimed** (its "side finding", written 2026-09-13): that
`reggies.ccmesh_pc`'s own stored, unskinned vertices are "unambiguously in
an arms-down, relaxed stance — bounds 1.386 (X) × 1.644 (Y), width visibly
less than height, nothing like brad/angel's arms-extended T-pose", while
`reggies.rig_pc`'s own rest positions are "the same T-pose as brad's" —
and that this was isolated to `reggies`, because `joleen` and `sophia`
rendered as "ordinary T-poses" the same way.

**Both halves are wrong, and the third clause — "isolated to reggies" —
is true only in a sense that has nothing to do with pose.** Measured
directly, with a new tool, plus a population sweep and a re-look at the
very PNGs the original claim was written from.

New tool: **`tools/validation/probe_bindpose_residual.cpp`** (built to
`build_verify/probe_bindpose_residual.exe`; it needs the anim objects, so
the stock `build_one.bat` object list is not enough — the working `cl.exe`
line adds `animated_pose.obj animation.obj payload.obj sample.obj`). Two
modes: a detailed single mesh/rig pair, and `--sweep <archive>` over every
`<stem>.ccmesh_pc` / `.gcmesh_pc` / `.rig_pc` triple in an archive.

#### The measurement that settles it: arm droop, computed WITHOUT blend indices

`spec-rig-format.md`'s rig space is Y-negative-up; `sr3rig::rigToMeshSpace`
(`(x, −y, −z)`, §9.13, CONFIRMED) flips it. In mesh space,
`reggies.rig_pc` puts

```
l-clavicle rest = ( 0.0522, 1.4273, −0.0757)
l-hand     rest = ( 0.5915, 1.0693,  0.0099)
```

— the hand sits **0.3580 BELOW the clavicle** while extending 0.5393
outward, i.e. **33.58° below horizontal. That is an A-pose. The rig is not
a T-pose, and never was.** `brad`/`angel`/`joleen`'s rigs are numerically
identical over bones 11–44, so they are the same A-pose too.

The mesh half was measured with a statistic that touches no blend index at
all: take the extreme +X vertex (the outermost point of the left arm —
whatever the stored geometry says that is), and measure the angle from the
rig's own `l-clavicle` rest position down to it.

| mesh | extreme +X vertex | droop, mesh | droop, rig | diff |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `reggies` | (0.6932, 0.9307, 0.1222) | **37.76°** | 33.58° | 4.19° |
| `brad`    | (0.6926, 0.9379, 0.1226) | **37.38°** | 33.58° | 3.81° |
| `joleen`  | (0.6891, 0.9341, 0.1182) | **37.75°** | 33.58° | 4.18° |

Three meshes, a **4.1 mm spread in X and 7.2 mm in Y** on the outermost
arm vertex. `reggies` is not in a different stance from `brad` and
`joleen`; it is in the *same* stance, to within a centimetre.

#### The original inference could never have separated the cases

"Bounds 1.386 × 1.644, width visibly less than height" is a true
measurement — this tool reproduces it exactly: all-vertex extent
**1.3864 × 1.6441 × 0.5105**, which is what `sr3_viewer mesh` prints as
`1.386 x 1.644 x 0.510` (draw-group 0 alone is 1.3864 × 1.6437 × 0.5027,
so the two are not identical and the viewer's line is the all-vertex one).
But **`brad`'s own bounds are 1.3852 × 1.7348 and `joleen`'s
1.3781 × 1.8264** — width less than height in both, and both accepted as
normal in the same paragraph.
`reggies` is in fact the **widest** of the three in X. The X extents agree
to within 0.6%; only the heights differ, because `reggies` is a short,
bulky, **headless** body mesh (its top vertex is at y = 1.6248, the
collar) while `brad` and `joleen` carry a head stub. §3's own rule applies
exactly: *a test that gives the same answer for the accepted and the
rejected case has not decided anything.*

#### Population sweep: there is no T-pose anywhere in `characters.vpp_pc`

`probe_bindpose_residual --sweep`, **275 mesh/rig pairs**:

* `droopRig` takes only **7 distinct values**: 33.58° (127 pairs), 35.02°
  (73), 34.99° (61), 21.47° (9 — the large `brute`-scale rig), 31.60° (2),
  31.21° (2), 80.28° (1 — `tiger`, an animal). **Not one rig is a T-pose.**
* `droopMesh`: **273 / 275 lie between 23.01° and 49.88°**; 262 of them
  inside [30°, 45°]. The two exceptions are `professorgenki` at −26.46°
  (arms *above* horizontal) and `tiger` at 73.71° — and `tiger`'s own rig
  is at 80.28°, so it agrees with its rig as well as anyone. **Not one
  mesh is a T-pose.**
* `|droopMesh − droopRig|`: mean **3.952°**, median **3.95°**. `reggies`
  scores **4.19°** — 187 pairs closer, 82 further, 6 tied. Dead centre of
  the population. The genuine outliers are `professorgenki` (60.03°),
  `shaderballz` (16.31°), `el_jose` (6.71°), `tiger` (6.56°).

The systematic ~4° gap between mesh and rig is not a per-asset defect: the
extreme +X vertex is a *fingertip*, past and slightly below the `l-hand`
joint the rig angle is measured to, on every character.

#### The visual claim, re-checked against the original images

I re-rendered `reggies`, `brad`, `joleen` and `sophia` with identical
settings (`sr3_viewer mesh ... --mode checker --size 720 900`) and looked
at all four. **All four are the same A-pose**, arms angled down ~37°. I
also opened the previous session's own scratchpad PNGs —
`reggies_check.png` and `joleen_check.png`, the images §9.56.2's side
finding was written from — and they show the same stance as each other.
The images do not support the claim drawn from them. What makes `reggies`
*look* different at a glance is that it is short, bulky and headless, not
that its arms are lower.

#### Four hypotheses tested, with exact results

**1. File-pairing mistake / more than one `reggies` candidate — RULED OUT.**
A string sweep of all 38 `.vpp_pc` archives finds `reggies*` in
`characters.vpp_pc` only. `vpp_dump` confirms exactly one
`reggies.ccmesh_pc` and one `reggies.rig_pc`, both inside
`saints_male_reggies.str2_pc`. The new tool prints its own provenance:
`reggies.ccmesh_pc` entry #0 (5,064 B), `reggies.gcmesh_pc` entry #1
(235,044 B), `reggies.rig_pc` entry #4 (7,312 B) — **same nested
container**. The bounds figure and the rig figures in this section come
from one process reading all three, so the "did two tools read different
files" question (§9.56.2 never asked it) is answered: they could not have.
*One relevant find anyway:* a near-duplicate sibling asset exists under a
**different stem** — `reggie` (singular), in `npc_luchador_reggie.str2_pc`
— 6,364 vertices against `reggies`'s 6,360, identical extents
(1.3864 × 1.6441), identical droop (37.76°), identical rig anomaly (below).
Same body, two characters. No pairing hazard (the stems differ), but worth
knowing it exists.

**2. The mesh is baked at some idle/stand clip's frame 0 — REFUTED.**
First, **no `.anim_pc` in any archive has `reggies` or `reggie` in its
name** (0 matches across all 38). Second, posing `reggies.rig_pc` with
frame 0 of three clean generic idle clips — via `sampleClipAtTime` +
`computeAnimatedSkinningMatrices` + `conjugateToMeshSpace`, the confirmed
§9.53/§9.56 path, unmodified — makes agreement **worse in every case**:

| clip (t = 0) | mesh↔bone residual, bind | posed | arm group, bind | posed | posed bone X extent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `gang_rfl_sd_idle_1` | 0.4845 | **0.5225** | 0.5362 | **0.6372** | 0.6487 |
| `cml1_bs_sd_idle_c`  | 0.4845 | **0.5188** | 0.5362 | **0.6301** | 0.8084 |
| `life_bartender_idle`| 0.4845 | **0.5249** | 0.5362 | **0.6283** | 0.8302 |

A real idle clip's frame 0 pulls the arms **in against the body** (posed
bone X extent 0.65–0.83 against the mesh's own 1.3864). That is what an
actual arms-down pose looks like in these numbers — and the stored mesh is
nothing like it. The residual is *minimised at bind pose*, which is the
positive form of the same statement. (The residual statistic here is the
primary-lane cluster metric — see the control note below; it is used only
to compare two bone-position sets under one unchanged metric, never as
evidence on its own.)

**3. An undecoded sub-header or extra reference in `reggies.ccmesh_pc` —
RULED OUT (structurally).** First 0x60 bytes of `reggies` / `joleen` /
`sophia` / `brad`, same shape in all four: magic `54 38 04 00`
(0x00043854) at +0x00; +0x04 a name-block length (0xBA / 0xBC / 0xAA /
0x9F); +0x0C a texture count (9 / 9 / 8 / 8); +0x10..+0x1F all zero;
texture-name strings from +0x20. Same single vertex channel (layout 3,
stride 32, skinned), same 4 draw groups. **No field present in `reggies`
and absent elsewhere, and none differing other than by the per-asset
lengths/counts the spec already assigns meaning to.**

**4. Bind-pose assumption end to end — HOLDS.** Covered by 1 above for
provenance. Additionally, §9.13's weighted-centroid rank test recomputed
here from scratch: the nearest bone to a bone's own weighted centroid is
that bone in **7/53 (13.21%) for `reggies`**, 8/54 (14.81%) for `brad`,
7/56 (12.50%) for `joleen`; mean own-bone residual 0.5706 / 0.5833 /
0.5988. `reggies` has the **lowest** residual of the three. Those figures
reproduce §9.13's published 14.9% / 0.6831, so the instrument is behaving
as it did then, and `reggies` is unremarkable on it.

#### A control that mattered, and a metric that did not survive it

The first version of this probe scored each bone by the centroid of the
vertices whose *primary* blend lane is that bone. On `reggies` it produced
alarming rows — `r-clavicle`'s cluster at ankle height, `r-toe0`'s at the
crown. **Run against `brad` and `joleen` it produced the same rows**, so
it was measuring a known, already-documented property (§9.13's 14.9% rank
rate: joints sit at the *end* of a limb, and helper/marker bones are
placed deliberately off-body) and not anything about `reggies`. §3's rule
— *a property shared by every failure is not a cause until you check the
successes lack it* — is what stopped that from becoming this section's
headline. Everything load-bearing above is either mapping-free (extreme
vertex, bounding box, rig rest positions) or explicitly cross-character.

#### One genuinely isolated, genuinely new finding — and a correction to §9.56.2's other claim

§9.56.2 states "bones 0–45 numerically identical across brad/reggies/angel,
confirmed via `dump_rig_bones`". **Re-run `dump_rig_bones` on the same
files and that is false at two bones**, and the exception is real:

| bone | `brad` / `angel` / `joleen` | `reggies` / `reggie` |
|---|---|---|
| `[0] root` | (−0.0000, −0.9269, −0.0000) | **(0.0423, −0.7892, 0.0068)** |
| `[45] spinebend` | (−0.0000, −0.9269, −0.0000) | **(0.0349, −0.9269, 0.0000)** |

Bones 1–44 and 46–49 *are* identical; 50/51 (`l-eye`/`r-eye`) differ
per-character on everyone, including between `brad` and `joleen`. Over the
sweep's 275 pairs: in **273 of 275, `root` and `spinebend` hold exactly the
same value**. The only two where they differ are `reggies` and `reggie`,
and both of those values are unique in the population (each appears
2 / 275). So there IS something isolated to this asset — **it is in the
rig, not the mesh, and it is not a pose**.

**Consequence, stated honestly:** *none at bind pose.* With identity
rotations `World_i = T(rest_i)` exactly, so every skin matrix is identity
whatever `root` holds — which is why this never showed up. Under animation
it is not inert: `root` is the parent of `pelvis`, `spine` and
`spinebend`, so its displaced rest position changes the pivot of the root
bone's own rotation and the local offsets `d_i` of those three children.
Whether that is an authoring artefact, a deliberate ground offset for this
body, or something the runtime reads, is **not** answerable from file
bytes here.

#### Tiers

* **[CONFIRMED — empirical]** The shipped humanoid rig is an **A-pose**
  (33.58° / 35.02° / 34.99° arm droop over 261 of 275 pairs), not a T-pose.
  Every shipped character mesh in `characters.vpp_pc` is stored in that
  same A-pose (273/275 between 23.01° and 49.88°; the two outside it are
  `professorgenki`, arms up, and `tiger`, an animal whose own rig is at
  80.28°).
* **[CONFIRMED — empirical]** `reggies.ccmesh_pc` is **not** in an unusual
  stance: its outermost arm vertex matches `brad`'s and `joleen`'s to
  4.1 mm / 7.2 mm, and its mesh↔rig droop gap (4.19°) sits at the
  population median (3.95°). **§9.56.2's side finding is RETRACTED, not
  narrowed.**
* **[CONFIRMED — empirical]** `reggies.rig_pc` / `reggie.rig_pc` are the
  only 2 of 275 rigs whose `root` differs from `spinebend`; §9.56.2's
  "bones 0–45 numerically identical" is corrected to bones **1–44**.
* **[REFUTED]** "Some clip's frame 0 is baked into the mesh" — no
  `reggies`-named clip exists at all, and three real idle clips' frame 0
  each move the rig *away* from the stored geometry, by 0.034–0.040 mean
  residual and 0.092–0.101 on the arm group.
* **[RULED OUT]** wrong rig pairing; multiple archive candidates; an
  undecoded `reggies`-only sub-header.
* **[OPEN]** What the displaced `root` / `spinebend` on `reggies`/`reggie`
  means, and whether the runtime does anything with it. Also still open and
  *untouched by this section*: §9.56.1/§9.56.2's actual subject, the
  full-skeleton fragmentation — nothing here bears on it either way,
  because the near-degenerate cross-limb clearances it is about are a
  property of the A-pose these meshes are genuinely stored in.

#### The lesson worth carrying

**Two false halves reinforced each other into a confident finding because
neither was ever measured against a denominator.** "Mesh looks arms-down"
and "rig is a T-pose" were each read off a *single* artefact — one PNG and
one prose description of a rest pose — and each is refuted the moment the
same measurement is run on the neighbours that were being called normal
(`brad`'s bounds are the same shape; `brad`'s rig has the same 33.58°
droop). The third clause — "checked whether this is systemic: `joleen` and
`sophia` are ordinary T-poses" — *was* the right instinct, and it was run
on the right files; it failed because the comparison was made by eye
against a stance nobody had measured, so "ordinary T-pose" and "arms-down,
relaxed" got applied to two images of the same 37° A-pose. **An eyeball
comparison needs a number attached to the reference class, not just to the
suspect.** The suspect was measured (1.386 × 1.644); the reference class
never was.

#### Independent re-verification (dispatching session, same day)

Re-ran three of this section's own commands directly rather than trusting
the summary: `probe_bindpose_residual.exe` on `reggies`/`brad`/`joleen`
(BIND-POSE RESIDUAL + arm/leg-group lines), `dump_rig_bones.exe` on all
three (`root`/`spinebend` rows), and `--sweep` over `characters.vpp_pc`.
**Every figure quoted above reproduced exactly** — arm-group weighted
means 0.5362/0.3809/0.3532, leg-group 0.4171/0.9038/0.8940, droopMesh/
droopRig/diff 37.76/33.58/4.19 for both `reggies` and `reggie`, the
displaced `root`=(0.0423,-0.7892,0.0068)/`spinebend`=(0.0349,-0.9269,
0.0000) on `reggies` only, and `SWEEP: 275 mesh/rig pairs measured`.

**Worth recording honestly: my own first move was to look at the actual
PNGs myself, per this project's own standing practice, and my initial read
disagreed with the retraction.** `reggies_check.png` vs `joleen_check.png`/
`sophia_check.png`/the new `chk_brad.png` — measured directly on the
720px-wide canvas, `reggies`'s hand sits roughly 50px lateral from its
shoulder, `joleen`'s roughly 100px, a real difference in on-screen silhouette,
not a subtle one. That's not compatible with "the same 37° pose" at first
glance. **What resolved it**: the section's own *mapping-free* metric — the
raw extreme-X vertex's angle off the clavicle, found without touching a
blend index at all — puts `reggies` at 37.76°, `brad` at 37.38°, `joleen`
at 37.75°, a 0.4° spread. That is far more decisive than a pixel count on a
checkered render, because it doesn't depend on body proportions. The
likely reconciliation: `reggies` is a visibly bulkier build (its own extent
box is the widest of the three in X, per §9.58's own table), and a thicker
torso/upper-arm shrinks the apparent shoulder-to-hand gap on screen at the
*same* joint angle — an optical effect, not a measured one. Flagging this
rather than silently dropping it, since "I looked at the picture and it
looked different" was wrong here and is exactly the kind of claim this
project's own methodology (`HANDOFF.md` §3) says to verify, not defer to,
even when it's my own eyeball.

**One real residue not fully absorbed by the retraction**: the arm-group
weighted-centroid residual is genuinely elevated on `reggies` (0.5362)
versus `brad`/`joleen` (0.3809/0.3532) — about 40-50% higher, not
noise-level, even though it's nowhere near the scale a true different-pose
explanation would require. The leg-group residual runs the *other*
direction (`reggies` 0.4171, lowest of the three) which argues against
"reggies is uniformly further from its own bind pose." Left **[OPEN]**,
same tier as the section's own `root`/`spinebend` question, rather than
folded into either "fully matches" or "still anomalous" — this specific
number was not explained by anything tested here.

**Bottom line: the retraction stands.** Independently reproduced, not just
trusted, and the one objection my own initial visual check raised has a
concrete, checked-against-the-actual-metric answer rather than a hand-wave.

#### One more data point on the `root`/`spinebend` displacement, then deferred (2026-09-13)

Before letting the `root`/`spinebend` mechanism sit as OPEN, checked
whether the divergence is really isolated to those two bones by dumping
`reggies`' and `brad`'s **full** 68-bone lists side by side (the original
sweep only compared indices 0-45). **It isn't isolated to two bones —
`l-eye`[50]/`r-eye`[51] differ too**: `reggies` (0.032,-1.684,-0.021) /
(-0.032,-1.683,-0.021) vs `brad` (0.036,-1.706,0.012) / (-0.036,-1.706,
0.012). Every other bone, 1-44 and 46-49 and 52-67, is byte-identical.

**This doesn't explain the mechanism, and isn't being written up as if it
does — it's one more honest data point, not a resolution.** Eye-bone
position legitimately varies with head shape between characters, so its
divergence here is unremarkable on its own — but it doesn't make
`root`/`spinebend`'s divergence *less* notable either: those two are
structural/foundational bones expected to be authoring-convention-driven
rather than anatomical, which is consistent with (not proof of) the
already-established population figure that 273 of 275 rigs share one
exact `root`≈`spinebend` value while only `reggies`/`reggie` don't. No
new mechanism found by widening the check.

**Deferred here rather than pursued further, per the standing policy
recorded in §9.61**: the concrete leads available from file data alone
(file pairing, idle-clip frame-0 matching, header structural diff,
cross-tool provenance check, and now the full-bone-list widening above)
are exhausted without a mechanism, and the next step would mean
speculating rather than discovering. Left **[OPEN]**, explicitly
deferred, not further chased this session.

#### The headline finding: the chain is in THREE parts on disk, not one

`spec-physics-format.md` §4.1 describes all 8 sub-parsers as one shared
idiom — 16-align, read a count out of the fixed `0x140` header, record the
cursor as a resolved pointer, advance by `count × stride` — and the obvious
implementation is one cursor threaded straight through all 8 from the end
of the header. **That implementation reproduces zero real files.** It is
scored explicitly, beside the real walk, in the harness output:
`SPEC-LITERAL one-cursor walk : 0 / N land exactly`.

The reason is a step §4.2 names but does not size: `FUN_007499d0`'s tail
resolves one further reference through `thunk_FUN_00e3e590` into `+0xb8`.
In every real file, that single reference's payload is the whole material-
definition + render-Mesh-sub-block region — hundreds to thousands of bytes
— and it sits **between the chain's first two arrays and all of its
remaining ones**. So:

```
  HEAD    bodyStart .. headEnd     FUN_007499d0's two 8-byte-stride slot
                                   arrays, back to back, then the
                                   count(+0x48) embedded Mesh sub-blocks
  MIDDLE  headEnd  .. tailStart    the +0xb8 reference's payload — OPAQUE,
                                   no header field sizes it
  TAIL    tailStart .. EOF         FUN_00749b40 .. FUN_00749e80, ending
                                   EXACTLY at end-of-file
```

`LevelMesh` reports all three, and the middle as an explicitly-labelled
opaque range rather than something it pretends to walk.

#### The go/no-go test, and the numbers

This format has exactly one structural landmark a walk can be graded
against: **`FUN_00749e80`'s trailing nested group is the last structure in
the file**, so a correct walk of the tail ends exactly at EOF, to the byte.
"Parses without throwing" would have proved nothing here — the counts are
zero in the overwhelming majority of files, so a do-nothing walk sails
past.

**The population.** `.clmesh_pc` exists in exactly **five** shipped
archives and no others — measured, not assumed, by walking all 38
`.vpp_pc` files in `packfiles/pc/cache/` and recursing into every nested
`.str2_pc`:

| Archive | `.clmesh_pc` entries | magic `0x4fe66afa` + version 20 |
|---|---|---|
| `dlc1.vpp_pc` | 846 | 846 |
| `dlc2.vpp_pc` | 2,633 | 2,633 |
| `dlc3.vpp_pc` | 753 | 753 |
| `sr3_city_0.vpp_pc` | 41,555 | 41,555 |
| `sr3_city_1.vpp_pc` | 54,597 | 54,597 |
| **every other archive, incl. `sr3_city_missions`** | **0** | — |
| **total** | **100,384** | **100,384** |

These are *entries*, not distinct assets — the same prop appears in many
tile bundles — which is the right denominator for a structural test but
not for "how many props exist".

**GO/NO-GO — `validate_clmesh.exe` over the COMPLETE 100,384-entry
population. Every archive that carries the format, not a sample:**

```
                             dlc1-3   sr3_city_0   sr3_city_1      TOTAL
entries attempted             4,232       41,555       54,597    100,384
header parsed (magic+ver 20)  4,232       41,555       54,597    100,384
  header rejected                 0            0            0          0
tail lands EXACTLY on EOF     4,232       41,523       54,500    100,255  (99.8715%)
no start lands exactly            0           32           97        129  ( 0.1285%)
distinct layouts: one         4,047       39,602       52,279     95,928
                  two           179        1,885        2,216      4,280
                  three           6           36            5         47
CONTROL start + 4                 3           10            5         18  ( 0.0179%)
CONTROL count(+0x70) + 1          0            0            0          0
CONTROL count(+0xfc) = 4          3           10           27         40  ( 0.0399%)
CONTROL spec-prose order          0            0            0          0
SPEC-LITERAL one-cursor walk      0            0            0          0
```

**100,255 of 100,384, to the byte, with every control at or below 0.04%
and the obvious spec-literal implementation at exactly zero across the
entire format.** The controls are what make the 100,255 mean anything: a
walk that cannot be broken by shifting its start or by adding one element
to an array is not measuring the file. Two of the four never fire at all —
perturbing an array's element count or swapping the trailing group's two
arrays is *structurally* impossible to satisfy by accident — while a start
shift or a changed trailing-group count occasionally lands on another
valid layout in a file that has one.

The ambiguity figure is reported rather than hidden: **95,928 entries have
exactly one tail layout landing on EOF, 4,280 have two, 47 have three.**
For those 4,327 (4.3%) the reader keeps the earliest and **which is right
is not established** — see the open items below.

**The 129 that do not land are a coherent, named subpopulation, not
scatter.** 125 of the 129 have `count(+0x48) == count(+0x58) ==
count(+0x70)` of 2, 4 or 14 (multi-reference files); the remaining **4 have
`count == 1`, which by itself refutes "multi-reference is the cause"**.
Every one of the 129 has all other counts zero and the `+0x78` sentinel
set, and every one is an `~l1` LOD variant — overwhelmingly highway
signage: `hwy_sm_green~l1`, `hwy_sm_orange~l1`, `hwy_sm_blue~l1`,
`hwy_sm_yellow~l1`, `hwy_red_ls~l1`, `hwy_green_sa_r~l1`,
`terminal_sign_a~l1`, `terminal_sign_c~l1`, repeated across tiles. And
they are only a *subset* of their own shape: 65 `sr3_city_0` entries carry
`count(+0x48) == 2` and 46 of those land fine. So the shared property is
**not** the reference count. Left **[OPEN]** — this is a small, exactly
enumerated, easily re-found set of files, which is the good kind of open
item.

census below is the same population, measured independently with a

